WEEKLY CHAT. GIGANTIC CLEARANCE SALE. Mr. W. H. WORSLEY has pleasure in announcing the most Gigantic Clearance Sale ever held in Manchester. It is a patent faet that concerns which operate the largest in the purchasing powers. thereby acquire the means of selling to the public atvery muck reduced prices, as compared with their competitors. CONCEITED people are seldom jealous. SOME people have two great object in life—first, to become rich; and, second, to become richer. IT is a wise lover who can tell when his heart is broken. UTOPIA is a land whose inhabitants are all engaged to be married. IT is risky to praise a woman's husband to her, 'an 41 still more risky to disparage him. NEVER judge a man by the coat he wears. Eq may have borrowed it for the occasion. MAN wants a little more than he will ever get Jere below.

A MAN'S most difficult lessons in self-restraint comes when he finds that he has a stomach that is not what it once was. POET TO EDITOR: "I send you a poem, "Why Do I Live ? " Please answer." Editor: "Because you send your poem by post." MOTHER-IN-LAW "The doctor said I was all run down, and needed strychnine as a tonic. Now, I don't want to take too much. How big a dose do you recommend ? " Son-in-Law (hopefully) "I wouldn't take more than a gallon to begin with. GRANDMA: "you'll hardly think it possible, but I can remember the time when people couldn't see through a stone wall at all !" Little Grand- daughter: "Couldn't they, really? What strange stories you do tell, grandma !" PARSON (to youngster fishing on Sunday): "My boy, I'm' surprised to find you here." Youngster (innocently) : "Do you know some other place where they bite better?" MAMMA: "Why are you always beating your doll? That isn't nice." Elsa: " Yes, it is. I must beat the doll, because I don't want papa to tell me, as he always tells you, that I am spoiling my children." FR. HEALY'S wit seldom had a sting to it. On one occasion, however, some vulgar people asked how he got on so well in fine houses. "Faith," said Fr. Healy, "it must be from my mother I got it, for papa was as common as any of you." COULDN'T HELP HIMSELF.—Lawyer (investi- :gating client's story) : "Now, you must keep nothing from me." Client: "I haven't. I paid you every cent I had in the world for your retainer."

" DID Miss Howell's voice fill the hail?" "Well, it filled the lobby. Nearly everybody went out there when she sung." MR. UMBELL : "Even the worm will turn." 'His Wife (scornfully) : "You are scarcely a worm." Mr. Umbell (reminiscently) : " Possibly not now, my dear, but I can remember in past days hearing folks say something about an early bird when you got me." THE MODERN WAY.—Mrs. Henry Peck: "Men have degenerated sadly since the days of chivalry. Sir Walter Raleigh spread his cloak on the ground for the queen to walk on. Women do not walk on men's cloaks in these modern days." Mr. Henry Peck : "No ; they walk on men's necks now." "WHEN I was once in danger from a tiger," said an old East Indian veteran, " I tried sitting down and staring at him, as I had no weapon." "How did it work?" asked a bystander. "Per- fectly. The tiger didn't offer to touch me." "Strange ! very strange! How did you account for it?" " Well, sometimes I've thought that it was because I eat down on a high branch of a very tall tree." A CONFUSING OCCASION. —Willie Wishington was gazing into space with a look of intense anguish. " What is the matter, Willie?" said one of his friends. "Have you been having trouble 7" " Ya-a-s. I'm afwaid that I've gone and made myself vewy unpopular with Van Diggles and his wife, don't you know." "In what way?" "Why, you know they both wide a bicycle." " Yes." "In costume." "Certainly." "And I met them this afternoon. They passed me one aftah the othah." "And didn't you speak to them ? " " Y-A-A-s. I wish I hadn't, foh, do you know, evewy time I think the mattah ovah I'm half convinced that I lifted my hat and bowed to Van Diggles and said, Hello, old man,' to his wife."

A BOY'S THANKSGIVING. —The following inci- dent is vouched for by parties well acquainted with the boy, now a young professor in one of our large cities. He was the son of a clergyman, and though only five years old, bright and clear beyond his years. It was at a dinner given by his mother to a few intimate friends. Master W— was allowed his usual place at table, but, becoming unruly, was, by way of punishment, transferred to a side table, whither nurse had removed his little plate, knife and fork, by mamma's orders. No sooner -was he seated in his high chair again than, bowing his head and clasping his hands on his soiled bib, he lisped with apparent reverence and great gravity, "0 Lord, I thank Thee that Thou hast prepared a table for me in the presence of mine enemies." It was with difficulty that the "grown ups" kept their smiles from becoming audible. A TANGLED RELATIONSIIIP.—" I tell you how it is," said the mild-eyed patient to the asylum doc- tor. "I met a young widow with a grown step- daughter, and I married the widow. Then my father met 'our step-daughter and married her. That made my wife the mother-in-law of her father-in-law, and made my step-daughter my .step-mother, and my father became my step-son, See? Then my step-mother, the step-daughter of my wife, had a son. That boy was of course my brother, because he was my father's son; but he was also the son of my wife's step-daughter, and therefore her grandson. That made me grand- father to my step-brother. Then my wife had a, son, my brother-in-law. The step-sister of my son is also his grandmother, because he is her step-son's child. My father is the brother-in-law of my child, because his step-sister is his wife. I am the brother of my own son, who is also the child of my grand- mother. I am my mother's brother-in-law, my wife is her own child's aunt, my son is my father's nephew, and lam my own grandfather, and I can't stand it." Ha GOT THE Jon.—He called at the house and asked if she had any carpets to beat, adding that lie had been in the business over 20 years. "How much to beat the parlour carpet?" she asked. "Five shillings." Why, that's awful I There was a man here yesterday who offered to do the job for four." "Exactly, madam, but how was be prepared ?" "He had a stick in his hand." -" I presume so. He intended to take the ~earpet out on a vacant ground, didn't he ? " " Yes; our yard ia too small, you know." • " Exactly. That is the tapestry Brussels -carpet. It is badly worn. It has numerous holes tin it. He would make a great show in get- ting it out and in there. Out on the ground • he would give you away to everyone who asked • who the carpet belonged to. Is that the way to .do a job of this sort?" "How do you do it?" "I take the carpet out through the back. I wheel •it home. I beat it in a yard surrounded by a high - board fence, and while lam returning it, all nicely rolled up and covered with a cloth, if anyone asks me what I have, I reply that it is a velvet carpet for NJ. 24, Blank-street. If no one asks me any questions, I call at the houses on either side of you and ask if they have ordered a new Wilton. They watch me and see me come in here. Maclaine, in the language of the Greek, do you twig ? " II; was given the job.

It is sincerely to be hoped that the most com- plete success will attend a recent departure by the Iztrnbeth Board of Guardians in respect to a certain number of the unfortunate children who are com- mitted to their care. Taking advantage of the fact that a new Board school had been opened immediate vicinity of their own 1`;Orwood schools, the guardians of tlie.ltirgg parish in South London have had 126 tneir children entered as pupils therein ; and as these are to be permitted to attend nAnner, from. ter4 to fifteen schoolm inuteisnbtehi lei g ordinaryaiuow d for the journey to and from the school, the experiment, commenced last week, ought to prove a success. The change to the chil- dren, and the fact that they are to be treated as ordinary pupils, ought to be beneficial in itself, whilst it goes without saying that the education must be of a superior character to that imparted in Poor-law schools, many of the teachers in which are uncertificated. In this matter Lambeth has fol- lowed the example of Bethnal Green, and other parishes might do worse than note the progress of the experiment.

It is pretty certain that the revelations as to the condition of the released dynamiters will lead to an important discussion and a demand for an inquiry into the matter of prison discipline as soon as the House meets next session. It is recognised, believe, in official quarters that some form of in- quiry may prove desirable, if only to set the public mind at ease upon the matter. The promptest course open to the Government would, of course, be for the Home Office to appoint a departmental com- mittee, on which the medical profession would be represented, to look into the question of prison treatment ; and it is believed that Sir M. White Ridley, whose humane feeling in mattc73 ot this sort is beyond cavil, would be quite willing to take this course or any other which would be likely to satisftheitublic mind and prevent a repetition of suchmainfui result:3 as those which litu'e shown trase of 'billite,liead.

Mr. Rudy2rti Ti-ipng cannot continue to write patriotic British ballads and live in the United States. Be might as well go to live in Russia, and there continue bis Simla stories. He is coming to live in England,, where he has some relatives in business in the city, as well as immediate relatives he is much prouder to recognise. If any min wants to do effective literary work he must either live in Paris or London—that is, assuming he is an Eng- lishman. But to go and live in America wag always regarded as a mad enterprise by most of Mr. Kip- ling's friends. He is quite of their opinion now himself, and one of his first strokes of business when be reaches London will be to arrange for the issue of a new work, which he has nearly com- pleted.

Mr: James Mackenzie Maclean, M.P., the aew president of the Istitute of Journalists, bails, as his name indicates, from North of the Tweed. His father,who came from the Hebrides, went abroad— Jamaica,to wit—and prospered,after the manner of his race,and on his return married,and settled down at Liberton ,near Edinburgh,whero James Mackenzie was born,iu 1833. At nineteen years of age he be- came a mathematical tutor, but some essays he wrote attracted the notice of a London editor, and be was advised to go in for journalism. Mr. Maclean took the good •advice, and at the age of twenty he had become editor of the " Newcastle Chronicle "—then a weekly paper. He left his post three years later in 1858 to become leader-writer for the" Manchester Guardian," and in 1859 he went out to India to edit the " Bombay Gazette." The post, however, proved anything but a desirable one, and a year later he resigned, and started the "Bombay Saturday Review." In 1861-64 Bombay waxed fat on the cotton boom, owing to the American %V or ; money was easily made, and by the Pad of 1863 Mr. Maclean was able to buy the " Gazette "for fifteen thousand pounds.

lie at one reorganised the oilice on English lines and brought over a competent 6taff from the old country. Amongst his contributors at this time were Mr. Rudyard Kipling's parents. In 1865 Mr. Maclean returned home, and in 1867 married Miss Anna Maria WhitbreLd. In 1879 be sold the "Gazette," and fn 1882 he bought a large share in the Cardiff " Western Mail," for which he still writes the weekly political letter. Mr. Maclean has always been a politician, and is one of the fathers of the present municipal systr3m in Bombay. In 1880 he was defeate:l for Elgin Burghs, in 1885 and 1886 he was returned for Oldham, losing the seat in i 892; while at the last General Election he defeated Sir Edward Reed at Cardiff by 824 votes.

We are on the eve of the great strikes in London, anyone of which, if carried out, would produce great suffering among the working population. Mr. 1 illett's arrest at Antwerp has given a great stimulus to the fermentation at the docks, and events are ripening, at least here, for the contem- plated universal or international dock strike. Then the members of the Cabmen's Union, almost to a man, having voted against the continuance ef ;he system which gives certain privileged cabs access to the railway stations; but the union includes only a third of the cabmen of London, and the opinion of the remaining two-thirds remains therefore unas- certained. Next, as to the dispute in the tailoring trade, parties are as far from an agreement as ever, and before the week expires perhaps 30,000 hands will be out of work. Mhe latest phase ef this quarrel is that while the middlemen strike against the firms, the working tailors and tailoresses will strike against tk e !middlemen, so that the middlemen are not likely to improve their position by their present agitation.

There is more than one" dossers' parson" in the East End. The correspondence about the Rev. T. C. Collings has brought out the fact that he has a serious rival in a clergyman whom the poor know as " Smiling Millership.” This gentleman,aided by the Lodging-house Mission, haunts the "doss- houses" which swarm in East London. Not find- ing this field of operation large enough, though most people would think it too great, if not too re- pulsive,he frequents the lowest neighbourhoodsilate on Saturday night, his object being to help the wretched. Belleving,like Mr. Collings, that poverty and misery have much to do with crime, he always offers food for the body before spiritual food. At present he is taking it holiday,but only one in name for he is labouring among the poor hop-pickers. Mr. Millership has been in the East End for thir- teen years.

Mr. Horace Marshall, whose death is announced, r'as the pioneer of the railway bookstall. The first cookstall was opened at Fenchurch-etreet Station ty him in 1840. Ten years later be branched out on a larger bcale, and had the bookstalls on the Stepney and Tilbury line, and on the Great Western Railway. But for the accidents of business the firm of Horace Marshall and Sons might have had the place which W. H. Smith and Son occupy. Messrs. Marshall and other competitors retired from the railway business in 1860, and gave way to the great firm which now holds nearly all the railway bookstalls in the country. The Marshalls, how- ever, had more than one branch to their business, and they secured a great proportion of the whole- sale news trade, handling a greater number of papers and periodicals than any one firm after W. H. Smith and Son. For many years the deceased gentleman not only made the business, but did it. For thirty-five years he opened his w arehouse every morning at half-past one to receive the morning newspapers. Be was a quiet member of the City Corporation and of the City Buard of Guardians. He was one of the leading London Wesleyans, not well-known perhaps as a speaker or a worker, but as a generous contributor to Wesleyan institutions.

Active steps are now being taken at the " head- quarters" of • both political parties to organise a vigorous campaign in the constituencies during the autumn and winter. There is a strong feeling among leading Liberals that the present recess c ffers a eingularly,good opportunity tor a spirited attack on the position of the Government. Its fail- ures at home and abroad have spread bitter dis- appointment among its supporters, and,by the same token, given heart to its critics. The importance of making good use of the present recess for Liberal " propagandist " work it emphasised by the consid- eration that as the next general election comes nearer the Government is likely to adopt a less reactionary policy in legislation. The Landlord's Relief Bill and the Anti-Education Bill will be dead ani buried, and the attention of electors will be con- centrated, if possible. upon Mr. Chamberlain's "unauthorised pogramme of "social " legis- lation.

such letters as a thoughtless youth might have written to a woman who confessed herself in love with him and false at heart to her husband. They stung me to fury„ ; accusqd Barbara of loving You. ii l'eiCented my words, but she proudly refused to defend herself. Then I declared that she should never have back the child until she swore to me she was worthy to take charge of it. And she would not swear. We were both proud, and both passionate and imperious. We quarrelled, and she said she wished she had never seen me. Then I proposed that we should live apart, and she eagerly acceded. Before I left the country, I went for the child, intending to restore it to her. It was dead. And its grave lies between us, Ames. If I had restored it when she asked me, it might have been living to-day, a girl on the threshold of womanhood. Ames, I, too, have grieved for the little life untimely lost. That smiling babe was my first and only child. No father can bear easily the loss of the life that sprang from his. I have grieved for my dead baby. I have wept over its small grave ; have wet its coffin with my tears; but my grief is weak and vain beside Barbara's." "Poor Barbara !" breathed Ames. "I know that she has mourned all these years for her dead child. The instinct of maternity is strong within her. But surely you can comfort her, Champney. Your grief should be a tie to bind you two together." "Barbara cannot forgive me. She told me that when I restore our child to her arms, she would take me back, and not before. And I know, if she were to forgive me, that little grave would be always between us. You see how hopeless it all is, Ames."
Willard linked his arm in that of the baron, and the two moved slowly down the path, between the masses of sweet-breathed flowers and shrubbery. " Yor r.ill remain at Saltair, Champney ?" lle

"Yes. Barbara cannot deny me the shelter of her roof, and I cannot go away from her again." " You do right to stay. .Your presence is a shield to your wf. I v.-)nder that people have never nt yo,7r strange separation.
. - Have you limy have forged those letters,' Champuey, which wrought all this trouble ?"
- "None. 1 have not an enemy—at least I had not one at that time."

"But Barbara might have had," suggested Ames. " Will you give me leave to speak freely ?" "Certainly. Say on." "Well, then, Champney, who would be most in- terested in effecting a separation between you and your wife? Who, in default of your having issue, would succeed to your title and estates ?" "My cousin and secretary, Felix Warner." "Exactly. Cannot Felix Warner be at the bottom of this trouble ?"

- His lordship started, his cheeks flushing. "Impossible !" he ejaculated. "Felix has never said anything against Barbara—at least, he has always declared his belief in her innocence of any intended wrong against me. Felix ! Why he is the truest friend I have in the world! I would as soon believe in an angel's guilt as in his ! You don't know Felix, Ames 1" "I own that I am but little acquainted with him," said Ames. "I have not seen him for years. I have no proofs against him, not the faintest shadow of a proof, as I must con- fess. But he has so direct an interest in your separation from your wife—in your dying child- less—" "Nonsense, Ames! Felix never thought of such a thing. He is jealous of my honour, and he would dread to have me become the dupe of an unfaithful woman, such as Barbara has seemed; but he is ever thoughtful of my happiness. He is like a brother to me. Since, as you acknowledge, you have not a shadow of proof against him, bat have simply fixed on him, in casting about for some one to father those forged letters, dismiss your suspicions of him. Felix was not in London at the time. That simple fact proves his inno- cence." "Then who could it have been ?" asked Ames, his theory shattered. "That is a mystery which time may or may not reveal4:' said the baron, sighing. "I acquit Barbara and you of all blame in the matter. Barbara declared to me to-day that toe letters were forged. No doubt I have been the dupe of some mischievous person, who never dreamed of the prssible results of his performance." " Your trust in Barbara is restored ?"

" Perfectly. I have been a jealous fool, and I have myself to blame for the ruin of my happiness," said his lordship, bitterly. The two, arm in arm, walked up and down the garden path for a little while in silente.

Ames was tempted to narrate to Lord Champney the particidars-of Col. Etlinghion's persecution of the Lady Barbara; but he refrained, knowing that he would only arouse the jealous passions which were now lulled. Besides, he reflected, Effingham would not dare repeat his insulting attentions, now that Lord Chanipney had returned. It was only a solitary and defenceless woman Effingham dared insult. "That matter will settle itself," thought Ames. "When Effingham hears that Lord Champney is at home with his wife, he will ga away, for, of course, he will comprehend that Barbara's husband is her protector. lie is cowardly enough to war upon an unprotected woman, but he would never dare brave Lord Champney's indignant rage. The presence of Barbara's husband protects her. I will say nothing that can arouse Champney's jealous anger, No pro- voke him to an assault upon Effingham. No scan- dal must touch Barbara's name."

With these thoughts Ames decided to say no- thing concerning Effingham, fully convinced that the colonel would leave Cromer un learning of Lord Champney's presence at Saltair. After a few turns up and down the garden-paths the baron said: "Ames, I have wronged you in my thoughts all these years. Fargive me. iou have my hearty approval to your contemplated marriage. Let us be friends."

The two clasped hands warmly. "And now," said the baron, "Leave me, Ames. Go into the drawing-room. No doubt Barbara is anxious lest we come to blows. I will follow you as soon as I shall have walked off a little of my superfluous excitement." "I will go," said Ames. "Don't despair, my lord. I know that Barbara loves you yet., She may answer differently a second pleading." He wrung the baron's hand and hurried toward the house.

"I will try to soften Barbara toward her husband," he thought, full of generous sympathy. "Surely she can forgive him. I will have a long talk with her to-night about him." He paused on the steps of a side porch and looked lyaek at the tall, dark figure stalking to and fro in the garden, and then, sighing deeply, he entered the house.
Gaiety reigned supreme in the drawing-room when he catered it. Lie young people were absorbed in some parlour game, and scarcely noticed his return. _ _
He looked around the room for the Lady Barbara, _ _ _

The flutter of thin black drapery on the balcony of one of the open windows caught his wandering glances, and he moved toward it. As he expected, the Lady Barbara was on the balcony. He stepped out beside her, and the lace drapery of the window floated down, shutting them off from the drawing-room. " Well ?" said her ladyship, turning toward him her strangely pale face. "All is well, Barbara," he answered, taking in his her cold hand. _ _ _ _

The Lady Barbara breathed more freely. "I followed you to the garden," she whispered, "and stood in the shade of a bush until I saw you walk down the garden arm in arm. Then I knew there was no more danger. How dia you manage to charm him so, Willard ?"

"By telling him frankly of my love for Ada, and assuri:ig him of the brotherly character of my affec- tion for you. He knows now that your heart has never strayed from him." "You did not speak of Colonel Effingham ?" "No. The colonel won't trouble you now that Champney has returned. It is useless to excite your husband in the matter, since you will never hear from the colonel again. You can tell Champ- ney, yourself, Barbara, when you become reconciled to him. An, he is coming in now! Remember your appointment at eleven o'clock, Barbara. I have much to tell you. He left her abruptly, going into the drawing- MOM.
A minute later, Lord Champney, pale and worn, entered the room.

Willard directed the husband by a glance to the balcony, hoping th,:.!.; he would join the Lady Barbara there. Bu c the baron, uncertain about his reception, shook his head and sat down at a centre-table, busying himself with a portfolio of engravings. . .
arter the Lady Barbara rejoined her guests.
The evening passed, music and conversation lending wins. to the hours.. It was fully. eleyep
o'cloci•i when the party separated, retiriDg to their several chambers.

Lord t2lndnpney went up to his Ow MOM, rest- less and unhappy, turned down his light, and sat down at his •,% indow, looking through the ,moveable shutters pon tile moo:Wt sea. The 1t was very still, and calm, anti fair, such a night as is (July seen in perfection by the summer sea. The waves beat lowly against the c ill's, and out upon the bright waters Lord Champ- ney fancied he could detect the glimmer of a sail, The sweet influence of the night brought a strangs- sense of peace and cluietne:f.s to the baron's restless,. soul.

But suddenly the charm was brohen by the low murmur of voices, coming up from below. At the same moment he beheld on the cliff, in the shadow of a group of trees, two figures. Oue of these he recognised at Once as that of his wife.

Her corupan;on—VVilliard Ames—had his back to the house, and stood further in the shadow. Lord Champney did not detect his identity. "Ah !" he muttered. ".Nly wife is taking a stroll by moonli;4ht %%ith some one she cannot meet at her house ? I must know who it is !"

He bent out further in Ins earnest scrutiny, and at the same moment, the Lady Barbara saw him. With the rapidity of a deer Lord Champney hurried from his room, springing down the stairs, and made his way to the front door. It -was locked. lb; hastened to undo the bolts and chains, and, at last successful, bounded out upon the lawn toward the chit'.

Too late ! The figures were gone ! The Lady Bu bare and her kinsman had re- entered the house by a private door, and had already separatt,l for the night. His lordship t.starched the cliff, but in vain. At length he slowly retraced his steps to his room, muttering, : _

" I'm outv,it-;,,,,, tms time, hot hel,neforth on my guard. 1-low do 1 know whom Barbara sees—who are her friends? She may baNe formed new affec,tions since 1 left her seventeen years ago. She she has not toll me for keen-
—hut how Oo
I mast be kec...l and watchful—l :.aabt iiowthe truth 1"
CHAPTER VI. THE RIVAL SUITORS.

As the sound of a horse's hoofs behind her on the pleasant country road, and of a voice calling her name, struck Dora Chessom's hearing, after leaving the tea-garden of the Hare and Hounds Inn, she started, half halted, and looked back. "Good-morning, Miss Dora," said the rich and pleasant voice of the horseman. "A lovely morning !" "Oh, it's the young squire 1'" said Dora, her pale face brightening. "1 beg your pardon, Squire Weir. lam getting into the general habit of call- ing you the young squire.'" "It used to be Noel," observed the horseman, smiling, yet half reproachfully. "May I keep you company to the Grange, Miss Dora? I was on my way there when I so fortunately overtook you." Without waiting for a formal consent—perhaps reading his answer in her friendly ey es—the young squire dismounted, and walked slowly at her side, leading his horse. He was Noel ‘Veir, who had come into possession of Weir Hall and a fine fortune while a mere lad. He was now some three or four and twenty years old, and one of the finest specimens of young man- hood to be found in the kingdom. He was tall and straight and stalwart, with a bright, gay and frank face, lighted up by honest, bold blue eyes, and by a glorious smile. Above his massive forehead tossed masses of flossy blonde hair. A curling blonde moustache shaded a firm yet tender mouth. Brave and honest and true, grave when there was need of serious- ness, he was gifted with one of those rare and sunshiny natures whose counterpart Dora her- self possessed. " Papa isn't at home," said Dora, cheerfully, putting her personal griefs into the background. "He went to Horsham on business, and I don't expect him home before sunset." "I didn't care about seeing the squire to-day," said the young man, with a sudden glow on his face. "I wanted to see you, Dora—that is, Miss Chessom." His earnestness rather embarrassed Dora, who began to entertain a sudden conviction of his errand. She became silent, and walked along the footpath wondering how she could best ward off the confi- dence he was about to make to her.

"Dora," he exclaimed, in a voice that trembled —" Dora, can't you guess what I want to say? Do you know why I have haunted the Grange ever since I came home from Oxford? It was to meet your sunny smiles, Dora—to see your lovely face You don't know how dreary and dark the old Hall seems to me after I have paid a visit to the Grange. Dora, I want to transfer the light of the Grange to my home I I want you! I love you— I love you I" He spoke eagerly and impetuously, all the ardour of his nature glowing in his manner. "Don't, Noel !" murmured Dora, her heart thrilling with a sudden pain. "Have I beeu too abrupt, Dora ? " asked the young squire, softening his ardent voice into a persuasive gentleness. "I have loved you so long, and I thought you understood me. Have I spoken too soon? Only give me the smallest straw of a hope, and I will wait for you as long as you wish. But don't say No, Dora! I love you with all my heart and strength. I could serve for you as Jacob served for Rachel—" _ _

"Don't, Noel!" repeated Dora, in a low, pained voice. "I had not dreamed of this I regard you as a friend—as a brother ; but not—not in the way you wish ! We can never be more to each other than we are now !" The young squire breathed hard. His face be- came shadowed with a great grief. "Never, Dora ?" he said, huskily. "Did you say never ? " Never, Noel! I appreciate the great honour you have done me, and I shall always pray for your happiness. I cannot be your wife, but let us continue to be friends ! " She held out her hand with a deprecating move- ment. The young squire took it and held it in his, his tPars dropping on it. "Don't grieve so, Noel," said Dora, in tender pity. "I am not worth your tears." 'You love another, Dora?" asked the young squile, in a broken voice. His tone was so gentle and so humble that the maiden could not resent his inquiry. I—l don't know 1" she stammered, her face burning with blushes. "I don't know my own mind, Noel." "I had feared that you would like Mr. Warner, with is city breeding and foreign manners," said the young man, in a grieved voice, yet without bitterness. "I do not trust him, Dora, yet I trust you will be happy with him, if you consent to marry him. Whoever you wed, and wherever you go, Dora, I pray that you may be happy. But if sorrow and trouble ever come to you, and you need a friend, send for me. If seas divide us, and half the world lies between us, I will come. Promise that when you need a true and staunch friend, you will send for me."

"I promise," said the girl, softly. Thpy walked on together to the gate of the Grange, and Dora then asked her suitor to enter the house. "Not to-day," said the young squire, forcing a faint smile. "I will wait until I can bear to see you with him. Good-bye, Dora." He pressed her hand earnestly, led his horse to the block, mounted, and dashed furiously away in the direction he had come.

"There goes one of the truest, noblest souls that ever lived," said Dora to herself, as she looked after him. "If he had spoken sooner—" She sighed, leaving her sentence unfinished, and walked up the short path to the house. The front door was open, as was also the door of the drawing-room. Dora threw off her sun-hat and went into the room, a troubled look chasing the brightness from her face.
As he eStered, a gentleman arose from a sofa by the wide west window and greeted her with a profound bow. In an instant Dora's face was stained with a wild-rose hue.

"Mr. Warner "she exclaimed, in a bright con- fusion. "This is a surprise !" "A pleasant one, I hope," was the quick response. "I met the squire on his way to Horsham, and he told me 1 most cheer you up in his absence. I am glad to have you to myself an hour, Miss Dora. The squire has never seemed to appreciate, or even see, my efforts to see you alone. Some strange good fortune has befriendea me to-day." He laughed softly, and reseated himself. Dora stole a sly glance at him. He was just the man to captivate the fancy of a romantic, country-bred girl. He was tall and commanding in form—nearly as much _so as.his_co_usin,Jord Cbampney. He was

tc type ur ton rasnwnarne !mu or Its class, wearing his hair parted in the centre like a woman's, and having long, tawny bide whiskers, which nearly reached his shordders. Re had a distinguished air —the result of long study abroad—was a master of the art of flattery, and was a consummate hypocrite. He seemed earnest, truthful and honest ; so much so that Lord Champney fre- quently called him " Honest Felix ;" but under his fair seeming he was t,cherning, plotting and deadly. He had a small income of his own, insufficient, however, for his fashionable necessities, and during his cousin's residence abroad he bad lived with him as confidential fricad and secretary, gaining by artful wiles and feigned devotion, astrong influence over his lordship. This was Dora Chessom's favoured suitor—the man for whose sake she had just rejected the truest heart in Sussex.
" You lo(,k pale this morning, Miss Dora," said Warner, as the glow faded from her cheeks. "You look ill !"
" I am net well," answered Dora--" that is, I do not feel quite myself. The morning is quite sultry."
"It is, assented Warner, sympathizingly. "The heat must be insufferable in town. I dread to go .back to it."
"Why must your' asked Dora, lightly. "You were there the other day, were you not?"
"Yes, to meet my cousin, Lord Champney, who has just returned from Germany. I spent a few hours with him at his hotel."

"I should like to see him," said Dora, thought- fully. "You have told me so much about his lord- ship that I fancy I should know him at sight. How strange that he should live abroad so many years, while his wife remained in England. Ii LadlSl.ampnt..; an_ invalid?" " 011,.n0 : the Lady Barbara—she was an earl's daughter, and is always called by her given name, because she prefers it to that of her husband—is the very imper2'oration of health " " s "
.las-the beauty of a goddess. She is a nagnificent woman r declared Warner, with enthusiasm.

"And they have no children ?" "None. Their only child died in her infancy, many years ago. If I survive my cousin, I shall be the next Lord Champney ?" said Warner, with half-concealed complacency. "How long his lordship has been away?" re- marked Dora. "Of course he has paid frequent visits home to his wife, but they must feel glad to be together again for good, now that Lord Champ- ney has resigned his post abroad." " Together !' repeated Warner, with an in- voluntary start. "They are not together. I left his lordship in London, where he has reports to make and business to transact with the govern- ment. I must go to him in the course of a week or two, and, indeed, I may be summoned to him sooner. My valet is in London, and has orders to forward to me any message that may arrive for me. I only hope my cousin may not summon me for a fortnight, and that I may have inducements to remain here," he added, significantly. Dora looked away out of the open window. How lovely she looked, with the hawthorn scented breeze lifting the curling tendrils on her jetty hair, with the faint colour flickering in her cheeks, and with her innocent eyes drooping in a sudden confusion.

Felix Warner felt his heart stirred as it had never been stirred before. He had looked coldly upon the charms of stately and beautiful women to fall in love at last with a little country maiden! And he did love with all the ardour of which his selfish nature was capable. He drew nearer to her, and gently lifted the little hand that lay in her lap. "This is a prize," he said, caressing the hand, "for some happy fellow. Is it reserved for Squire Weir, Miss Dora 2" " ! " said Dora, her cheeks scarlet.
, "I thought not. It is too lofty a prize for a clodhopper like 'the young squire, as your father calls him—"
Dom made a motion to withdraw her hark'.

"Squire Weir is not what you think," she said, warmly. "He is noble and good. He is a graduate of Oxford, and came off with high honours. His integrity is a proverb. Everybody respects him and looks up to him. Under all his gaiety, he has a grand and solid character." "He has an earnest defender," smiled Warner, refusing to release her hand. "I don't deny all you say, Miss Dora. No doubt 'the young squire' is a very worthy fellow; but he's so plain —no style, you know. And then his family! He is nothing but a country squire, after all, and they Bay his mother came of a manufacturing family in L'irmingham, and that young Weir has inherited an ir,terest in some plodding manufacturing business. He is well enough in his place, but I understand he superint‘ ~ds his own farm, and is his own man of business."

"Is that anything against him?" demanded Dora. "I don't admire idlers, Mr. Warner. I don't see how human beings, gifted with in- tellect and sense, can sink into drones and do- nothings! I respect the man who works. We were placed in the world to do—not simply to be—and I respect the man who takes up the burden of life bravely and gallantly, and does his share in the world's work. Better to break stones, or work in a smithy," she added, " than to do nothing I have no sympathy with fashionable idlers, the thoughtless butterflies of humanity ?"

"I can't come among those you denounce, Miss Dora," said Warner, with a slight laugh. "I am a worker too, only of a different sort to our young squire.'" He said truly. He was not like the bee, but rather like the spider. His work lay in the weav- ing of webs. " I—l didn't think of you," stammered Dora. "Then won't you think of me now ?" asked War- ner, still lightly. "I don't like to be lost sight of. How well your fair brow would become a coronet, Dora I You would make a glorious Lady Champ- ney Nature never meant that such a jewel as you should be wasted on a simple country squire. It meant, rather, that you should have a fitting setting of rank and worldly honours." Dora did not answer. She appeared absorbed in watching a group of brown birds on the sunny lawn, but Warner knew that she was listening to him.

"Dora," he continued, "innocent as you are, you must have guessed why I have loitered here these three months. I have seen the fairest women of the Continent, but I never loved until I met you. My cousin wishes me to marry, but until now the thought has been untearable. My heart has never bowed before any shrine till now. Dora, my con- queror, will you fetter me with your love, or will you condemn roe to the dungeons of despair ?" Dora's heart fluttered. The glow came and went in her cheeks, and her eyes drooped yet lower. A strange happiness took possession of her, yet, even then, she could not help but mark the difference between the two proposals she had received that morning, and in her heart she liked best the plain and straightforward declaration of Noel Weir.

"Dora," whispered Warner, with soft gentle- ness, "you are strangely silent. You have not been playing with me, after all? Say that you love me, Dora. Say that you will be my wife! Will you give me this little hand, and the heart with it ?" He laid down the hand upon her knee. It fluttered there a moment softly and then stole back into his cool grasp. "My own Dora," he whispered, bending over as if to kiss her. Dora gently put him away, and looked up at him, her face pale, her eyes glowing. "Mr. Warner," she said, in a low and troubled voice, "are you sure that you love me ?" " Sure ? I would lay down my life for you, my peerless Dora." "You do not think our stations in life too unequal ?" "A nt too unequal. Dora. And our station will be the same when we are married."

" But," said Dora, desperately, " suppose— suppose that I were not really a Chessom—not the squire's daughter, but only a poor girl whom he had adopted out of generous pity. Would you love me just the seine? Would you want me for your wife ?'' Warner's face clouded, and he looked at her keenly. Then he fingered his long side whiskers in an embarrassed manner. After a minute's silence he exclaimed, his brow clearing: "I see, Dora, you want to try me. You want to make sure that it is not the squire's riches I am after, but yourself. Lot your little heart be at rest. 1 should love you jut; the Caine if your origin were obscure, or if you were simply a dependent upon the squire's bounty. It is you I love, Dora, not your probal,le dowry." He spoke with an earnestness that convinced the young girl of his sincerity. A smile like April sunshine broke over her face. - _
"I believe you, Mr. Warner," she said, quickly.

----'7Kfid now may I seal our betrothal with a kis° asked Warner. "Call me Felix, Dora. You ar my promised wife, and this is the token a yo troth." Again be bent over her, and this time his touched lightly the girl's shrinking mouth. .4. "You are like a wild bird, Dora," he sall: tenderly. "I must be careful not to frighten 337"; It seems like a dream that you are going to be 11/1 wife. I must ask the squire's consent this lel night. 1 will ride over for the purpose." Despite her happiness there was a shadoW c'S flora's face which Warner exerted himself to reml soon succeeding in the effort. He lingered an Of longer, and then ordered his horse and rode E4M. his mind in a state of supreme contentment. Dora stood by the window and looked after bm- 'With a wistful gaze. "Will his love stand the test before it ?" lb/ thought. "Will it survive the discovery 0I birth? If that woman's story is true—and that it is—papa must tell Felix all. Of course will love me just the same. He said he w 0111,6 And yet, somehow, I feel strangely ginolll,4'. There is trouble ahead for me, I believe. JO— a strange foreboding of it." (To be continued).

OR, A WAR OF THE HOUSEHOLD,
By Oa la:tither of •- Double Life," "The Bailiff's Scheme," &c., &c.
CHAPTER V. AMES AS A MEDIATOR.

Despite the shadows brooding over at least three of the party, the dinner at Saltair passed off very agreeably. Lord Champney took his place as host, as a'matter of course, and exerted himself success- fully to be entertaining. The Lady Barbara was apparently in fine spirits, and Willard Ames had never been gayer. Not one of the guests dreamed of the dark reality under all that fair and pleasant seeming. The dinner over, the Lady Barbara led her guests hack to the drawing room. Lord Champney and Willard Ames joined the group, but soon after, when conversation was in full tide, the former ex- cused himself, on the rretence of wishing to smoke a cigar, and wcnt out hit° the garden. A- few minutes later Ames also withdrew, and went in quest of the Lady Barbara's husband. He found him in the flower garden, walking slowly up aui down the shaded, moon-lit paths, puffing at a cigar. His lordship turned, halted abruptly, as Ames's step crunched the gravel path, and drew up his tall and commanding figure, and flung away his cigar as he awaited Ames's near approach. A moment later the two stood face to face; the one dark, haughty and stern, the other fair and proud, and no less haughty. ‘• Ilave you asked me to meet you here as a friend or as an enemy, Lord Champney ?" asked Ames, quietly. His lordship sneered. " Did you think it possible that you and I could meet as fr,n, ?" !:• demanded. . ...hies, eThnlv. v should
alm,%,ys • a dear b6t._,, --for such she has been to :Ile. I was her fathel.'s ward; you know, and Barbara and 1 were brought up like brother and sister."

Lord Chainpney looked keenly and searchingly into Ames's face ; but the bright blue eyes met his gaze openly and frankly. " Yes, I know you were brought up together," his lordship said, stiffly. "Barbara is nearly of my age," said Ames, coolly disregarding his companion's unfriendly manner. "She is hut a year or so my junior. It is rather odd that she will be my aunt by marriage —that is, if AO la will consent to marry me. lam going to risk my fate to-morrow." "1)0 you mean that you love and want to marry Ada Gower ?" demanded Lord Champuey, looking at Ames as if he would probe his soul. "I do," answered Ames, his face lighting up with a happy glow. "Ada has encouraged me, and I believe she returns my love. I know that you are not Ada's guardian, my lord, but neverthe- less she is an inmate of your home, and I ask your, as I have asked Barbara's, consent and approval of my suit." Even Lord Champney, suspicious as he was by nature, could not discredit this statement. His face flushed, and an uneasy look crept into his eyes. "You have my consent and approval, if they will do you any good," he observed. "Barbara Is willing you should marry Ada ?" "Not only willing, but she is well pleased," said Ames. "She invited me here on this present visit, that I might have the opportunity to woo and win Ada. Oh, my lord, is she not the fairest, sweetest being you ever beheld ?" " Who ? Barbara ?" cried Lord Champney, start- ing jealously. " No—Ada ? Barbara is a magnificent woman, but she has not Ada's gentle sweetness." "There is no comparison between the two "said Lord Champney, curtly. "The one is a pretty, unformed girl; the other, as you say, is a magni- ficent woman As well compare a candle to a star!"

The baron turned away, walking moodily and reatlesoly up and down the path. Ames watched him carelessly, a smile creeping about his girlish mouth, as he slowly plucked the pink petals from the roses on the bush beside him.

After a little, Lord Champney returned to his companion. " Ames," he said, abruptly, fixing his eyes in an eagle glance on Ames's face, "1 had a fancy that you loved Barbara once. Did you ?" "I loved her as a brother loves a sister—in no other way," said Ames, meeting Champney's gaze fully and honesty. " Barbara was but a child when she married you. She was not seventeen. When you left her and went abroad she was but little more than eighteen, and I was not yet twenty. I was not old enough to think of love, even if you did me the honour to be jealous of me," and Ames smiled. "I was at the university then, but I can't forget my surprise when I learned that you had gone abroad as attaché to an ambassai,lor. You have become ambassador, and resident minister abroad, since then. You must have been born with a genius for diplomacy, Champuey, else you would have never given up home and friends to serve your country all these years." "You are mistaken," said the baron, with a bitter smile. "I was formed for a domestic life. You cannot find a man in England who appreciatee a home more than I; yet, like him who wrote the song of Sweet Home, I have been all my life homeless." - -
"It's never too late to mend," suggested Ames. The baron sighed bitterly. "It's too late for me I" he said. "Too late ! Those are the saddest words in the language, Ames. Too late ! " _ _

" 'W hen they're true, but in your case they are not true. The most miserable man is he who makes himself miserable. Do you still love Barbara?" "Love her? Yes—a thousand times better than I love my own soul 1" cried Lord Champney, with a passionate fervour. "Ames, when I asked you out here to-night, it was to upbraid you and to quarrel with you. I believed, I confess it in shame, that you loved my wife and that she loved you. I am jealous, suspicious and unreasonable. With my dark skin, I have all the quick passion of the natives of the tropics. I have wronged my wife beyond forgiveness in my cruel treatment and neglect of her. Yet I have loved her all these years. Never for one moment has my heart swerved from her—never have I once been untrue to her even in thought. She has been exalted in my mind above all other women, even when I have believed her lost to me. A thousand times I have been on the point of returning to her and begging her forgiveness, but always 1 resolved to wait a little while longer, hcping that she would make overtures to me. I waited in vain. There is grey in my hair, Ames—there are lines on my forehead. I seem to have grown old, while she is in the glorious prime of her beauty. It is too late! if she ever loved me, her love is vanished ! No love could survive the treatment I have bestowed upon her, yet I would die to regain her love !" " Why don't you tell her so ?" asked Ames, pityingly. " 1 know Barbara well. She has a grand, broad nature ; a noble soul, a proud spirit. She has nothing small nor petty in her composition. And I believe—despite all that has passed—that she loves you still. When a woman like Barbara loves she loves for ever." Lord Champney shook his head in silence. He took a few turns up and down the walk, and then halted ag do, saying in a choked voice : " Allied, 1 Juice told her. I have laid my heart at her feet. I have prayed her to forgive me " " And she?" _ _

"Site spitted me, as I must confess I deserved to be spurned. She does not love me. She told me I had lived seventeen years without her and I could live without her to the end. Sha is cold and stern and unforgiving, but just. In my despair and my anguish I could have knelt to her, but she repulsed me." The heart of Willard Ames thrilled with pity 9.8 he regarded the despairing face of the unhappy husband, "Be patient, Champney," he said, clasping the baron's hand. " She will soften yet." " Never She said there was a grave between us—the grave of our child. She can never forgive me for my e'ruelty about the child. You know how it was. Barbara was ill for months of a fever, after the child was born. The doctor ordered that the baby should be sent into the country until the mother recovered. Barbara grew better at last, and mended slowly. I told her where the child was, and she approved of its having been sent away. It was then I found in her private desk a packet of love-letters, signed with your name—" "I never wrote them, Chant puey—l give you my word of honour. 1 never wrote a line to Barbara that you might not have seen." "There were in the letters allusions to expres- sions on Barbara's part of hatred to me and regret for hes marriage._ The. letters_ were ar4ent-71u8t

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
Y DEAR NELLIE,

Ostrich feathers, if they are of really a good quality, are possessions to be prized by smart women, and I hope all of you who are the fortu- nate owners of such treasures have put them away carefully during the summer, where the moths have not been able to work their wicked will on them. Now is the time for the feathers to be brought out of their retirement, and sent to a reliable cleaner to be renovated and curled. I have seen two entirely new hats, one was of white felt, the broad brim bent up slightly in a singularly becoming style, and the rather high crown trimmed with a band of satin ribbon, a rosette, and two jetted quills. The second was of shrimp-pink velvet, with high, full-topped crown of pink and gold brocade; the brim is softened by a row of tiny curling tips, and three long plumes and a tip are adjusted at the side.

A hat which is much worn has a Tam-o'zThanter crown of semi-transparent white crinoline straw and a brim of yellow Tuscan straw, the connecting link ;being a twist and bow of green and blue shot glace, with a mount of white swan's quills. Just towards the front is a trail of roses with delicate pink and white petals. Little boys are rather more difficult to dreg" .gracefully and becomingly than little girls, especi- ally when they are ,emerging from baby frocks, Air id have not attained the dignity of ;knickers. A pretty dress for a 'laddie in this transition state, from two to three and a half years old, may -consist of navy serge, worn with a vest of fine striped flannel, and a detachable sailor collar of white flannel or linen. This is made with a small band having several buttonholes worked in it, and small pearl buttons are sewn inside the neck of the tunic in a carseqponding position.

For a young girl a very -pretty wariiing frock might be made of embroidered grass lawn, with a yoke and sleeves of pale pink cambric. The hat has a crown of burnt straw, with a brim of pink cambric to match the dress. In consequence of the el, in the weather many muslin and lawn toitottes intended to be worn at outdoor functions have had to be laid on one side in favour of slightly thicker materials, which have been made up with a great deal of elegance. ,One of these costumes is in grey canvas grenadine over pink silk, with a pink silk vest and tight under-sleeves of the same, with full grey chiffon wrinkled over them all the way down the wrist and ending in a frill. The back and side pieces of the corsage and the epaulettes are in the grey canvas, and the pink vest is covered with grey chiffon, drawn down to the waist. The straps over the shoulder, neck, and watetbands are of grey -satin, dotted with silver sequins, and the latter has a xichly-wrought, but not large, silver buckle.
A costume of hark blue 'canvas, looks very pretty bound with white linen; a vest and cravat of white chiffon, and a white felt hat with white wings, and baud and rosettes of cherry-red velvet.

• V. • .0••• The flounced skirt is without doubt upon us, and the flounces take various outlines.; now they twill be put on in a rounded scallop, now in a van. .dyke, or again straight round the skirt. Such skirt have I in my mind's eye, made of pale pitir lace silk, with a deep flounce hanging from the knees in points bordered with a fringed ruching and resting upon a second flounce with a straight hem also ruched. The skirts which hear flounces should not be so full as those which are plain; indeed all the skirts should not be so full as they have been, for we are again realising the advantage of not carrying about with us 25 yards of material. Your lovints ELWIE.

The list of bridegrooms of the month include,s no fewer THE MAYOR'S ABSENCE. than twelve military men and eleven clere:finens The Mayor and Deputy-Mayor being absent,Alderman From the Tyrol we have news of altwast umarecedent- Sutton was on the motion of Councillor Higaroar,elected i edly early snowfall, but this does not necessatily mean to thechair. that the coming winter will be eith'ar early nrprolonged. Last year, my readers will remenlber, we had snow in October, and all the rustic signa of a severe winter,but a spring like November followed, and the season was most unusually mild. The departure, aswell as the arrival aK the -swallaws. is always most carefully watched, and the time is chronl icled as regularly as if they were members of theeiZoya, Family. It seems these dates vary not only accardin" to the season but alao with the locality, last year for in stance the swallows all deserted Lmbleside before the end of September, but lingered on at Dover until N9V- ember the 9th and honoured Bethill with their presence as late as the 16th of that month, ere finally taking wing for the sunny south. Opponents of bull-fighting, who are numerous in Paris, will be sorry to learn that Madame Sarah Bernhardt' enthusiastically patronises 'the popular Spanish sport. , It is announced from San Sebastian, that having been cresent at a bull-'fight, she was so delighted with the toreador who killed 'fivehdils. that she presented him , with a valuable pin ornamented with brilliants. Accord- ing to a Parisian theatrical journal, the d:va has given a commission to a well-knewn Russian-French dramatiat to prepare for her a new I lay, founded on "Carmen." The new version, it is said, will be a more faithful adaptation Of Prosper Igerimes's novel-than the operatic , libretto, and the English version performed at the Gaiety Theatre, London, not long ago. Apropos of actresses, in Vienna the pressure is so great that at thirty years of age they are, as well as singers, regarded as too old for much more use, and are relegated to Obscure parts or put &IT the stage. In the last two years 7.3-.0 or 40 such actresses have become beggars, and not a few have died on the country roads along which they have been begging for food. chorus girl is most fortunate if she can nut get £517. month, many girlstreceive but £1 each a month. This however does not apply to the Court Opera where the pay is better. Durand the Parisian, who makes a precarious living by hanging himself for the delectation of the French public, has been forbidden by the German Government to give his gruesome exhibition anywhere in the Father- land. He has therefore passed on to Switzerland, and when he' has rejoiced the people of that country suffi- ciently he intends to conquer America! One cannot help thinking-that if all the morbib-minded peaple who take, pleasure in degrading spectacles of the kind could be hanged, the world would benone the poorer for their absence. It appears that a French workman is constructing an' aerial machine with which he pronoses to tempt fortune inthe skies. The apparatus is to be supported by a series of small cylindrical balloons, and the pilot will have wings attached to his arms wherewith he can pro- pel himself through space. Truly the threatened dangers ,of the streets multiply fast. The cycle abates nothing of its blood tax, a cloud of -auto-cars, which no man or , woman knows yet how to dodge is waiting to break on the town, while the flying machine threatens us from labove.

MISCELLANEOUS. The minutes of several committees which were printed in last week's " Examiner," were confirmed without discussion.—ln m wing the confirmation of the minutes of the 'Finance and Estates Committee, Councillor SHAW GREEN referred to the proposal that the sum of £2OO be accepted in settlement of the claim for' damage done by the recent fire .;o the premises in Bridge-street recently occupied by Mr. Thomas Daintith, and said that all the items were fully made out, and the committee decided to accept this sum in discharge.

Rag bag rugs are often very useful in the bathroom, I kitchen or servants' bedrooms, and the manufacture thereof is an excellent means whereby to employ restless 'little fingers, now the evenings are beginning to get long again. Commence by cutting half circles, measured on the bottom of a baking powder tin, of different kinds of cloth. Sew a piece of old carpet on a heavy foundation of bed ticking and then stitch on rows of the half. circles until it is covered. The rugeney be round or square, the circles buttonholed round the curves with bright coloured coarse worsted, scalloped, or pinked. One I made last winter was from old "jersey sleeves 'black and red, old stockings could be used in the same way, dyed if necessary. Silk tartan hose will be worn this coming winter by up-to-date folk, but the striped specimens that have lately been much en evillenve are unlikely to retain their popularity, owing to the increased size they give the ordinary toot. Plain black cashmere, with lace fronts are being shown now, and very useful thesewill doubt- less prove. Apropos of hosiery, we should all do our best to prevent our menkind from purchasing crimson ,or scarlet socks. Owing to vanity or some other cause operating on the male mind, men are particularly fond of indulging in these colours, with the result that they run the risk of blood-pois ming if they are out of health or have a slight scratch or wound. Even the best socks in these colours are unsafe, and the cheap manufactured article ;s a source of real danger. Opera cloaks are unusuailiy ,rich this autumn. Time was when cashmere lined with pongee was considered s fficiantly smart for almost any occasion, but now materials must be of the rit'hest, and linings of the finest to bring them up to date. 'Some of the silks employed in the building of these cloaks are beautiful beyond description. We used totbe content and have a plain or a figured one,now one effect is set over the other, and a silk that in itself would be rich enough to stand alone,is not only interwoven with alloral design but displays a superstructure of some large fern leaves, or a huge flower in brocade. Moires, in a great variety of water- ings, recalling a shower of rain, or knots of wood, are woven in black and colours,plain and with satin stripes, while mirror velvets have meandering designs in white all over thennthrown on singularly pure colourings that appeal to our most cultivated tastes. Although the little girl's reply to a question from the teacher, to the effect that the 'United States was "governed by machinery," cannot be described as an ahheether true statement, there is no doubt that many things are done in America by machinery which are here done by hand. For instance, the 'United States Post Office has introduced machines for counting and tying postal cards and small teindles. These two machines are capable of counting 503000 cards in ten hours, and wrapping and tying the same in paekages of twenty- nave each. Speaking of the post offices, the annual report shows that we write more, letters than we ever did before, forty-six letters, newspapers, or boek packets lacing the average for every man, woman and child in the Ue;ted ITineclem. Considering however that many persens write this number of letters in a day, the amount is not co enormous as it seems. Ireland with its less than 5,060:00) of population claims to have more centenarians than any country in Europe. perhaps in the world. They number -578. 'ln Spin 401 persons have crossed the century limit, in France 213, in England 145, in Germa.ny'7B, in Scotland 4E, in Norway 23, in Sweden 10. in Belgium 6, and in Denmark 2. There is however, in Moscow, a man who claims to he something more than a centenarian, for according to a Russian newspaper he has ,reachedl39 years of age. His eyesight is undimmed, his hearing good, and he is a splendid pedestrian, so the Russian parOr says. There is an excellent method whereby to use up odd pieces of soap. Make a small 'flannel' bag, leave one end open, and when a few have accumulated sew up the opening and an excellent bath bag is evolved. As only pure soaps of reliable make ought tote used it pays to utilise every scrap. Potato Biscuits.—Take half a poznel,of cooked pota- toes, rub them through a wire seive add to them one pound ofteur, and a little salt. Put two ounces of dripping into a saucepan, melt, and add enough to mix the flour etc.te a paste sufficiently stiff to roll out easily. Turn the paste on to a floured board, knead well, roll to an eiehtae of an inch thick and stamp out rounds the BiZ9 of a teacup. Bake a pile isrown in a moderate oven. " MADGE ."
