div.head: BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: THE BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT.

' At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting l'Committee it was resolved that a plan showing the line of frontage on the west side of Bridge-st fram Rylands- street to Market-gate be signed and deposited. The CHWARMAN, in moving the a.deption of these minutes, said that it was provided on this plan that the average width of the street would be 80 feet, and it was very necessary that they should pass this resolution, as it would enable the Town Clerk or the committee to act in any case which might come before them when it was necesgary to interfere and make the line in the street. In case they thought it necessary to make any altera- tions in property it was very necessary that they should be in a position to define the line of streets. Councillor SHAw GREEN suggested that they should postpone this matter and bring it up at the end of the business when the question of street improvement was to be considered in committee. This suggestion was adopted. The rest of the minutm; were comfirmed. LOCAL SUCCESS.

'ln movinc, the adoption of the minutes of the Museum and Technical Instruction Committee, Councillor RnEERTS menthned that there had been some satisfac- tory ,riccesses in both the art and science classes. The elaq., which only commenced last season, had qucct-ssful one of the students obtain- medal offered to the whole country. Two r tç Co,lncil exhibitions had been secured and also a br.ot.z,i medal in the art section. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Council would be pleased that the successes which had characterised the work of the committee for several years were still maintained. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: ELECTRIC LIGHTING.
div.p: THE ELECTRIC LIGHTING.

Councillor HEATON in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Gas Committee remarked that it would be seen that the Chairman had been requested to bring the question of electric lighting before toe General Purposes Committee, and he had no doubt he would do so. Councillor BENNETT said he cordially congratulated the committee upon their prompt acceptance of the sugges- tion he made at a recent meeting with regard to electric lighting. He hone] that before very long they would have a very desirable improvement in Warrington in that respect. Councillor ROGERS asked for an explanation why the committee had entered into arrangements with the Lan- cashire Asylums Board to supply gas at 2s. 91 per 1,000 feet? He contended that if any one was entitled to a reduction it was the workingman. The Towls CLERK : Allow me to explain that the price is the same that a person consuming the same quantity of cas in the borough would have to pay. Councillor ROGERS : But they are not in the borough, and they are a rich board and well able to pay. The Tnwrq CLERK It is a public body. Councillor HEATON said t.,e Board would be a very important customer, and they could afford to pay. T'ne Asylums' Committee intended to make their own gas. Public bodies were not private individuals, and he con- sidered that the Gas Committee had done a very proper thing in securing such good customers. The Corpora- tion had obtained a sum of £2OO towards the eost of ex- tending the main. The minutes were then agreed to.
"THE HORRIBLE STENCH AT WILDERSPOOL." RUNCORN PEOPLE TO BLAME.

Councillor ROBERTS moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Rivers' Committee which had resolved that the Manchester Ship Canal Company be urged to proceed forthwith with the construction of the penstock in the new road over the disused portion of the Mersey. He remarked that the company had a certain time given to them in which to construct the penstock, but the committee was endeavouring to get it done earlier if possible. Councillor Murex seconded the adoption of the minutes. Alderman FRANCOME said he was very pleased that the Committee were doing something to cure the horrible stench at Wilderspool. Two months ago they were promised a sewer from Wilderspocil to St. James' Church, and a® take the sewage out of that part of the river. The work was not done, and the following month they were in the same position, and at the present time they were as far off abating the nuisance as ever. He had seen the Town Clerk within the last few days, and he had told him that the Runcorn authorities would net sign the agreement, whereas, on the other hand, Mr. Brandreth had told him (Alderman Francornb) that the Town Clerk of Warrington had not •kept to his agreement. Whilst these two great authorities were ,quarrelling the people of Wilderspool were being poisoned alive. His own house at the present time was like a hospital, as every- one in it had sore throats, and the whole neighbourhood was in the same condition. Some strong pressure ought to be brought to boar upon the Runcorn authoritiesto do something to relieve the people of the horrible stench there. Councillor Woons said he could fully realise the condi- tion of things at Wilderspool on account of the nuisance arising from tne river. Mere was no need to go to Wilderspool, he could smell it from his bedroom in San- key-st., and the smell was simply disgusting in Bold-st. Th smell was carried to the centre ot the town, and he thoueht such a condition of things should be remedied for the health of the inhabitants. Cciuncillor SHAW GREEN' said the matter was a very serious one, and after the manner in which Alderman Francomh had put it,and the repudiation on the part of the Runcorn authorities, he thought the Town Clerk should tell them publicly where tne bitch realty was.

Councillor HEATON said the committee wanted a Dro- ver agreement fur their money, and they were quite justified in acting as they were now, whatever the con- sequences might be. They were not responsible. They must have the money before thny could spend it, Alderman FRANCOMB : That is speaking without feel— ing. I should like to hear what the Town Clerk has to say. This is ton serious a matter to wrap up. The TOWN CLERK : There is nothing to wrap up. Alderman FRANCOMB : lam not referring to you; I am referring to the people of Ttuncorn. Councillor Ilnkron : But you put it as if this Council were to blame. The TOWN CLERK said when the negotiations were in progress with regard to the borough bounda.rr,which ,was to include Stockton Heath, he met the Runcorn people the night before the Local Government Board inquiry,and it was agreed what the terms should be. But in drafting the terms of :the agreement, counsel .made a mistake and words were used which did not ,carry out the agreement. He (the Town Clerk) altered the agreement to carry out what was actually decided ,•upon but the Runcorn people would not new sign it. He ' was determined not to give way to.them. Tin was sorry the delay had taken place but it had been causcd by he •Runcoro people. Councillor LEE said he understood from the Town Clerk that he had come to terms with Colonel Ashton, clerk for the Runcorn Authority, with reference to the sewer.

--The Towx CLERK : Yes, terms were come to, and the agreement drawn up. It was sent for signature but he '(Mr. Whittle) got a telegram from Colonel Ashton saying the Runcorn people would not sign it. 'Councillor SHAW GREEN: It is a very serious matter? The TOWN CLERK: Yes, it is. _ _

Councillor ROBERTS said with regard to the discussion raised ,bv Alderman Francomb it was really not a matter for the River's Committee. But he (Councillor Roberts) was not sorry it had been raised bee tUqA it would enable the Council to feel the responsibility that they all laboured under with regard to their duty to the unfor - tunate people living near to the old portion of the river. Although they oil regretted the nuisance, at the same time it ras hardly fair to expect the Corporation to take upon itself a position which might make it solely re- sponsible for the expense of the drain which it was pro- posed to lac' down. He did not wish to say one word wiaieh might te in any sense likely to strain the friendly relations which had existed uri to now between Runcorn and themselves.and he did not think any member of the Council would wish to de so, and they must, therefere, walk a little warily until the matter was settled. They might safely leave any question of law in the hands of the Town C!erk. (Hear,hear.) If the Town Clerk felt an advantage was attempted to he taken on a technical omission from the first terms of the agreement he was justified ia standing o it until what were really the term: of the agreement morally, were howier)hly carried out. As far as the River Committee were concerned they were determined to give what assistance they could to purify the old river. They were not a Health Committee, but they were anxious to

work in conjunction with the Health Committer. This was certainly a most serious matter, as one heArd or; 311 hands of a class of sor, throat a hich was being called the " Ship Canal throat" for want of a better nt•firlition. It was undoubtedly attributable, accordin:z to the ined - cal men,to the impurities which were given off by the Ship Canal, the old river and the river itself. Where they formerly had one stream they now had three and conse4uently they were three times worse in bad smells. The CHAIRMAN said he thought it should be mak) clearly known that neither the Council nor the Town Clerk were responsible. The Town Clerk had submitted the agreements and as the Runcorn people had refused to signlit, they were responsible. The Committee's minute was then passed.
THE FIRE BRIGADE CONGRATULATED.
OUTSIDE INTERFERENCE: LIVELY DISCUSSION.

Alderman HUTCHINSON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Fire Engine Committee including a new article from the Warrington Order, 1896, with reference to cohducting the brigade in case of fires, a copy of which was given in our last issue. He alluded to the duties of the Superintendent of the Fire Brigade, and remarked that it was necessary that lawlessness should be pit down at a fire. The police had given the brigade great help in the past in preserving order, and it was hoped they would continue to do so. He was sure the brigade would be pleased to acquit themselves in manner which would reflect credit upon them and upon their Superintendent. Mr. Turner was called before the committee at the last meeting and congratu- lated upon the very efficient manner in which he and his staff worked in extinguishing the recent fire in Bridge-st. (Hear, hear.) The committee were adver- tising for additional firemen, and they hoped soon to have the brigade in a very efficient condition. Counoillor SMETHURST seconded the motion.
Alderman BOLTON: Will the Superintendent have power to order the police off? The arrangement looks rather one-sided.
Alderman HurcanisoN : We expect the police to as- sist us. _ _ _

Alderman BOLTON: But the article sacs "it any per- son shall wilfully obstruct he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding £5." The CFIAIRMAN : But we don't suppose a police officer will wilfully obstruct. Councillor Tienewei said he was glad that the Fire Engine Committee had seen their way to congratulate the brigade on the manner in which they worked at the fire at Mr. Daiatith's premises. The fire brigade had been a sort of mark for anyone to have a shot at, and it was only fair now that they had acquitted themselves well that they should have the credit, and that the Council should acknowledge it. He thought by adopt- ing the new articles the fire brigade would in future be able to combat fires in a much better way than formerly. Ile thought it was not so much the fire brigade which had been to blame, but the public, who had interfered with them. He hoped there would be no friction be- tween the police and the firemen under the new arrange- ments, and that they would be carried out in a proper spirit. Councillor SHAW Gum; said he believed it was only fair to repeat an observation whicb was made by one of the assessors who came down from the Insurance com- panies. He was a man who had had a large experience of fires, and he remarked that it was almost a miracle that the fire was confined to such a small area, and the fire brigade were to be congratulated in keeping the fire within the limits they did. (Hear, hear.) He would like to ask whether the Superintendent had not formerly been in full charge at fires ? The CHAIRMAN : There have been complaints. Counciller ROSERTS said there had been some criticism , in the Town Council—and it had been very vigorous in days gone by—about the operations <if the fire brigade, and probably the new regulations were the outcome of it. If the committee had realised the necessity of cen- tralizing the power of the authority for the time being in the heal of the brigade it was no doubt a very sensible decision, which every member of the Council would sup- port. As one of those who had not hesitated to speak warmly In the past in adverse criticism of the conduct of the brigade, be did not think he would be fair in that matter if he did not congratulate them new upon the manner in which they worked on that particular occas- ion. It did not do to be constantly kicking people, and when they turned over a new leaf they ought to be as ready to recognise that fact as they were to recognise it to the contrary. (Hear. hear.) Councillor BENNETT added a word of congratulation to the fire brigade for their work at the recent fire. Councillor WOODS: As another who has criticised the fire brigade,and the only one present who saw the fire— The CHAIRMAN: Did you interfere? Councillor WOODS: I had more sense. Continuing, he taid he went there with the object of assisting in the saving of life,and he appreciated all the fire brigade had done. He advised the committee to have the fire escape taken to any fire there was in any house more than two storios high. He saw what took place and saw the danger that the family were in, and he felt what would have happened if it had been Alderman Blackhurst's or his (Mr. Woods') shop on fire. If the fire took place be- hind the shop,they could not get out except through the window. He quite agreed that one or more of the escapes should be in an accessible place in the centre of the town. They would be run to the scene of the fire and preveat the possibility of an accident by a woman jumping through the window when there was no neces- sity for it. He was told that the new escape was in Warrington, and was not brought out. Ho thought it should have been brouzht out as it wmuld have been a. good opportunity of testing it. All he could say in refer- ence to the remarks that had been made about the people interfering were entirely wrong. He could not forget the work the police had done. The private de- tectives were on the spot ten minutes after the bell was rung, but he could not say there was the same prompt- ness in getting up steam. It was about twenty minutes before the engine was working. Councillor SMETHURST stated that complaints had been made to the committee that some members of the Coun- cil interfered with the fire trigade.—Voice " Name."— Councillor Woods was one. _

Councillor Woorm (interrupting the speaker) : It is a deliberate lie. I say it publicly. I heard this was com- ing on, and this is the reason I am here, though I am not 'fit to be here. lam here to protest against the charge that has been made against me. Councillor Smethurst is the one who interfered in the other fire. I strongly object to what he has said. The CIILIRMAN:: But if you are satisfied- Councillor WOODS: lam satisfied I did my duty and did not interfere. The CIIAIRMLNI I think you could afford to let those remarks pass by if you are sati-fied that you did not interfere. It is not a matter for discussion.

C.,unciltor SMISTRIIRST The report came from the superintendent of the fire brigade, and if we cannot rely upon what he has to say then I think it is high time we "chucked " up our positions as members of the Fire Engine Committee altogether. The Superintendent reported to me and the Chairman of the committee that Councillor Woods ran up the street with his arm.; raised above his head endeavouring to stop the Saperintendent with his hese. If that is not interfering I don't know what is. The CHATametr-: Hearsay evidence is not of much valise.

_ Councillor SMBTIII7IIBT -: But we have the evidence of our Superintendent, and if we can't rely upon what he says- Councillor Efiwrow: If the resolution is left over this sort of interference will not occur af.Tain, and Coun- cillor Woods and every other member of the Council will know that he must not interfere in the future.
--Councillor Smwnionsr 1 That is all very well, but am on my feet--
Councillor ROBERTS IC is quite obvious. (Laughter.

Councillor SMETHURST: t tiave as mnch right to speak as anyone else. I feet the resolution is a very im- portant one. If it is carried out we shall have to sum- mon such men as Councillor Woods and Alderman Wright. It is very hard lines if a man is to be locked up if he does not go away when he is rendering a service. Councillor SUAW GREaNI Who is going to be locked up? Councillor Smwraustsr 1 Two or three of pm& (Laughter.) At the same time, lam pleased to hear the kind remarks that have been made with reference to the efficient manner in which the brigade discharged their duties at the recent fire. With regard to the fire escape we did not know at the time that it had arrived. Councillor WOODS explained that he simply put up bis hands to show the Superintendent and the Dremen where the fire plug was, and if that was to be looked upon as a diabolical interference with firemen and a steam fire engine he should be regarding himself as a Samson. (Laughter.) The GRUBMAN : I think the resolution on the agenda will do away with any misunderstanding at fires. Alderman HIITCEIINSON said the fire escape had only just arrived, and they had arranged for a gentleman to come over and instruct the firemen as to its use. With respect to the fire plugs, it was unnecessary for anyone to show the Superintendent where they were in Bridge- st. or in any of the principal streets. He was perfectly fami:ar with them. The minutes were then p.ss,cl. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.— THE COUNTY COUNCIL GRANT. WARRINGTON UNFAIRLY TREATED.

The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the G.lnei al Purposes Committee's minutes,which contained a resolu- tion tint the County Council having refused to allow the payment of various items amounting in the whole to £335 from the Technical Instruction Estimates for 1896-7, it was resolved that the deficiency be made up out of the rates. Alderman FRLNOOIIII seconded.

Councillor ROBERTS with the permits:ion of the Coun- cil explained why it had been necessary to request the Corporation to make good the deficiency en the Techni- cal Instruction account. He stated that during the first two years of the establishment of technical schools, the committee sui mitted estimates to the County Cows- 4 cil, and those estimates were adopted by them without ' comment. When they came to the session Zof 1891-5 the County Council submitted an agreement in which the committee bound themselves to spend the grant ! made by the County Council in accordance witn the ! Technical Instruction Act. The committee did not an- ticipate that there would be any deviation from those terms. When they submitted their estimates, to their intense astonishment the accounts for the previons year which had to be sent up to the County Coucil after hav- ing been passed, were sent back to them with items amounting to £242 struck out and brought to their debit. He had only got to say that the agreement under which their operations in the sessions 18941-5 and 1895-6 required the committee to spend the money in accordance with the Technical Instruction Act, and the terms permitted them to spend it in the way they had done. The County Council it seemed had adopted certain rules for dealing with technical instruc- tion authorities of smaller size than Warrington. The Corporation of Warrington he might say was the largest subordinate authority in the jurisdiction of the County Council,in fact Warrington was the largest non-county borough in England. That being so, they had an equit- able right to ask that the grant made to Warrington should be on the same terms and conditions upon which boroughs which were county boroughs received their grants. But the County Council had treated them all along the line as if they were of no greater Importance than such places as Earlestown, Newton, Leigh, Widnes, and other places smaller in size and in rateable value than Warrington was. He was not going to blame the County Council as a whole, but the pettifogging and mean manner with which the Technical Instruction Committee of the Ccunty Council had dealt with Warrington was beyond words which he could find to express it. 'The Warrington committee were disgusted. The accounts for 1894 and Mt did not come back to them until they were well advanced in 1896, and the Council would see how impos- sible it was to make the accounts tally. The County Council not only required that the estimate of 1896 7 should be ia accordance with the agreement entered into but also required that it should be in accordance with the agreement and rules which had been framed by them for dealing with smaller authorities. They would not allow them to charge certain establishment charges against their ac- count. When be reminded the Council that they were entitled to £BOO a year, and of the further fact that their grant had been reduced by the County Council to a little over £5OO, and a portion of this grant had been further interfered with by the fact that they refused ta pay certain establishment charges which they allowed in the first two years, the Council would see what an awkward position they had been placed in. They were not only deprived of £3OO a year to which they were en- titled, but they were also not allowed to; spend the reduced grant in the same way as they were allowed in the first two years, which was unreasonable. The com- mittee had the management of the School of Art, and before it became the property of the Corporation there were certain establishment charges. Be did not mean in the shape of rent but in cleaning, iightiog,and warm- ing. Those were charges which were inevitable in the control of any institution. But the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council refused them the payment of a penny for those establishment charges. The position was becoming intolerable,and the commit- tee did consider whether they should stop the whole con- cern and throw the responsibility upon the County Council or continue as well as they could, asking the as- sistance of the Corporation to help them out of the diffi- culty until they might claim to be a county borough. The committee shrank from stopping an institution so successful and one which had done such good ;work dur- ing the past four years. Nor did they like to entertain the idea of disbanding their staff and sending their scholars to the four winds of heaven in order to get over the difficulty. They hoped the representations they had made to the Cc unty Council would some day take effect. They found that the money which rightly belonged to Warrington was going into the agricultural districts, which were very well supplied. Special inducements were offered to farmers' sons in order that they might be educated in agriculture, whilst the students in War- rington had to do the best they coulci for themselves. It was also a fact that a place like Preston, which was a county borough, and which had net applied a penny to technical instruction, hut to the reduction fits rates had received one sum of £l,OOO from the County Coun: cil, a moiety of which was contributed from Warrington The whole position was one which he felt himself impos. Bible to describe. The committee had to throw themselves upon the consideration of the Council—when they ought not to need a penny if their equitable p.isition was con _ sidered—rather than allow their work of technical in. struction in Warrington to be disbanded. The Cumestart said he had not the slightest. doubt that the action of the County Council would induce Warring- ton to apply for itself to become a county borough as soon as possible. Councillor SHAW GREEN expressed his gratitude to Councillor Roberts for the explicit way he had put the position before the Council. He had put the mater to them very forcibly and shown to them how inequitable ; was the action of the County Council, that he did not think the members of the Council would refuse to grant I the amount asked for under the circumstances. They had carried out the agreement with the County Council to the letter, and although the County Council had laid down certain ruletethey had not kept to those rules din- inc the two preceding years. Councillor Roberts and himself went to Preston and explained to the County Council Committee the difference between a small rural ; area such as Winwick or neighbourtng townships and Warrhagton, and pointed out to them that the rules in existence for these small agricultural districts were in. ▪ applecable to a small town like Warrington. But they a were told that the charges were too high and that they a had no right to claim them. They went felly into the ; matter with the committee but they had to come away ; disappointed, and felt that there was no sympathy with urban authorities. The County Conned's sympathy ; was with the rural districts and they were offering 10s. , a week to induce farmers' sons to he instructed in avi- culture. Why should not the County Council give War- rington 103. a week for their tanning students ? Or why should not the youths at their iron works in War- rington be offered that amount to attend the metallur- gical school at Wigan ? He thought it was just as reasonable that they should have the same advesstages r as those living in the districts outside. At present War- • rins.,ten had to spend £5OO in order to get a grant of 1 £3OO. But they couli nut !itnp an institution whieh sees

dom. such a vast amount of gond, and the committes sinrQrelv hoped that the money asked for would be granted. Alderman BOLTON hoped that in future the Technical Instruction Cnmmittee would submit their estimates to
the Council seeing that some of the money was to come mit of the rates, and let the Council have a voice in the

• spending, af the money. Councillor TINNION said as one interested in the gym- nasium he was exceedingly pleased to hear that the negotiations with reference to its transfer to the Corpora- tion had at last corns to a satisfactory conclusion. He did not know what the scheme for the future was to be, but he had sufficient faith in their Town Clerk to know that it would he a scheme for the best interests of the institution. (Hear, hear.) He might say that it had been suffering from the fact that it had been short of money. It had been a usefulinstitution in the past, and now that it was in the hands of the Corpo.ation he believed it would do a still greater amount of good in the future. He was one of those who believed in the advan- tages of athletics of all kinds, and he hoped a committee would be formed to take the management in hand. Councillor ROBERTS in reply said the question which had been raised by Alderman holton was a reasonable one, and one the Committee would agrm to and carry out. The Committee did not want to continuo to beg money from the Council, and if they reviveci what rightly belonged to them they would not have to ask the Council for anything. The OFIAIRMAN said with regard to the Committee of management for the Gymnasium, the subj?ct would he considered by the GenEral Purposes Committee at the next meeting.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

Traffic has been well maintained during the past week the number of ocean-going vessels using the waterway having been 79. Of these 44 were arrivals and 35 de- partures. Fereign traffic accounted for 21 arrivals and 12 outward sailings, whilst of vessels sailing coastwise 23 entered and 23 left the canal. On Saturday ships were in dock loading for London, Belfast, Dublin, Barcelona, Brazil, Bombay, China and Japan, Paris, Antwerp, St. Petersburg, and Hamburg, whilst other! were discharging carg,e from the Mediterranean,London, Mobile, Bristol, Laguna, and elsewhere. The prosoecta of a heavy cotton season, both of the American mid the Egyptian staple, are bright, and ample arrangementS have been made for frequent sailinc,,s both from the Gulf ports and New Torkiand also,from Alexandria. It will proqablv be some time in October before the first consignment of the new season's cotton is received. It is announced that in response to a demand for an early sailing the Knutsford will be berthed at New Orleans, where she is doe OR the 5h prox. The Lucina is due at New Orleans ten days later, and will follow the Routs- ford to Manchester. According to a statement prepared ' by the canal authorities,on a representative carg0,3,022 tons, of cotton and grain from New Orleans last season, over £735 was saved by shipping to Manchester as com- pared with the cost via Liverpool. This averages 43.104 d per ton.

It is estimated that within the Turkish Massacres last six or Bevan days no fewer than 5,000 or 6,000 more Arnonian: have been foully murdered in Turkey. Tbia11:t?01 massacre of defenceless Christians by farla Mohammedans did not take place among the mountains of Armenia or in any Par,t of the inland and scarcely accessible Par!, of Asia Minor, but actually in the street ef Constantinople and under the eyes ° the representatives of the English and other European Governments and under the guns of the small war vessels which are attached to the en bassies. Yet there was practically no effectO interference with the emissaries of the Sultsl3' They were permitted for hour after hour to 1111_,St the poor Armenians from their shelterlB6 places and to brain their victims with clubs or t° hack them to pieces with knives in broad daylight' Some most vivid and shocking accounts of tlie wholesale slaughter are given by various eorreet, pondents. The Servian Minister at the Turkl9 capital writes that although hardened by what he ' had experienced in his life as a soldier, in Const: tinople " with his own eyes he saw scenes of silus. fiendish bestiality: that his nerves gave vrtr. 'Armenians of rank who were driving in a carrieF through Galata were surrounded by the 111°Ilt strangled and cut to pieces. Hundreds of Arra° ian women girls and boys were outraged and after wards killed." Another pathetic incident is thus late. Three boys and a girl of a noble Armenia?, family were being taken to a boat when some Tin ish softas noticed them aid gave chase. A violelle struggle took place between the boatmen and the Turks, but in spite of the heartrending cries of Oa children the softas did not stop until the craft alit the little ones were buried beneath the waves° the Bosphorus. One young Englishman who 119:e.. been for some years engaged in Constantinople commercial pursuits writes home to his par°o°. that he could hear from the stores in which b was engaged " the terrible screams of the Armen; inns, chased through the streets like hares, the howling of the ferocious mob as the battered to death their victims." " The streeto he adds, "are like shambles, bodies taken awe9l wagons dripping with blood on the way to th.l cemeteries, leaving the road marked with the trll of death. Crossing Galata Bridge I saw dried 1190 pools of blood, showing that the poor creature had been hacked to pieces and bled to death v.° their wounds." Such are:the scenes which e been enacted at Constantinople at the very t 11330 the precious "Concert of Europe" is supposed be devising methods for protecting the Christi% subjects of the Sultan. The Turkish Governnieoilf has shown its defiance of the Christian nations a, Europe:by tolerating this massacre, and, dition to this, evidence is accumulating fro' for many sides to show that a diabolical plot ad the further destruction of Armenians bilis actually been concocted by the Sultan and sl4 advisers. The immediate cause of the outbre was an attack upon the Ottoman Bank by an °lse band of twenty or twenty-five men under the Oar of Armenians. As, soon as these men had co tured the Bank bombs were thrown ana Ater appears to have been the signal for the slant, to begin. Turks of the lowest class had neje brought into Constantinople, from the Asle'the side of the Bosphorus, and as soon 88 ocl bombs wen exploded hundreds of Turks into the streets,armed with clubs,knives and They were assisted in their fearful work hlll, soldiers and police, and by Kurds and Laz,ase hills had committed similar atrocities amongst t'
and vales of Armenia.je thig The question that is now being asked to country is, how long is Lord SALISBURY Vil4;ted tolerate this sort of thing? It is that the Sultan has formed a deliberate 13"—

ftterminate all the male Armenians in his domi- The fate of the females and children may be Surmised but cannot be described. Is this atro- tolls Ruler to be allowed to complete his dread- N. Schemes? England is in a special sense pledged to protect the Christians of Turkey, but, apart al- tc,gether from diplomatic responsibilities, Lord S4LISBURY surely does not propose that the People of this country should stand aside while a /?. hole nation is beihg exterminated simply because It is Christian. Our Government does not shrink from force when a Sultan of Zanzibar or a King of 4shantee has to be dealt with, but as yet it has ithown little else than weakness in dealing with kore powerful offenders. The writer from Con- stantinople whose letter we have quoted, speaking lor the British residents says "we blush with Shame for being Englishmen, and feel humiliated 411 d dishonoured."

A LONDON newspaper has Conscience Money. been gathering some more or less interesting information With regard to "conscience:money." It appears that the Imperial Exchequer is annually some £2,000 Or 523,000 the richer owing to the uneasy con- Rciences of people who have in one way or another defrauded the public revenue. Many people, it leeins, have an invincible objection against setting forth the full amount of their earnings upon iecome-tax papers and as a consequence they benefit at the expense of the public. In some cases, however, after years have rolled on, there comes a sudden fit of repentance and reisiorse and a cheque or a registered letter is sent to the Treasury containing a sum of money which is estimated to cover all arrears. The income-tax is the greatest source of conscience money, and after that comes the custom dues, but many little sums are also obtained in connection with the evasion of taxes on the wearing of armorial bear- ings, the keeping of servants or carriages or dogs. It is neeciless to say that the conscience-stricken Party rarely or never puts in a personal appear- ance at the offices of the Inland Revenue Com- kissioners. When the money is surrendered per- eonally it is generally a third party who hands it over. He often, it is true, has a surprisingly close acquaintance with all Use circumstances of the case, but as he persists la asserting that he is only acting on behalf of a.friend, he is not troubled with too many ques- tions. The Treasury officials take the sensible and Philosophic view that they are receiving money Which could only be obtained through the volun- tary action of the offending party, and they do not throw unnecessary obstacles in the way. Clergy- teen in not a few instances act as the go-between Members of their flock come to them with the confession that they had sadly under-stated their incomes on such and such occasions, or that whilst returning from a pleasure trip they smuggled through certain dutiable articles, and ask them to forward the amount necessary to cover the lapses from straightforward dealing. This, of course, the obliging cleric unelertakes to do and the Trea- -41117 is, therefore, so much the richer. It has been 'laid that "conscience does make cowards of us "but it has also been discovered that in refer- %ce to the particular kind of omissions or cora- 121issions referred to conscience,does not as a rule effectually operate till after many years. It has been found that people who are making up their last accounts with this world are the largest con- tributors of" conscience money." "They want to depart with a clean slate—and they remember the Chancellor of the Exchequer."

A pleasing incident took place at the meeting of the Runcorn School Board Tuesday. The Clerk,Mr Moss, had in attendance two blind children,inmates• Of schools in Liverpool, for similarly afflicted child- ren and the School Board members kindly had the ithildren in the room. On being questioned they iloth showed signs of average intelligence and evi- lently appreciated the kindly interest the Board took in them. An impromptu collection was levied Itlod the children left with sufficient small change to keep them in lollipops for at least a month.

The recent fire at the Runcorn Workhouse will not cost the ratepayers anything owing to the fore- sight of the Guardians who have the premises fully ensured. Mr. Aaron raised the point at the last Meeting as to the best method of dealinglwith fires Vhicil may break out at that institution. Luckily for the Board the one that has recently taken place Was caught in time, for had it obtained a strong hold, the house would have had to go. Though there ore fire appliances at the house there is,it is alleged, tif) sufficient supply of water so that even a fire brigade would be helpless if anything in the shape of a serious outbreak took place. The Guardians Would do well to look into the matter.

Dr. Gastaldi is trying, through the School Board, ta have set up in the town a system of advanced or ascondary education. So far as this goes it is all right. but Dr. Gastaldi goes further and says that the institution when started will be self-supportin g Here is where there may be some difference 13f opinion. While education is indeed the strongest factor in our daily life we do not think in Runcorn there will be many parents desirous of sending their children for further edu- cation after they have complied with the laws of the school Board. The children who would go to School go elsewhere as Dr. Gastaldi pointed out, but fees from that class of scholar together with the grants they might earn would not make a second- ary school self-supporting. The difficulty is to get the children to school now-a-days up to a reason- able age, as parents are so very anxious to get their

eons well-placed in situation where they can help the bread-winner to provide for the children rising after them. A secondary school might be started but there will be an additional burden cast on the rateplyers. _

PROSPECTING FOR NEW WORKS AT RUNCORN. On Thursday a gentleman representing a firm of soap makers visited Runcorn and examined the town with a view to finding a suitable site for new works. Mr. Welding, the surveyor to the District Council, placed facilities before the visitor, and accompanied him in Lis search.

SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN. On Wednesday a number of teachers and officers con- nected with this institution had a picnic to Frodsham. The weather was fine though dull and an enjoyable afternoon was spent. The journey there and back was made in vehicles supplied by Messrs. Booth and Son. REGISTRATION OF VOTERS AT RUNCORN AND DISTRICT. Notices are out calling attention to the fact th tt the Revising Barrister, Mr. D. A. V. Colt Williams, will hold a revision court on Thursday, October Ist, for Runcorn and District. Trie districts included are the Aston-by. Sutton, Halton, Runcorn North, Runcorn South, and Wiston polling districts. The court will sit in the magistrates' court house, Runcorn. RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. The Committee have decided to hold their first annual prize distribution on Friday, the 18th inst., and Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P., has been asked to perform that duty. The British Association meetings will be held in Liver- pool the same week, and an endeavour will be made by the local committee to secure some prominent member of that body to address the Runcorn meeting on science and art subjects. On Friday morning about 11 o'clock Miss Mary Dut- ton of 3 Victoria-road, sustained very serious injuries by ' falling from the back bedroom window. Miss Dutton was engaged in cleaning the windows when ehe wa3 seized with a fit of dizziness and fell from the window, backwards, into the yard. Dr. Ormesbv who was promptly called found her suffering from scalp and other wounds of a serious nature.

A FOOTBALL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. A rather severe accident occurred to a juvenile devotee to the football game on Wednesday night in Runcorn. Joseph Powell, a schoolboy, was playing football with other boys on the fair ground when he slipped and an her boy fell on him. Through the fall the lad's arm was broken. P.C. Nicholls who happened to be in the vicinity rendered first aid and set the injured limb tem- porarily after which the lad was taken to his home in Sutherland-street. RUNCORN „WORKMEN's EXCURSION. On Saturday last Messrs. Earp and Company gave their workmen and wives an excursion, the place selected being Southport where a substantial dinner and tea were provided. A thoroughly enjoyable day was spent. After dinner the health of Mr. Earl) and family was proposed by Mr. Hollingworth, ably seconded by Mr. Sandbach, and a vote of thanks to Mr. Jones, the manager, for the admirable arrangements he had made for the trip, was also cordially passed. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. The choir held their annual social evening on Wednes- day. The proceedings commenced with an excellently served tea, and was followed by a miscellaneous pro- gramme. Mr. A. Robinson led off with "A warrior bold," in his usual style. Mrs. Temperley followed with the song "Annie Laurie." and was encored. Mr. T. Parry gave a reading entitled "The man with a bald head," which elicited much laughter. Mr. M. Thomas favoured the company with the song "Hearts and homes," after which a mandolin and pianoforte duet was contributed by the Misses Warburton. Mr. and Mrs. C. Leathwood rendered the duet entitled "The singing lesson," and were recalled. Mr. F. Littler gave a humorous recitation, entitled "The perils of contradic- tion," and the programme was brought to a close by Mr. A. Robinson rendering a mandolin solo with piano accompaniment. There was also a speaking competi- Mon, Mrs. Temperley and Mr. Thomas dividing the first prize. Fruit was distributed during the evening, and games were afterwards indulged in. Mr. J. Richardson presided, and Miss Warburton acted as accompanist. HALTON-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. The annual choir sermons in connection with the above church were held on Sunday, when the Rev. W. Arrowsmith, one time of the Runcorn circuit, preached two appropriate addresses. The evening service was particularly well-attended and the rev, gentleman's dis- course based upon the words " Who touched my clothes" was closely followed by his auditors. During the services special hymns and anthems were admirably rendered by the choir. In the morning Miss C. Taylor sang" But the Lord is mindful of His own" (Mendels- shon) with fine effect; while the choir rendered the an- , theme " I will sing of Thy power" (Sullivan),and "Like as a father pitieth his own children" (Balton). In the evening four anthems were given by the choir. Miss C. Taylor gave a beautiful rendering of the " The Better Land," and the solo in the anthem was taken by Mr. R. Yates. On the conclusion of the service Sullivan's "Say, Watchman "was given with marked effect, in memory of the Rev. C. de P. Gliddon. Collections amounting to over £lO were taken. RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB. —IMPORTANT RAGES.

On Saturday last the Runcorn Cycling Club brought off a ten mile road race for which six competitors were started by Messrs. Mundy and Stubbs. After some good travelling the following results were returned :-Ist,W. Wray (10 minutes start), time 34 minutes; 2nd, R. Wellington (10 minutes start), time 351 minutes ; 3rd,C. Peacock (4 minutes start), time 31± minntes ; 4th, J. Charlesworth (2 minutes start), time 311 minutes. Medals were presented to the first, second and third. The course lay over a good road slightly up-hill and the weather was favourable to fast riding. The judges were Messrs. Wellington and Flindley. On Wednesday a 25 mile road race took place for which there were seven starters, the results supplied being as follows :—Fastest time, G. Whingates (scratch) time 1 hour 26 minutes ; Ist, S.Webster (1 minutes start),time 1 hour 27 minutes; 2nd, W. Wray (5 minutes start),time 1 hour 31 minutes; 3rd, J. Cbarlesworth (21 minutes start), time 1 hour minutes. Mr. Whingates takes a gold medal for the fastest time, and silver medals with gold centres were given to the first, second and third men in. The judges and starters were Messrs. Mundy and Rushton. RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB COTTAGE HOSPITAI7 FIINTI.

On Sunday last the band of the 2nd (E.C.) V.B. Cheshire Regiment gave a aacred concert on Runcorn Hill. The concert was held under the auspices of the Runcorn Cycling Club and should have taken place the previous Sunday. The weather on that date was so bad i that the committee deemed it advisable to postpone the concert until last Sunday when it took place under very favourable circumstances. There was a good attend- ance and the programme was greatly appreciated by those present. The concert was opened by the hymn "0 God our help in ages past," and was followed by the grand march " Tannhauser " (Wagner) ; selection from Weber's Mass in G ; cornet solo "The Soul's Awakening" (Haddock) ; selection from " alevy's Works ;" intermezzo from Cavalleria, Rusticana (Mas- cagni) ; Kyrie and Gloria, Mozart's 12th Mass, conclud- ing with the hymn " Lead kindly Light." The band was conducted by Sergeant T. Outhwaite. Collections were made on behalf of the Cottage Hospital Fund the following being a list of the individual efforts of the col- lectors :—Mr. W. H. div.head: SAD DROWNING CASE AT WESTON POINT.
div.p: SAD DROWNING CASE AT WESTON POINT.
INQUEST.

Mr. Wereley held an inquest in the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on the body of Thomas Henry Stevenson, who was found drowned in the Weston canal on Tuesday night.—Rebecca Stevenson,wife of Richard Stevenson, of South-road, Weston, labourer on the canal,said deceased was her son, and was 7i years old. He went out about 3-30 on Tuesday, and did not say where he was going. The next she heard of him was from a boy named Poole, who told one of her children that her son was in the canal. That was about 5-30. She went to the canal side and saw them grappling for the boy. He had been accus- tomed to fishing in the canal, and she had beaten him several times for going on the canal side.—Alfred Poole, a boy residing with his mother at Weston Point,said he saw the boy who was drowned oatching fish in the canal at Weston. Deceased was standing on the bank, and he slipped in. There was no one about. He told Harry Myers and the mother of deceased ,hut did not know how long it was after deceased tell in the canal.—Frederick Myers, a clerk, said he saw a crowd of people on the canal side and he got grapples and after a short time he recovered deceased. He thought that the body had been in the wlter at least ten minutes. He tried to restore life but could not do so.—On the advice of the Coroner a verdict of "Accidental drowning" was returned.

div.head: • F RODSHAM.
div.p: • F RODSHAM.

SuomiNo ACCIDENT.—On Friday morning shortly after ten o'clock, George Guntrip, a porter at Frc,dsham Station met with a shocking accident which ended fatally. He was closing one of the carriage doors of a train running between Ditton and Helsby when he slipped and fell between the platform and the vehicles. Though the moving train was promptly stopped it was found that the deceased had been shockingly injured, indeed one leg was completely cut from the body, while the other was almost severed. The injured man was taken at once to Chester,but his condition was such that despite every attention be succumbed the same day.— An inquest was held at the Chester General Infirmary on Saturday afternoon, by Mr. F. Turner (deputy city coroner). A verdict to the effect that deceased died from shock was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
PROPOSED HIGHER GRADE EDUCATION.

The monthly meeting of this board was held in the Town Hall Runcorn on Tuesday evening, present the chairman Mr. J. Pritchard, Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., F. J. Norman, J.P., and G. Moss (clerk).—Dr. Gastaldi moved that the District Council and the Technical Instruction Commit- tee be invited to confer with the Board on the question of the desirability of providing secondary education in the town. He thought it was their duty to provide eduriation for the children of the town as far as was consistent. Both! the Board and elementary schools were giving the best education possible and they found them vieing with each other and obtaining the best re- sults. He pointed out that many children went early to school and were able to pass their sixth standard when they were not even 12 years old and as soon as they had passed they were free and did not go to school any more. Some of these children were sent outside the town to Liverpool but the majority could not afford to de this. This therefore involved upon the Board the duty to pro- vide some kind of higher education. Another argument in favour of secondary education was that the more they educated the children the more beneficial it would be to the town in which they lived. If they looked up the statistics on the subject they would find that most of the people in prison were there simply through ignorance, and even in Scotland which was at the head of the kingdom for education and knowledge a large percentage of those in prison were uneducated. He considered the more they spread the seed of knowledge the higher would be their standard of life and he thought it was their duty to do so and by so doing they would provide—if not for this generation— for future generations a better way of living and greater happiness both to the individual and society. Mr. Norman seconded and supported Dr. Gastaldi's remarks. The resolution was then carried.
FOOTBALL PROSPECTS IT RUNCORN.

Seldom, if ever, has the Runcorn Football Club faced a new season with better prospects than it does this year. Last year the highest honours were gained by the club and this year a strong endeavour will be made to uphold the prominent position Runcorn has always taken in Rugby football circles. Daring the summer the men have been practically idle, but this week practice matches have been held and the players have stripped and returned to the sport with renewed zest. As far as can be seen at present the team this year will be pretty much the same as last year, though Myers, one of the beat backs has recently been hurt while following his employment. All the old members are available though, and while other teams have representatives scouring the country in search of new blood the Run- corn Club will maintain its prestige by the efforts of the lads who have been born, bred and brought cut in the town. The committee this year have been able to see their way to make much needed alterations in the Irwell- lane enclosure, and visitors will find considerable improvement has been made in the ground. A new turnstile has been provided at the Norfolk-street entrance and a new dressing pavilion has been erected for the players. The field has been well looked after du lag the season and the grass is distinctly stronger than it was at the latter end of last year. Saturday next will see the men taking the field in real earnest, when they will play their first engagement with the well-known Tyldesley combination. With a capital ground, a good team, and a line list of engagements the prospects of the club for the coming season are indeed rosy. Many think that the cup will be kept at this side of the bridge for at least another season, but anyway the club which wreets the cup from Captain Faulkner and his merry men well fully deserve the honour they will gain by se doing. div.head: DINNER TO THE CLUB
div.p: DINNER TO THE CLUB

- -.- On Monday evaning the members of the 4lub were entertained to dinner at the Wilson's Hotel, from the balance of the fund subscribed for the purpose of cele- brating last year's achievement of winning the Lanca- shire Cup. The chair was occupied by the President,Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C A., who was supported by Messrs. Carroll, W. Faulkner, W.E. Dudley, and J.E.Longshaw. After dinner a toast list was commenced, and convivia- lity reigned supreme until near midnight.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

This Council met at the Workhouse, 'Dutt on, on Tues- day present: Mr. John Mclntyle J.P., chairman,Messrs. Joseph Knowles, J. Weir, T. Wright, T. Lewis. J. Bran- dreth, W. Bradford, H. E. Heywood, S. Woodward, J. Derbyshire, J. B. Chadwich, E. Aaron, J. Stokes, G. Pilling, Mr. Ashton (clerk),Mr. J. Ashton (deputy clerk), Mr. Farrington nuisance inspector, Mr. Diggle and Mr. Swinton, (surveyors).

HALTON PAROCHIAL COMMITTER. At a meeting of this committee held on Saturday afte-r- -noon, Mr. Wright presided, and there were present : Mr. C. Birch, J. Mannin., F. S. Jeacock, W. McCulloch, and L. A. Povey. The Clerk (Mr. Ashton), read a letter from Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, stating that he bad considered the complaint with res- pect to the scarcity of water to seven cottages on the 'Common and he could not agree with the District Coun- cil that the supply of water was insufficient. The Clerk was requested to look up the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Water Works Act, and ascertain whether the Urban District Council of Runcorn as the present pro- prietors of the Waterworks could be called upon to lay water mains to the houses and schools on the Common. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Jeacock, seconded by Mr. Looker, that application be made to the Local Govertnent Board under section 276 of the Public Health Act 1875, tr., declare the provisions of sections 45 of the Public Health Act 1875, to be in force, in the contribu- tory place of Halton and to invest the Rural District Council of Runcorn with all the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, and obligations of an Urban Au- thority under the provisicus within the said contribu- tory places. The minutes were adopted by the Council.
lIRLSBY ROAD.

Mr. John Collier, Helsby, wrote saving he had been requested by the ratepayers of Proffits Pit, Helsby, to call the attention of the District Council to the condition of the road leading from the highway to their respective cottages. It is during wet weather almost impassable, and the commencement of the road being adjacent to a pit the banks which are washed down made the road dangerous to pedestrian and vehicles. They asked that the road be made good.—The Surveyor in answer to a question stated that it was an occupation road and had not been repaired by the Board and was out of their jurisdiction.

div.head: WILDERSPOOL SEWAGE QUESTION.
div.p: WILDERSPOOL SEWAGE QUESTION.

Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk Of Warrington. writ- ing with reference to the Wilderspool sewage said the Corporation would not consent to the omission of the wards struck out of the agreement. He did not under- stand why they should object to them. The agreement was all to the advantage of the Council and would relieve them of the serious obligation of abating the nuisance caused by the discharge of their sewage in the old bed of the river at Wilderspool. Without the agree- ment the responsibility of the Council remained, and they would be compelled to abate the nuisance. All accounts between them would have to be adjusted under section 62 of the Act of 1888, and would suit the Cor- poration a deal better than the terms set out in the agreement.—Writing again on August 31st, Mr. Whittle said it was agreed that they should pay a proportionate part of the cost of the treatment of sewage and this was based on terms decidedly advantageous to the Council. It was agreed th it they should pay the cost of any works in excess of the requirements of the borough, not that they should pay only a proportionate part of such cost. The agreement as drawn did not carry this out and must be corrected.
The Clyde and Belfast shipbuilders have conceded an advance of five per cent, to the members of the ship- builders' and Boilermakers' Society.

div.head: LADIES VISITING COMISIITTEN
div.p: LADIES VISITING COMISIITTEN

The Ladies Visiting Committee reported that on Wed- nesday, August 26th, they visited the male side of the House and found everything in perfect order. They noticed particularly that the outlook from the windows was very desolate. They therefore begged to suggest that as the main hospital yard was about to be re- asphalted that a space on one side be left for the culti- vation of some greenery. Mr. Stokes said the House Committee would consider the matter.

div.head: RECIINT FIRE
div.p: THE RECIINT FIRE

The Clerk reported that the committee appointed to consider the outbreak of fire had resolved to make a claim of £33 upon the Insurance Company for the dam- age caused by fire. The company's assessor accepted this claim on behalf of the company and gave permis- sion to proceed with the work of repairing the damage. —The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Stokes. Mr. Aaron stated that ten years ago he brought the Question of how an outbreak of fire could be dealt with at the house. Plans and estiinates were drawn up by Mr. Charles Linaker of Froasham. Had Mr. Ashton got those plans. Tee Clerk in reply said that he had found a bundle of papers dated HU relating to fire extinguishing. There was na plan. Mr. Aaron said if the best fire engine in the world came to the house in case of fire there would be no water for it. The recPnt fire was a very lucky thing. Had there been any lives lost tnere would have been a Local Government Board inquiry and an inquest, and the Guardians would have been censured severely, and deservedly so. The inmates of the house were all cripples and there was only the master to deal with the fire, and there was not a suScient supply of water. He hoped the Clerk would find the plans, and that something would be done to prepare for extinguishing fire.—On the mo- tion of Mr. Stokes a special committee was appoiLted to consider this matter.

div.head: TOBACCO.
div.p: TOBACCO.
On the recommendation of the House Committee the male inmates are to be allowed an ounce of tobacco. THE VAGRANCY :'/LtrESTION.

Mr. Cunnah (the master) said that the:vagrants were causing a deal of trouble, and assistance was urgently needed. He suggested that the schoolmaster should be appointed assistant relieving officer at a salary of £5 per annum. Either this would have to be done or a separate officer appointed. In reply to the Chairman the Master said the school master would have time to attend to vagrants in a morning and late at night. Mr. Stokes said they were endeavouring to carry out Mr.Dansey's suggestion that they should keep the tramps two days instead of one ; and the tramps were very rough and troublesome. Mr. Lea moved; the Rev. J. Simpson seconded ; and it was reselved that the schoolmaster be temporarily appointed relieving officer, and Mr. Lea gave notice that he would move his permanent appointment at the next meeting.
BER MONEY.

The Clerk in reply to a question of which Mr. Hey- wood had given notice at the last meeting, said the beer money was included in the amount repaid by the ex- chequer. It came under the head of officer's rations.

div.head: VISITORS TO TER ASYLUM,
div.p: VISITORS TO TER ASYLUM,
It was moved tat Mr. Stokes. Mr. Mclntyre and Mr. Lea be appointed a committee to visit the County Asylum. This was seconded and carried. FINANCIAL MATTERS.

Mr. Heywood, chairman of the Finance Committee, stated that the committ9e had passed accounts amount- in. to £145 sd. The bulk was spent in outdoor relief, £9O going to Runcorn district, £2B to Frodsham district and £2O to the Budsworth district. The balance in the bank was £1,256.—Mr. Woodward seconded the passing of the minutes of the committee and they were adopted.

POOR LAW STATISTICS. Mr. Dansey's statement of thepauperism and expendi- ture of the 41 Unions in his district was submitted. It showed tbat Runcorn Union had an acreage'of 47,100 a population of 42,517,and a rateable value of £242,381. The number ot paupers re- ieved on January 1, 1896, was, indoor 169, out- door 747, total 916, as compared with 198 indoor and 791 outdoor, total 989, in 1895. The proportion of pauperism to population was 21.. The expenditure for the half- yaar ending Lady Dar, 1896, was in maintainance £616, out relief £1,743, total £2,359, a decrease of £209, compared with the corresponding half-year of 1895. The cost per head of population was is. lid.. as compared with is. lil. for Northwich, is. 21d. for Stockport, is. 1001. for Chester, 11id. for Taryin and 90. for Wirrall. The report was adopted.
RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Town Hall, Runcorn on Thursday morning, present— Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.A. (in the chair), J. Pritchard, G. H. Kirkham, D. Bisbrowne, F. Wisivall, H. J. Grice, J. Wilson, T. Dean, M. J. Sweetman, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, F. A. Lake (law eierk), E. Marshall (secre- tary), and J. Wilding (surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. - -

7 - Dr. Wright submitted Dr. McDougall's monthly report on the health of the district. The number of deaths registered was 15. There had been no inquest cases. Five of the deaths were due to diarrhceA, 4 to phthisis, 1 to cancer, 1 to bronchitis, 1 to paralysis, 1 to convul- sions, 1 to infantile jaundice, and one to a disease of un• certain origin. The deaths show an average death- rate of 91 on the twelve months. During the month 45 births were registered.—The Chairman remarked that the presence of Dr. Wright in the place of Dr. McDougall showed that Dr. McDougall was unable to attend. They were very sorry that he was prevented from attending through illness, but they were glad to hear he was very much better. He would be glad if Dr. Wright would ex- press their kind sympathy with Dr. McDougall in his illness.

div.head: HIGHWAYS AND EIIILDINDS COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAYS AND EIIILDINDS COMMITTEE.

The following minutes were submitted, that a memorial be sent to the Directors of the London and North Western Railway Company,asking for a reduction of tolls in respect of the foot-bridge across the river Mersey,and that the seal of the Cnuncil be affixed to the Memorial.—That notices be put up in several streets declaring such streets to be highways and repairable by the inhabitants at large. Mr. Bisbrowne in moving the adoption of the minutes referred to the first item. He thought that the mem- bers ought to give the matter their serious support. He believed that some of the members were of opinion that it was hopeless for them to obtain a successful issue to the petition. He thought that they might seriously hope, because in the memorial a strong case was made out and he considered it deserved consideration. The bridge had been open 28 years, and they were quite sure that the profits had been enormous. Only two attempts had been made tw the Council to obtain a reduction, they were in 1884 and 1889, and they were quite in order in making a move in the matter. The tendency throughoutithe country was to reduce tolls or wipe them away altogether if possible. It would be a great benefit to the town and to the working classes, and he had pleasure in moving the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded, and said he felt certain that the Railway Company would consider the matter laid before them for the sake of the poor people of Run- corn who were the people who made the greatest use of the bridge. He considered there was hope for the petition, and he looked forward to a reduc- tion in charges which had been obviously great.— Mr. Grice supported the resolution and thought the time had came to put the matter before the railway company once more. The connection between Widnes and Run- corn was of the utmost importance to both towns and he eonsPered that the railway company by reducing the fares would be acting in their own interest as well as in the interest of the towns. He had great pleasure in sup- porting the memorial and he hoped the members of the Council would support it very strongly by an expression of opinion. Dr. Gastaldi suggested that the Chairman 'should personally place the matter before the directors in London.—The Chairman said he would only be too glad to follew the work up but he thought it would be best to send the memorial forward in the first instance. —The minutes were then passed.
WATER COMMITTER.

The Water Committee in their minutes recommended that the wage of Thomes Bell, plumber's assistant, be increased 2s. per week annually until he attains the age of 21 years.—Mr. Pritchard maved, and Mr Wilson seconded the adoption of the minutas,which was agreed

MARKETS AND CEMETERY COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that six months notice be given to Mrs. John Ball of the intention of the Coun- cil to discharge the loan of £3OO borrowed for the o..me- tery ; That a precept be served on the Overseers of the poor for £lBO for the six months ending 31st March. 1897, for the repayment of loans, and a precept for £lOO for Cemetery expenses for the same period ; also that the seal of the Council be affixed to such precepts.— Confirmed on the motion of Mr. Kirkham seconded by Mr. Grice.

TECIINICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTER. The committee reported that they bad received and considered letters from the department of science and art to the effect that this council has the option of being paid either on the results of examinations or by attend- ance grants, and they beg to recommend that with regard to the session 1895-6 this council elect to continue to work and receive wants under the rules of the direc- tory for 1885 6, that is, to be paid on results of exam- inations. The committee recommended that the fees for the shorthand and dressmaking classes be 33. per session instead of 3s. per quarter, and that the fee for laundry work be is. 61 per quarter instead of 3s. per session ; that a class for the advanced course of naval architecture be held and that the lecturer be paid a minimum salary of £l2 and railway fare for such advanced courso ; that a class for practical carpentry and joinery be held, and that the requisite tools be obtained. (estimated cost of

tools £6) ; that the terms of payment in respect of the chemistry classes for the forthcoming session be as follows :—A minimum salary of £l2 10s. instead of £lO for each class, the science and art grants on results of examinations, in excess of such minimum salary to be paid to the lecturer ; that prizes be presented to the sue- cesqul students in the science and art subjects. (Estim- ated cost of prizes £l6) ; that the committee be empowered to take all necessary steps in connection with the public presentation of prizes and certificates.— Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wilson seconded and the resolution was carried.

div.head: TRE TRADE COMMITTER
div.p: TRE TRADE COMMITTER

Dr. Gastal3i asked whether anything had been done in connection with the Trade Committee that ceuld be made public.—The Chairman said they were well aware that there had been a deputation from the captains of the p r as he had made it clear then, the committee had no power to command any private firm in any woe. Everything they could do in their private •cap4city, he was glad to say they were doing. He could only say that the interview they had had with one or two firms on the question of future trade in Runcorn made him feel satisfied that the lines they were going on would bear fruit. They had already seen during the week a very great improvement down at the docks, but he might point out that the Warne was not altogether on the side of the Ship Canal Company. He had an interview with Mr. Mead° wcroft the other mornini, which was most satisfactory. He could assure them that the Trade Com- mittee was doing its best to improve the trade of the town.—Dr.Gastaldi asked whether the water at the lay- bye was being kept up totthe promised 24 feet as it was reportsd that it was only 22 feet a short time ago.—The Chairman pointed out that this was another matter best dealt with by the Trade Committee in their private capacity arid in this matter as well as others he could assure them that everything was being done that could be done. _
The meeting shortly afterwards terminated.

div.head: FLOWER SHOW AT MOORE:
div.p: FLOWER SHOW AT MOORE:

Under the auspices of the Moore and District Horticul- tural Society, a show of fruit, flowers, and vegetables was held in a field near Moore Hall, kindly placed at the disposal of the committee by Mr. C. Roylance. It was the second annual show in connection with the society and was opened on Thursday afternoon by Lady Brooke. The exhibits which surpassed in quality and quantity those of the previous year, were tastefulls, arranged in two tents supplied by Mr. Cotton of War- rington. The exhibits of flowers were particually fine, and reflected great credit upon their owners. In addi- tion to the exhibits in the competitive classes,there were several attractive stalls of flowers and fruit shown by nurserymen outside the district, Messrs. William Clibran and Son, nurserymen,seedsmen, and florists,Altrincharn, had on view a choice collection of dahlias, phloxes and other flowers, and also a large variety of herbaceous plants. Mr. George Tandy, nurseryman and florist, of Ackers-lane, Latchforn, also made a fine display of flowers and plants. Mr. Massey, of Acton Grange, exhibited fruit and flowers, and an attractive feature of the stall of Messrs. Dixon and Robinson, of Manchester, was the collection of gladiolas. There were also exhibits of plants by Mrs. W. C. Jones, Mr. John White, J.P.,and Lady Brooke. Amongst those present were :-Lady Brooke, Rev. H. T. Clarke, Mrs. Clarke, Miss Dutton, Miss Tinsley, Mr. Vere Davies, Mrs.%ll. Woods, Miss Woeas Miss Seeker, Mr. J. E. Seeker, Miss Groome, Mrs. and Miss Middle- ton, the Misses Litton, Miss Willis, Mr. J. L. Jones, Mr. ' Rovlance and others. The President of the Society (Rev. 13. T. Clarke) in introducing Lady Brooke said he would like to remind those present that the society was only in its second year, and was therefore quite in its infancy. He did not see the show last year but if it was comparable with this year's show and making allowance for the twelve months' growth, it must have been a prodigious infant. The present was an excellent show and was one which Moore might well be proud of. The secretary told him that the number of exhibits was one hundred in excess of last year, and so far as he was able to judge, the quality of the exhibits was excellent. The committee had worked hard to make the show a success and their task had been anything but an easy one. Whilst con- gratulating those who had been fortunate enough in gaining prizes, he trusted that those who had been less f srtunate would not be discouraged and would sick now - led ge that they had been beaten only on their merits. (Anplause.) Lady Brooke said she had very much pleasure in be- ing there for the purpose of opening that flower show, because she took a practical interest in gardening, and especially in the culture of flowers. She thought. there was no pursuit which gave greater pleasure. All the year round-even in winter-there was always something to do,something to be seen,or observed. The cottage gar- dener, she believed, got more real satisfaction from his, garden than raany who dwelt in large houses, and who had more extensive gardens, and that was because ,flowers seemed to extend to the affection and sympathy of those who cultivated them. She often saw more beau- tiful flowers in a strip of garden near a cottage than in a garden round a large and imposing mansion, and it ' was the result of the love and regard lavished upon them. ' They must have given pleasure to many a tired way- larer. She thought the people of Moore had attained excellent result., and she hoped the society would con- tinue to prosper for many years to come, and that more and more would enter into the competitions. She had pleasure in declaring the show open. (Applause.) A large number attended the show during the day notwithsanding the unpropitious weather, and music was supplied by the Preston Brook brass band. Appended will be found a list of the prize-winners. The judges were as follows : Mr. Kipps, Walton Lea ; Mr. Lock- hart, Walton Hall ; and Mr. Slater, Norton Priory ; pro- duce, Mr. C. Linaker, j (Frodsham) and Mr. C. Baguley. The officers of the society who are to be con- gratulated on the success of their efforts are as follows : President, Rev. Es. T. Clarke, vice-president, Mr. John White, J.P., committee, Rev. J. W. Gilbertson, Messrs. J. L. Jones, Gleave, Seeker, J. Weir, Litton, W. Oulton Tandy, Calder, Hamblett; Wilkinson, Sander- son, Judd and Hayward. Mr. Arthur DePrez was hon. secretary, and Mr. T.
