div.head: HELSBY.
div.p: HELSBY.

SUDDEN DEATII.—On Tuesday, Mr. Churton'held an inquest at the Horse and Jockey, Ilelsby, on the body of Thomas Forkin, aged 52 years, of Darrinabeck, County Mayo, Ireland, labourer. The deceased worked for Mr. John Dutton, farmer, Woodhouse, Frodsbam Lordship, and after working in the fields on Monday he fell back dead while lighting a stove at noon. A verdict of "death from natural causes "was returned.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

DROWNING FATALITY.—On Tuesday night a boy named Thomas Henry St3phenson, aged 7, son of Richard Stephenson, of West n Point was fishing in the Weston Canal with several other children. It was sup- posed that the deceased lad was reaching over into the water for he slipped and fell into the canal. Another boy ran and gave the alarm and the body was recovered by means of grapples very promptly. P.C. Bancroft rendered first aid but life was extinct and his efforts to resusticate the body were futile. MARRIAGE OF Wig B. ROSENBREG.-011 TUFF, day, at the Parish Church, Runcorn, the nuptials betwem Miss Kate Rosenberg, second daughter of Mr. L. Rosenberg, agent of the Trustees of the River Weaver Navigation at Weston Point, and Captain D. H. Griffiths of Appledere, Devon, were celebrated. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. D. S. Bowen of Christ Church, Weston Point. The bride and bridesmaids (Miss Rosenberg and Miss Mar- shall) were prettily attired,and each wore a gold brooch set with diamonds, the gift of the bridegroom, and also carried beautiful bouquets. Mr. L. Rosenberg jun., acted as best man. After the ceremony luncheon was served at Weaver Villa, the residence of the bride's parents, and the happy couple 'shortly afterwards left for Ilfracombe where the honeymoon will be spent.
GRAND SWIMMING GALA AT WAR RD GTON.

One of the most popular forms of athletics in War- swimming. and the various War- rington is undoubtedly aquatic festivals which have been held from time to time have met with universal support. The best gala of the present season was held on Tuesday evening in the Cor- poration Baths, which were crowded to the utmost. A excellent programme of events had been, compiled and some of the bes, swimmers in the district were compet- ing. including J. H. Tyers,the amateur champion. The building was better ventilated than usual and the spec- tators were, to a groat extent, protected from wholesale splashing by a screen which ran round the side of the bath. Dr. Canneil occupied the chair. The officials con- trolling arrangements were .—Judges, Messrs. Walsh, Critchley, Hatton, and Derbyshire; Handicapper and ' starter, Mr. Joseph Derbyshire ; check starters, Mr. Stanley Wilson, and Mr. T. G. Grounds ; timekeeper, Mr. Fair Turner ; hon. secretary Mr. F. Garside. •
50 YARDS OPEN AMATEUR HANvICAP.

The above was the first event of the evening and for it over 50 swimmers had entered in competition for the prizes, which were as follows :-Ist -prize, a ease of cut- lery ; aid, Gladstone bag ; 3rd, hand bag; and 4th, walking stick: Twelve heats were necessitated and the respective winners were—G. T. Waters, 0.W.5.C.; W. Creighton. ; J. Formby, E.C.; T. R. Towers, L.S.C.; J.H. Sanderson, S.S.C.: L.Purgold, L S.C.; J.H. Wright, 0.5. C.; A. B-scow, W.S.C.; J. Hampton,W.S.C.; ' J. Lowe, W.S.C.; D.Holland,N.H.S.C.; and W.Dunnett, W.L.S.C., and J. Graham, W.S.C. a dead heat. It will be seen that a good numner of Warrington swimmers were successful in their heats. Four heats were necessary in the second round and some very strong swimming was witnessed for places in the final ; these were se- cured by Waters, Towers, Boscow, and Lowe, the two latter being members of the W.S.C. For the prizos a most exciting struggle took place between theso four, who finished in the following order, Towers Ist, Boscow 2nd, Lowe 3rd, and Waters 4th. In the ninth heat of this race Tyers started at 12 but could not secure the first position. There was,however, a fast time prize of one guinea value,which he made sure of by swimming the 50 yards in 25 3-5 seconds. He was loudly cheered for his fine effort. J. Formby twice attempted to beat this time. In his heat he did the distance in 29 seconds or 1 2-5 seconds behind Tyers. His next venture in the second round was even better for he landed only 3-5 of a second behind the champion's titne.

div.head: POLICE UNIFORM RACE.
div.p: POLICE UNIFORM RACE.

Members of the local police force,for the evening, cast off their personation of law and order and adopted the new role af being food for amusement. Five of them, Sergeant Phillips, P.C. Elwards, P.C. Chrimes, P.C. Berry, and Detective Meacock, were competitors in a police uniform race,and entered the building arrayed in a cast-off suit of " blues," helmets included. They formed line on the steps of the spring board, and while the starter was giving the instructions P.C. Berry,think- log the signal givee,plunged into the water and had a most exciting race with himself. He swam valiantly and certainly came first, but to his own amazement the others had not started. The other four started properly and swam strongly considering the conditions. Meacock and Phillips were the best, the former coming in winner.

div.head: LADIES' HANDICAP.
div.p: LADIES' HANDICAP.

Far the members of the fair sex the following prizes were offered for competition in a 50 yards handicap :- Ist, lady's watch ; 2nd, preserve dishes ; and 3rd, lady's hand bag. Two heats were swum, the entrants in the first being Miss M. Baker, Warrington ; Miss A. Hyde, Droylsden ; Miss Pennington,St.Helens ; Miss M.Mather, Warrington ; and Miss Chesworth, Warrington. The two last named were first and second, respectively. For the second heat there entered the water Miss L. Molloy, Liverpool; Miss Cash, St. Helens; Miss B. Whitehead, Lshton-under-Lyne •, Miss J. Bolton, Warrington; and Miss A. Crompton, Warrington. This heat was won by Miss Crompton, Miss Molloy coming second. The final was warmly contested, and resulted in favour of Miss ' Mather, Ist •, Miss Crompton, 2nd • and Miss Chesworth, , 3rd. Miss Mollor, who was heavily handicapped, swam very pluckily, and it was decided to present her with a prize of equal value to the third. The CHAIRM&N made a short speech. and said he thought many people failed to understand what the baths were built for. Some thought they were built for the rich, but he wanted them to understand that they were built both for the rich and poor, more especially the latter. (A pplause.l

div.head: LIGHTED CANDLE RACE,
div.p: LIGHTED CANDLE RACE,

The above was a novelty for Warrington and proved the most popular event of the evening. It was confined to members of the Warrington S.C., and ten s,viminers participated in three heats. The rules were "each com- petitor must wear a night dress reaching half-way below the knee; and carry a lighted candle and a box of matches. If his candle goes out, he must immediately stop swimming and re-light it. Any competitor inter- ferine in any way with another, or splashing, or blowing out his light, will be disqualified. First and decond in each heat to swim in final." _Much laughter was occasioned by the appearance of the swimmers in the first heat, and they sustained a good deal of banter. Each entered the water, arranged his nightdress,secured his liehted candle and started. They were allowed to carry the candle any way,but the favourite method was in the mouth, while the swimmer travOled on his back. Occasionally a carille went out and had to be re-lit. The whole race was greatly amusing and those who got in the final were G. Smith, T. Hoghes, J. Hampton, A. G. Robert-on, A. Ashton, and T. Prince. The ultimate result was Roberston first, Hampton second, and Hughes third :—First prize, pipe in case (presented by Mr. T. Morris) ; second prize, gentleman's umbrella (presented by Mr. James Critchley); third prize, cigarette case (presented by Mr. S. Beaman). POLO MATCH.

A great deal of interest was taken in the league water polo match between NarrinE,,ton and West Liverpool,the fixture being the last M the first round of the"A"division. The teams were composed as follows :—Warrington, goal, A. Robertson ; backs, Beaman and Boscow;half- back, T. Locker ; forwards, A. Ashton, G. A. Scotson, and W. Creighton. West Liverpool, goal, M. Collins ; hacks, C. Jones and J. Cowley; half-back, T. Bradshaw; forwards, J. Molloy, M. Simms and J. 0. Matchett. In the first half of the game Warrington defended the deep end of the bath. The visitors were first on the ball but a foul gave Locker possession and he transferred to Scotson. 'The latter was unable to utilise his chance and the ball travelled to the opposite end. Boscow was next instrumental in stopping a rush, but Cowley put in a shot which Locker held and retaliated by a throw right into the goal-keeper's hands. Some fast play ensued in the Liverpool goal and the Warrington forwards were very prominent. A good opportunity came to Bradshaw but he failed at the shot, and Locker by a splendid dribble reached the visitors' goal, only to lose possession at the critical moment. Creighton made a good attempt also.A foul gave the bill to Molloy and he, from a good position put in a shot which beat Robertson, Locker was again unsuccessful but RQbertson prevented further scoring by his dexterity. Half-time arrived with the visitors leading by one goal. The second half commenced with Warrington holding the shallow end. Some good exchanges took place which ' ended in Scotson trying one of his long shots. The attempt was a good one and the ball just missed passing through the goal. Locker and Boscow were both promi- nent, and the latter after a smart dribble along the side, equalised by a strong shot. On the restart, Warrington played with determination. Beaman prevented the visiting forwards getting too close and gave Locker another chance. He lost the ball and Bos- cow being again fouled he passed to Scut- son who rut in another rapid throw. Locker was in tinie to receive it and put the leather throughommis- takeably. This put the visitors on their mettle and they became dangerous more than once. Cowley was pre- vented from scoring by Boscow, and Beaman almost achieved success. Collins fisted out right into Seaman's

ITan.ds:and the latter made no mistake this time. Several othyr vigorous attempts were made on the Liverpool goal, and on one occasion Locker struck the posts. Even- tually the game concluded in favour of Warrington by 3 goals to L This was the last item on the programme and the en- tertainment closed after lasting over two hours.

div.head: BELL-RINGING IT ST. PAUL'S.
div.p: BELL-RINGING IT ST. PAUL'S.

On Monday evening, at St. Paul's Church, the ringers accomplished a date peal for practice, con- sisting of 1,896, changes made up as follows :-96 of grand-ire, 720 of College single, 720 Oxford single, and 360 Canterbury pleasure, arranged and con- ducted by Mr. A. Oxley. Time, one hour two minutes; tenor, 16cwt. Treble, W. Oxley; 2nd, J. Pornfrey ; 3rd, A. Oxley; 4th, F. W. Stout; sth, W. Brammer; tenor, E. Edwardson. This is said to be the first peal of this length ever accomplished in Warrington by this or any other band.

div.head: TRAGEDY OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE TRAGEDY OF IRELAND.

Oh, the Tragedy of Ireland must with anguish rend the cores Of those who love her lakes and hilhi,her silver-broidered shores ; Who pride in her old glories, learning, arts, and splendours rare, The wit and valour of her sons, her daughters, graceful, fair. flat erstwhile favoured land whereto in legions used to fink The philomaths of other lands, their minds with lore to stock— Now fast being decimated -and despoiled of men and wealth, While other nations grow and thrive, by rapid strides,by stealth. 'rho Irish Celt is dwindling fast within his native home, Each year his country's flower and youth still drained beyend the foana : And the Tragedy of Ireland in this fact doth culminate, With a vengeance most:appalling,with malignity of fate. That land where plenty, peace, and rural happiness should Long turned into a lazaret of poverty and pain : The wailings of the homeless, of tho sundered kith and kin, With the crash of falling rooftrees,make unceasing dirge and din. Old Ireland's bone and sinew ever driven o'er the

waves, To help build other nations, or to fill the paupers' graves. A delusive El-Dorado lures the youths and maids away, While were the naked truth but known, at home they'd strive to stay : For one, whose dreams are realised in Emigration's

! curse, : A score find disappointment, slavery, death—or even worse ! In genius, daring, energy, capacity, emprise, The Irish race can well compare with any 'neath the skies ; Yet to-day the Irish Nation, her advantages withal, Is the poorest, p'rhaps, and most distressed upon this earthly ball. For ages long her surplus wealth unj us IF drawn away By" Absentees," while peasants pinch and starve, this rent to pay ; Whereas a country's produce, or its value to a cent., To encourage Arts and Progress, should at home be wisely spent ; Ever taking out, ne'er putting in, the bottom soon is reached— Here's Ireland' state exemplified, her management impeached ! Poor Erin ! Now nigh helpless as a hulk mid storm-lashed waves, Long the shuttlecock of parties and the " Tiddler's ground " of knaves, Though many an earnest effort, ardent struggle, noble fight Has been made by pure-souled patriots, thy crushing wrongs to right ; Yet ever when fruition all but crowns the work of years, Some recreant or wreeker to frustrate thy hopes appears. And bars the goal from out thy reach, through madness' spite or whim, Whilst a host of minor wreckers is most sure to follow him. Then recklessness, disgust, despair, from disappoint- ment spring, And the confidence essential to success takes rapid wing ; The Unity that wonders wrought, tri factious strife gives place, While Ireland reaps but growing ills, disaster, and dis- grace. Oh, the Tragedy of Ireland has its most heart- rending phase In the fact that oft it happpens, he ; chiefest part who plays In the smashing up and wrecking of her dearest hope and plan. Is some well-loved and trusted—once truehearted— Irishman ! Such inscrutable defections, where all looked for honest zeal, Are the rocks whereon are shattered ever Ireland's hopes and weal. Oh,the lesson plain herein contained's within the dullest reach ; But can prophet, man, or anga this great lesson ever teach ?
Warrington, August, 1896.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held rn Sunday afternoon. The chairman was Mr. Haviour,and in the few minutes allotted to him he spoke on the sub- ject of" Tile Family Outcasz.." He advised his hearers to lend a helpidg hand to the erring one and net despise I a man when he was down. If they were to raise human- ity tbey must mix amongst them and do something to help them. By • o doing they would be following in the footsteps of Chriat.—Mr. Walter Brough was the spe .ker for the afternoon, and delivered an inter:tsting, address on." Conscience." He urged those present to obey the voice of conscience, and not to quell it, and pointed his remarks by many apt illustrations. A special feature of the service was the singing of Mr. Edward Parton, principal baritone of the American Church, Faris. fie gave a capital interpretation of the hymn" Jean, lover of my soul," and the solo "A Dream of Paradise." Both were greatly appreciated.—The Rev. John Yonge asked for volunteers to canvass the town in the interests of the P.S.A..and asked his hearers te make the movement a still greater success in the town.—Mr • Robbins and Mr. William Beewick also took part in the service.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DESTRUCTIVE TRAMPS AT THE WORKHOUSE.--THERB MONT'S EACH. On Saturday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Mr. John Burgess, (in the chair), Mr. Chandley, and Mr. T. Birchall, two tramps, Mary Ann Marshall and Elizabeth Smith were charged with having, while casual inmates of the vagrant ward of the Workhouse, refused to perform their allotted task on Friday, they were further charged with breaking windows to the extent of 235. Bd. damage at the same time.—Prisoners admitted both offences and behaved with considerable bravado.—Mr. Basil Shearer, enquiry officer, prosecuted and informed the magistrates that the prisoners were admitted to the workhouse as tramps. It was the custom for all females stopping a night to pick a lb. of oakum. The pris‘ners were offered the usual amount but refused to work at all. The master was sent for and he ordered them to be locked up. They then deliberately smashed almost every pane of glass in the room. There was no provocation for it. When the windows were broken they kept shoving their heads through, and as it was a visitors' day, jeering at people who passed. Be (Mr. Shearer) was instructed to prose- cute and he asked their worships to deal as severely as possible with the prisoners.—Marshall : I helped to break the windows and I am only sorry that the brick did not go through the Governor's head.—Smith said I am sorry too.—The magistrates sent each prisoner to gaol for one month's hard labour on the first charge and two months on the second.—When leaving the Court Smith remarked complacently that she could do it on her head.

ATTEMPTED SIIICIDE AT WARRINGTON.—ALLEGED RESULT OF BETTING. Before the magistrates at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, Peter Quinn, 17 Town Hill, a brewer's labourer was charged with attempting to com- mit suicide by cutting his throat at his dwelling-heuse on Saturday night.—The Chief Constable said this was anather case of self-inflicted injuries where the prisoner was actuated by an endeavour to attract sympathy. He had been drinking more heavily than usual for several days and on Saturday he came ho:ne about eight o'clock, had his tea and made a remark about having " backed " four horses and lost on every one. Prisoner then went upstairs and in a few minutes was heard to say "I have done it now." His brother William Quinn went up- stairs and found prisoner bleeding from a wound in the throat. Information was riven to the police and P.C. Jones and Sergeant Hollingworth went to the house. They found a penknife (produced) staived with blood. He (the Chief Constable) sugge-ted the desirability of remanding prisoner in custody for a week to bring him to his right senses. Since the affair he had denied that he had backed any horscs whatever.—The magistrates rflnanded prisoner as Suggested.

, SATURDAY.—Before Captain Witbington (chairma Messrs. Wm. Houghton and J. Hartley. DRUNK AND Dls-RDERLY.—Maria Kenny was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly at Newton. REFUSING. TO QUIT LICEIiSED PREM SES.—Michael Callig- han, of 28, Derby-street. Earlestown. was charged with being ,drunk on the licensed premises of James Henry Forster and refusing to quit when requested by the landlord to do so on the 10th August. Defendant was further charged with being drunk and disorderly on the highway. He pleaded guilty and was fined 10s. and costs. A CYCLIST IN TROUBLE.--Dower Cooper, Swan Inn, Win- wick, was charged with having on th. 14th August ridden a bicycle on the footpath of Warriugton-road,Whawick,and was flied is. and costs. CART WITHOUT NAME.—Mark Schofield, 26, School Brow. Warrington, was summoned for having on the 14th Augast at Winwiok driven a cart without having the name painted thereon. He was fined one shilling. CHARGES OF CRUELZY TO HORSES.—Thomas )c- Dermott, a boy, son of Mr. McDermott, cab proprietor, Barlestown, was summoned at the Instance of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, on a charge of having on the 12th August cruelty illtreated a horse by beating the same.—Mr. R. Swill. of St. Helens, defended.—lnspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A. stated that at 6.30 on the date named he was at Newton Fair. and saw the defendant driving a black mare up artn down the street near to the Oak Tree public house. He had the stick produced (a blackthorn) in his hand and was bat- ing the horse with the knob end of the stick. He saw the defend Int give the animal about a dozen strokes with it. and also to hit e grey mare with it as the nimal passed him. Witness stopped the defendant and took the stick from him, telling him he had no reason to beat the animal at all. On examining the tense there were no wales on the back, but the horse showed signs of being in pain—ln cross-examina- tion, witness said it was untrue that he had half-a-dozen Stinks at the Oak Tree Inn. The stick produced Wee not one calculated to make wales, but it would make bruises. ' He had received a letter from Mr. Hazelton, who was in partnership with Mr. McDermott, but he did not know what it meant. Ile did not get anything for a coeviction. The half-penalties were generally given to the Police Superan- nuation Fund. The officers of the society were not paid by success.—Mr. Hill, veterinary surgeon, Altrincham, gave 1 corroborative evidence as to seeing the defendant strike the 11 horse several times with the stick produced. To beat a horse with such a stick was cruelty. He examined the horse, and found it very tender and contused on the off-side.--In cross- examination, witness denied that he made a practice of going about with Mr. Luff, or that the fee he received from such a source constituted the greater source of his income. Ha had not been in a similar case for six months. He never made an appointment with Mr. Luff to meet him at Newton.— Inspector Liaff said as a suggestion had been made with reference to his condition he would like to call a polee sergeant who was there.—P S. Baneks said there Wee No truth whatever in the suggestion that I nape lea Luff was tros worse for drink. He did not show the slightest signs of it. and was perfectly cool.—Mr. swift for the detence said he had not the sliehtest objection to the Ser resent having ca:led and if he (Mr. Swilt) had m ide an imp:oper suggestion he would be the first person to witbd.aw it He had no in- tention of doing Inspector Luff an injury by a suggestion which he could not maintain He was instructed that In- spector Luff was at the public-house mentioned for a consi- derable time, but in the face id the serge int's evidence he must contess that it was a suggestion that ought not to have been made, and he would withdraw it. With re'erence to the facts of the case, the defendant was the son of Mr. McDer- mott, who did a large business at harlestown, and Mr. Hazelton was jointly interested in the business. On the day in question both of them went to the fair for the purpose of disposing of souse horses. accompanied by some men. The defendant was not thee for the purpose of driving one of the horses, and it was only during the temporary absence of one of the men that th: defendant was allowed to erive the black mare for 50 or 63 yards up Ashton lane. The bay only hit the anithar once and then not sever .Iy. When the stick had be n taken off the boy by Inspector Luff, Mr. McDermott and Mr. Hazelton examined the lioree and saw no signs of ill-treatment. Mr. Hewitt and Mr. Dixon of ot. Helens were imrned ately sent for and they found no marks upon the animal. The evidence for the prose- cution was far fetched, and he asked the magistrates to dismiss the case.—Samuel Hewitt, veterinary surgeon, said he went to the Oak Tree. Newton. on the date named. He arrived there at 6.45 and examined the black mare owned by Mr. McDermott. He failed to find any marks upon the animal, and if there had been any caused by the defendant he would have sten them —Mr. Dixon. veterinary surgeon, St. Helens said he examine hue horse in question at 7.20 the the same night. There was not the slightest truth in the accusation of cruelty. The animal did not show the slightest nervousness, and if there had been some severe blows struck there would have been some bruise on the body. He d d not see how a lad. like the defendant could hurt the animal. There was not the slightest sign of cruelty. Mr. Robert Stead employed by Mr. DI cDermtt, 38 and 40, Derby-street, Barlestown, and Mr. Hazelton also gave evidence for the defence. The magistrates dismissed the ease—John Carter was charged with having cm the 24th July, cruelly illtreatedia horse by beating andoverdriving the same. —Mr. htuart, selieitor, defended Inspector 3 Bilson. I de- posed that at 4 45 on the date named he a as in Market-street, Barlestoen, and saw the defendant driving a single hosse waggonette. It was being driven at a rapid rate, The conveyance was overloaaed and the horse was in a distressed condition. He stopped the horse, arid he count-d 3ln the waggonette wh'cla was only I eensed to carry 8. The eff-side of the horse was covered with wales and it was impossible to count them. Its back was a con- fuel mass ot wales.- Inspector Luff gave corroborative evi- eence.—ldr. Stuart. far the defence, contended that it was itnpotsible fo the defendant to be drivi .g at a furious r .te as there were a number of vehicles in front of him With regard to the overloading, he wished to po'nt out that the conveyance was registered to carry twelve ant not eig t as stated. , He submitted it was a case where the On !era had keen mi-tak en. -David Phillips, employe,' at the Viaduct Works, Barlestown stated that on the date named he was on the waggonette in question. He told the offi-ers that there were only eight passengeis. The convey-um was lieeasei to carry twelve.—llr. Hoskins said 11 was the owner of the horse, end when it was b. ought into the stable it did no", st.ow any sigas of distress. He had no waggonette licensf d to entry eight.—The a,eistra'es d'smissed the case. —William Forster. 312 Station-road. ONE THOUSAND LLAMAS LADEN WIfH GOLD. Who doesn't like to read about buried treasure? Who hasn't dreamed of finding it? What delight suddenly to possess vast riches? Shining gold, sparkling , gems Things for which we have not been obliged to scheme or toil ; that will free us from all need of scheming or toil- ing thereafter! At), let us not indulge such fancies. They make work seem like slavery and wages like pinches of common dust. Yet that such hidden masses of wealth exist there is no doubt. But where are they? About four centuries ago the Emperor of Peru was a captive in the hands of the Spaniards. His people sent a train of 1,000 llamas (a small beast of burden resemb- ling a camel) laden with geld to ransom him. While on their way, crossing the Andes mountains, the men in charge of the expedition heard of the death of the Emperor, and concealed this enormous treasure so effec- tually that not a trace of it has ever been found Go and dig it up, and you will never again feel the sting of

poverty. But clap the brakss down hard on the whesls of your imagination. What was money to Robinson Crusoe ? What would the wealth of Peru have been to Mrs. Jane Stranks during a certain period of eighteen months that she tells abeut P Dust, my dear fellow, countless pinches of common dust. Hear is the reason why—one more picture of that fearful furnace in which all earthly de- sites are melted into one prayer—" Oh, God, deliver me from pain !" "In June, 1891," she says, "I had an attack of in- fluenza, followed by bronchitis, which left me very low and feeble. I had no appetite, and the little food forced myself to take gave me pain and palpitation 01 the heart. I had a weary sinking feeling at the pit of ' the stomach and as obliged to fight for my breath. / had a continuous hacking cough, and spat up quantities of thick phlegm. Later on I had gout all over Aid, as it were my hands, face, and legs being puffed up, and was in agony day and night. I became so weak I could not raise my hand to my mouth, and had to be fed.' "For months I lay perfectly helpless and alm sst life- less, having to be lifted in and out of bed. Four doctors attended me for nine months without effect. Then they told me they could do nothing for me, one of them giving me a letter of recommendation to Guy's Hospital. At Easter, 1892, my husband took me in a cab to that hos- pital, and I was placed in the Miriam Ward, and examined by several doctors. "At this time a hard substance seemed to have formed in my stomach, which the doctors said was a tumour, and treated me for it. I got weaker and weaker, until one night the nurse told me that the doctors had said I was as bad as I could be, and would not probably live throuoth the night. " The nurse placed a s.:Teen aroand my bed, expecting me to die." "raking a slight turn for the better. I returned home, but was soon as bad as ever. After this I got a letter of recommendation from our landlord, and attended as an outdoor patient at Victoria Park Hospital. After being under treatment a month, I lost all faith in medicine and gave uppaking it. I was now little moee than a living misery. I was tired of life, and often prayed that the Almighty 'would take me. I now had fits of shakine so bad that the bed trembled under me. My head was so full of pain that I thought I was going mad, and several.times a day I lost conscionenese. "In this dreadful condition I lingered on until November of last year, 1892, when a bole was left at our house telling of a medicine called Seigel's Syrup. I had lost all hope of getting well, but my husband would have me try this medicine. To please him I did so; and, after taking it a few days, I felt a little relief. My breathing was easier and my appetite revived. Continu- ing with the medicine all pain gradually left me, and I gained strength daily. In six weeks I was able to go about the house and do light work, the first time I had done anything in eighteen months. lam now iv good health, and able to do any kind of work. I owe my life to Seigel's Syrup, and wish my case to be made known.' (Signed) Jane Stranks, 22, Gaywood-road. Hoe-street, Waltbamstow, near London. April 20, 1893." No words of comment can be too strong for a case so remarkable. We stand before it at a loss what to say. It is not a miracle, of course ; although many a reputed miracle has been less wonderful. How is it possible, that Seigel's Syrup could, with such apparent ease, nave restored to health a person in so desperate a strait ? Yet that it did restore her is certain. The facts have been thoroughly investigated and established beyond dis- pute. Mrs. Stranks was on the crumbling edge of the grave, and was thence brought back to the region of health, activity, and enjoyment. How was it done? Mere is the simple secret. The influenza left her whole system debilitated, as it usually does. Indigestien— which in the first place invited influenza—attacked her with increased power. Asthma, heart disturbance, nerv-. ous prostration, the infl tmed and congested stomach, which was mistaken for a tumear, etc.. etc.—ill results end symptoms of arrested dieestion—follovrecl. The priv- ate and also the hospital treatment failed, because it was directed to the symptone, not to the c4u7e. Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup was appeale I to, and responded by setting the digestive funotion in novration, expelling the pois n from the blood, end placing Mrs. Stranks at the head of her house, a saved women. But t was a marvel all the same. As to that pile of treasure hidden in the Andes. We should like to have it. Oh, yes N use el eine; we shoaldn't. But as between riches.rid he an _ye ve us health. For what would gold have bee' to Mr., Srsi ks the night she lay behind the screen ven up to .ee Ask yourself that question.

div.head: WORD IN CONkIDENCE.
div.p: A WORD IN CONkIDENCE.

It is a pleasant duty to give honour, where justly due, but in these times we reserve the right to exercise our discretion as to what is worthy of praise. We must not,however, in our caution fail to discrimi- ate. Must not condemn the Navy because an officer blunders ; must not ridicule or underestimate the value of our universities because one graduate makes a failure in life ; must not mock at religion because one member goes wrong ; must not sneer at the entire medical pro- fession because one physician makes a mistake, nor de- cry all proprietary medicines because some lack merit. While it is the duty of everyone to detect and avoid ardent pretender and the grasping impostor, sue should also give credit where it is due. You may with confid- ence rely upon the statement made by Mrs. Mary Wat- sen, 8, Fleming-street, Govan. Glasow. She writes :—" My husband was laid down with a very bad attack of Bright's Direase the latter end of August last year. We had first one doctor and then another, but neither of them seemed to do any good, indeed, one of them said from the first that it was a hopeless case. My husband had been about :ix weeks ill and still getting no better and getting.no rest night nor day, always with the feeling when lying down as if he would be drowned. About this time I met a friend who told me of a Mr. Dick who had been cured by Warner's Safe Cure. I went and saw him and he told me all about his own case, and he recommended me very strongly to get Warner's Safe Cure for my husband as he had never knoa n it to fail, he having told many about it. I got it for my husband, and after he had taken the fourth bottle the water came away as black as p4rter and with flakes in it like snow, but every day after this he got better, and was out in a fortnight from that day, and now he is able to be at his own trade, which is that of a carpenter, and but for Gods good. ness and Warner's Safe Curc, he would have been in his grave. It cannot be too highly recommended, I have told a great many about it."

--- MACMILLAN AND Co.—The twentieth of the Illu- strated Standard Novels is " Helen" by Maria Edgeworth. To this work Anne Thackeray Ritchie writ's an introduction. She says that " Helen" is remarkable as a piece of edna!rable writing. There is an extraordinary grip of life in its pages, a brilliant description of some of the best society in England, a deliberate vivacity." Interesting Personal particulars are given of Miss Edgeworth and a touching mention.ot the death of her brother, William. Illustrations in accordance with the high character of those throughout the series are sup- plied by Chris. Ilammond.—Among the many ad- mirable items in this month's " Century " magazine is a biography of Harriet Beecher Stowe, entitled 'The Author of 'Uncle Tom's Cabin,' "with pictures portraits and autographs.by Richard Burton. Many particulars of Mrs. Stowe's life are disclosed far the first time and one finds much to marvel at. Harriet Beech,....r early showed her bookish- . flees, and at six was finding delight in "The 1 Arabian Nights." At ten she was fascinated with the more often dreaded task of theme-writing I and at twelve she produced a paper with the fol- lowing title, "Can the Immortality of the Soul be prayed by the Light of Nature," a thesis gravely answered in the negative. Under the title of " Clave's Journey to the Livingstone Tree," are given glimpses of life in Africa from the Journals of the late E. J. Glave. The pictures are from photographs by the author.—As usual some very good reading is to be found in " Macmillan's Maga- zine " while " St. Nicholas " is replete in literary inar.,er delectable to the youthful palates—For is. one gets nine cleverly written stories by F. Hop- kiuson Smith. The hook, so tempting a bargain; is" A Gentleman Vagabond." The author in an inixoductory note says " There are gentlemen vagabonds and vagabond gentlemen. Here and there one finds a vagabond pure and simple, and once in a lifetime one meets a gentleman simple and pure. Without premeditated intent or mental bias I have unconsciously to myself selected same one of these several types—entangling them in the threads of the stories between these covers. Each of my readers can group them to suit his own ex- perienee." Such " grouping" as the author rsfers to of course necessitates perusal of the stories, and the reader will find them all well worthy of it. They are skilfully woven and highly interesting. CA.SSRLL AND Co.—These publishers announce the issue of" Pictorial England and Wales," a compan- ion work to "The Queen's London." Part 1 con- tains 32 pages of beautiful pictures prepared from copyright photographs. The most pictureNue places in the country are pictured and convey a stund idea of the beauties which abound in Eng- land and Wales. Altogether the work will be corn- Posed of 11 parts, containing 320 illustrations. Needless to say the latter are inishei productions of the printer's art.—ln view of the wide-spread interest evoked by the course of events in South Africa, the Soudan, and other parts of the African con'inent, Messrs. Csssell and Co. are publishing a s.ixosnny monthly edition of "The Story of Africa and its Explorers." Dr. Robert Brown is the author and there are about 800 illustrations, reliably accur- ate. The work furnishes a "lody of information sech as coul .1 only be obtained by the perusal et hundreds of separate volumes. With part 1 which is now before the public is a large presenta- Hen plate depicting an attack by Matabele on the Chartered South Africa Company's Laager. Graph- ically written knowledge of the dark continent is imparted in a pleasant forrn.—There is some sadness in the reflection that within a very short time the Magazine of Art has been twice enlarged by the addition of a biography of the late Presidents of the -Royal Academy. Subscribers to the magazine have herdly ceased the study of Lord Leighton's life before they are absorbed in the relation of his suc- cessor's career. The September number of the alaonzine of Art contains an extra 16 pages of an "In Memoriam "of Sir John Everett Millais, Bart., P R A., by M. 11. Spielmann. Toe biography is clearly the work of a loving hand. A number of reproductions of representative works by the late president come between the pages. MESSRS. F. WARNE AND CO.—From these pub- lishers we have received " For Such is Life" by Silas K. Hocking (price 3s. 6d.), ansl " Within Her Gra-p," by .Mary H. Tennyson (Is.). Both these novels will be reviewed sh, rtly.

THE WESLEYAN MINISTERIAL CHANGES AT WARRINGTON.

THE NEW SUPERINTENDENT. The Rev. Owen Watkins (superintendent of the cir- cuit) and the Rev. G. D. Mason closed their miniet,re in Warrington on Sunday. Speaking in Bewsey-road Wes- leyan Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. OWEN War' SINS said he had not preached a farewell sermon because he could not. He would only like to say the longer be remained amongst them the more he had learned to loveand esteem them all. He rejoiced exceedingly that he was leaving them a united people, one in heart, one in mind, and one in purpose. Weereter he aed hie wife and family went they would alwevs have a very plea3ant remembrance fef Bewsey-road. Of their great kindnesa towards him he could not speak too highlv,and he hoped they would sheet again when their travelling dave were over and their work had been done. Might the great Lord of all allow them in the end to be united for ever iit the land where there was no parting, where the people were never sick,and where God Himself wiped away the tears from all faces. He wished to -peak a word on be- half of his brethren who were coining. As they loved him,so let them receive the new corners kindly and well. He honed they would receive them as messengers of God. At Bold-street,the Rev. G. D.Mason preached his fare- well sermon and took as his text the words "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself.so that I might finish my course with joy. and the ministry ehich I have received of the Lord Jesus to testify the gospel of the Grace of God." He said that he had come that night to the close of a three years' ministry among them, and it was not without anxious thought and deliberatien that he had chosen that text for the occasion. During his stay in Warring- ton he had conceived an affectionate regard for many who were in that church that night. It was in all pro- bability the last time that they would meet in their pre- sent relationship, and very likely if he ever came again he would find that some had been gathered home. some had gone out into the world, and that some had been lost. He begged them not to judge him by wuat they had seen done,but by what had been attempted. He said to all " farewell." The choir then sang "May God be with you till we meet again." THE NEW SUPERINTENDENTT.—SKETCH OF HIS CAREER. Accompanying a portrait cf the Rev. J. Potts (the new superintendent) there is the following sketch of bis career in this month's issue of "The Warrington Circuit Wesleyan Methodist Church Recoid." "Mr.Petts was born in Manchester, but he can hardly be said to be a native of the Cotten Metropolis, for his parents removed thither from Derbyshire. On settling in Manchestar,the parents of Mr. Potts made their hothe at Great Bridge- water-st. Chapel. Mr. Potts received his early educa- tion in one of the Mothodiet day schools, but his real training for the work of life commenoed with his en- trance into business at the age of thirteen, when he not only sought to become efficient in his employment, but devoted himself to private study, in which he was largely aided by Cassell's Popular Educator,' tile first edition of which was then just published. At the age of 15 he joined the church. Mr. Potts' call to preach came through a sermon by the Rev. John Rettenbury, which was followed in due course by the call of the Church through the leader of the Theological Class, the Rev. Richard Smetham. In 1881 he was accepted 1w the Wesleyan Conference as a candidate for the ministry, and without any preliminary training was sent at once into circuit work. Leaving business on 'Thursday night he arrived the next day at the market town of Newbury in Berkshire, with four sermons in his pocket, three of which he preached on the following Sunday. Frain that day,in various parts of the country,he has been ectively serving the Methodist Church. His apprenticeship as a Methodist preacher was passed in country circuits, but important centres of population have also claimed hint. Whilst residing at Smethwick he was president of a dis- cussion class, numbering amongst its members no less than six alumni of Wesley College, Sheffield, most of whom are now leading members of the Wesleyan Church in Birmingham. Two of his most congenial a ppeint- scents have been in his own county of Lancasle e—at Widnes and Oldham. Six years of his life lei .e been spent in gallant little Wales, for the scenery, the people, and the religious history of which he has enthusiastic admiration. During his residence in Nottingham, Mr. Potts has steadily elos ei rho ,sfeem and :-fr-ntion of his people A- a prtaelier he delights not in speculations about the truth. In ..y wise and faithful application seeks to comm, tele- h itself. His sermons are thoughtful, wellvit,itited with ea perience. and reveal a mind familar with the deep things of God as well as a devout ed sympathetic spirit. He is pre-eminently a teacher. No erie can hear him often without receiving instruction and the knowledge conveyed is always made sut s qvient to the I,igeest ends. One secret of his power is the fact that the preacher himself is so much a part of the ser- mon. As a circuit administrator he has special aptitude. His sound judgment and delicate tact enable him to skilfully guide the business of a meeting, whilst. the at" solute confidence which his impartiatity inspires pre- vents opponents of his policy from feeling aggrieve? by his decisions. Be is prompt to deal with matters require attention, and. yet cautious enough to t sleeping dogs lie." He is no bureaucrat. With tellies confidence he trusts thc people, and seeks to carry them with him in his undertakings. He is an ideal colleaelle• His perfect brotherliness and absolute freedom fror3 assumption make it a pleasure to work with him, whilit his sound judgment and ability inspire respect. One who knows and loves him well, the Rev. John LeateileY, of Edinburg, has admirably summed up the leading features of his character : lam asked to give an impression of Mr. Potts. More than twenty years ago he made a good impression upon me, and to this present it remains. As a Manchester man ought to do. "he knows his way about," and makes few nets- takes and no enemies. Some men are like a little shop with a large window, and most of the stock can be seen at a glance—other men are like a wholesale warehouse, where they keep the stock out of sight and show samples only in the window, ATI. Potts does not tell all he knows in his first sermon ; if he did, his first sermon would last hree years, and then would he unfinished. He is better tan the hook ' Inquire within far eyeryt fling.' If there 11,-,ok, a picture, or a celebrity Mr. Potts does not know sntm-thing about, a sensible person will not trouble to inquire further if he gets Mr. Potts's opinion, or hears he tines not know it. This quality in Mr. Potts is well' known by his friends—till wi Je acquaintance with te eles. Then he knows where to buy and when and where to sell or exchange books. Ilis apt quotations from the hest writers all his intelligent hearers will notice. The modesty of the man is as conspicuous as his versatility. He never puts on side,' perhaps a little more confidence in his own powers might have been a blessing to himself and others. As I think I know him better than he knows hiniself, I shall take care he does not see this sketch, or he will want to delete some things. The thirst for knowledge is great in Mr. Potts. That I may know 'S surely one of his aims in life. Without robbing any circuit of time or his family of money he Yal seen more than most men. If he has to go to a synod or to an appointment in another circuit he will drop off the line and visit some ruin or explore some neighbourhood, and catch the next train." PRESENTATIONS. _ .

SHOCKING ILL-TREATMENT OF CHILD REN. AN UNNATURAL FATFIER.

On Friday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Alderman Wright (iii the enair), and Councillor Roberts, George Bailey, 27 Leicester-st., was charged with assaulting his children, Mary and Annie, on the 26th August, in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering. Inspector McAteer, N.S.P.C.C., prossouted, and said that about 12.30 on Thursday afternoon Mary Bailey, aged 12, was brought to his office by her brattier George and a Mrs. Harrison. At the request of the two he examined the girl and found her in a terrible state. She was suffering from contusions on the thighs, both arms, and both shoulders. She was one mass of bruises. Fie sent for Dr. Bowden who also examined the child. Witness went ti defendant's house at 4.30 and saw Annie,ap,ed 10, whom he examined also, and found her also greatly bruised. There was no doubt that the children had been cruelly assaulted. He pro- duced a heavy piece of machine belting with which the children had been thrashed. _ _ _

Mary Bailey,aged 12, a very intelligent child,said Olt on Wednesday night she was in bed and her father came up and thrashed both of them for not going to school. She did not go to school because it was raining and she had no shoes. The leather produced was that which he thrashed them with. A Mrs. Hughes came up and took the strap from defendint saying he had hit them enongh. Defendant had beaten them both before many a time with the same strap. The Chief Constable then suggested that the bench should see the child's shoulders themselves, they were so badly bruised. The magistrates agreed.-1. Harrison bared the girl's shoulders. They were very much bruised and one arm was in bandages, which it was stated covered cuts caused by the strap. George Bailey, son of defendant, said that on Thurs- day he brought Mary Bailey in company with Mrs. Harrison to the Inspector's house. His father had been in the habit of illusing the children since there mother died. On one occasion he threw witness downstairs.

M. U..lson stated that defendant olten Mused • his children. When the child was brought to her she gave instructions that she should be taken to the Inspector. e Chief Constable allo gave evidence as to the con- e seemed to be in a very nerv- :l his bad. ry

Dr. Bowden stated that he had examined the girl. He found extensive bruises on both arms, forearms, shoul- ders and thighs, apparently the result of considerable violence. Defendant said he had to correct the children for not attending school. He had been threatened with a sum- mons from the School Attendance Authorities. He thought he had not overdone it. Alderman Wright: What do you think of them this morning then. Defendant: Well it does seem worse than I thought. I am very sorry. div.head: LAMP THROWING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE LAMP THROWING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
COMMITTAL OF PRISONER.

At the Warrington Police Court on Friday, John Hares was again brought up on remand, charged with doing grievous bodily harm to his wife Annie Hares by throw- ing a lighted paraffin lamp at her en the 4th August. The Chief Constable briefly recapitulated the particu- lars of the case, (which have already been published)and called evidence. Be asked that the prisoner might be committed to the ssizes to take his trial. Dr. Langd t.le, senior house surgeon at the Infirmary, stated that Annie Hares was admitted to the Infirmary on Tuesday, August 4, about 9 p.m., suffering from a severe burn on the left side of the face, most severe in the neighbourhood of her ear, also involving the front of the face and neck. Her hands were also slightly burned. She smelt of paraffin and was suffering from shock and in great agony. The injuries were of a very serious nature. She had been in the Infirmary until Thursday last. It would be several weeks before her injuries were entirely cured. Mrs. Han s, who looked very weak and had her head bandaged said that on the 4th of August she met her hus- band in Bask-street and asked him if he was coming home. He said no and hit her. She told him he had no right to pawn his clothes for drink. The blow blacked her eye. She went home and hid in a neighbour's house. Prisoner returned at 8.30 and went to witness's mother's house a Ivre they had been living. She heard hire kicking up a row and went in. lie called her a foul name and picked a fender up to throw at her. Witness and her mother took it from him. He said he would take her life and took up the ashpan as a missile. That was also taken from him by her mother and he said he would b- well have something and took the lighted paraffin lamp from the mantlepiece and threw it at her. It struck her on the side of the head and knocked her down. It exploded and set her on fire. He had frequently threa- tened her life and often ill-used her. Prisoner was not drunk though he had had some drink.
Prisoner said he had no questions to ask his wife.

Catherine M'Ouire, 6 Berry's-yard, mother of Annie Hares, said previously prisoner and his wife had lived with her about six weeks. She corroborated the last witness's statement. She threw cold water on Mrs. Hares, and Mrs. Knight wrapped a shawl round her. Sabina M'auire, 18, Erwood-street, who was also present, gave further evidence as to prisoner's threats. Catherine Knight, 8, Berry's-yard said she saw defend- ant take the lamp and throw it at his wife. Witness saw it from the window. It exploded and set her on fire and witncss rushed in and tried to put the fire out with a shawl. Prisoner came to her assistance with his coat.

P.C. Evans stated that on the date in question be saw Mts. Hares being conveyed to the Infirmary and went in search of prisoner in company with P.C. Millington. They found him at Berry's-yard and he was slightly under the influence of drink but knew what he was doing. Witness charged him. He replied " I wish it had killed her ; I wish it had gone through her b-- heart." Witness then locked him up and at the Police Station he admitted;throwing the lamp at her. Witness returned to the house and picked up the scattered frag- ments of the lamp. Prisoner said he reserved his defence. He was committed for trial to the next Liverpool ss!zei.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD WARRINGTONIAN
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD WARRINGTONIAN

Regret will be felt by many Warringtonians at the death of one of the oldest and best known of them, in the person of Mr. William 'Longshaw Grappenhall• road, Latchford, who died at his red, deuce on Saturday at the advanced age of 87.- Though he had passed by many years the allotted three-score years and ten, Mr. Longshaw was in possession 61 all his mental faculties up to the time of his death, nor was he deficient in bodily vigour. He had a complete knowledge of old Warrington and could relate many interesting particulars rela- tive to the growth of the town during a large portion of the present century. Mr. Longshaw was born at Reddish Hall, near Appleton Thorn, and first commenced business at Lsige, where he founded a small wire mill. This business he subsequently gave up and came to Warrington to take the part ot manager for Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Limited. That position he maintained:with honour and integ- rity for 30 years., during which time the business developed enormously. He left the firm about the year 1869 and went to Sankey where he carried on the business of chemical manufacturer under the title of Messrs. Longshaw and Sons. It was while working there that one of the deceased gentleman's sons, Peter, lost. his life through drinking acid inadvertently. This business was also dropped and Mr. Longehaw finally came to ateli- ford in 1892, and lived there in retirement, until his death on Saturday. During his long life he was twice'married, first to Miss Newton, a Cheshire lady of good family, and secondly to the third daughter of the late Mr. Peter Phillips, of Warring- ton. This lady died in 1891, aged 81. For eight or nine years Mr. Longshaw was a very active mem- ber of the Board of Guardians. In politics he was an ardent, and at elections, a hard-working Liberal, while he was in religion, an Independent Methodist, and attended Friar's Green Csapel. His death removes from the town one of the few gentlemen who are truly "links with the past," and everywhere his loss will be felt. The remains of Mr. Longshaw were interred at the Warrington C3metery on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. W. Hudson, conducting the ceremony. Among those present at the graveside were, Mr. T. Long- shaw (eldest son), Mr. F. Monks, J.P., C.C., Mr. Dixon and Mr. Thomas Priestman.

div.head: MOO RE.
div.p: MOO RE.
THE INQUEST.

An inquest was held at the Red Lion Inn, Moore, on Thursday afternoon, before Mr. Worsley; eorimer, on the body of a man found in the canal on Tuesday night.—Job laberner, boatman, living at Lymm, sta;ed that he engaged deceased on Monday at Manchester to go with him to Runcorn, and to load and unload a flat. He only knew him by the name of " Alf." He had seen him doing similar work on the canal many times. He was not a drunkard. On Tues- day night they were going under Moore Bridge when he saw another flat coming. Witness called out that they would be run into. It was then about 9.15. Deceased, who was aft, went forward with a fender. When they were clear of the boat he called out "Alf," but he re- ceived no answer. He then shouted to the tug to stop. They went back and found the " fender" floating on the -water under the bridge. The body was consequently observed in the same place. The moon was giving a goou light at the time, but they were passing under some trees. It would be half-an•hour after the boats "touched "before the body was recovered. His idea was that the deceased had fallen off the fiat with the shock of the collision.—P.C. Robinson, statiqued at Moore, stated that he received information of the acci- dent at about 9.30. He proceeded to the bridge, where he found that the body had been recovered. Every means of restoring respiration were tried, but without any effect. There were no marks of violence on the body. The deceased was apparently 46 years of age. He was five feet seven inches in height, had dark brown hair, moustache of the same colour, and whiskers of about a week's growth. He wore a pair of corduroy trousers, well worn, a corduroy waistcoat, a striped shirt, blue socks, and a spotted blue neckerchief.—The jury re- turned a verdict of" Accidentally drowned."

div.head: NOTORIOUS ,INVINCIBLE DECLARED INSANE.
div.p: A NOTORIOUS ,INVINCIBLE DECLARED INSANE.

The Amnesty Association on Saturday received an official intimation that John Duff, who was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude at Warwick, in 1885, has teen declated*a dangerous lunatic. Duff's crime created a great:sensation in Birmingham. He made an Appoint- ment with John Gateley, a collector for the Irish Re- publican Brotherhood, at the Gardener's Arms, Solihull, called him outside, pulled out a revolver, and shot him in the stomach. The victim lingered for several days, and refused to say who had shot him. Duff escaped to America,but some years afterwards a detective saw him in London on the top of an omnibus. His arrest was effected, he was tried at Warwick, befote Justice Den- man, and sentenced to twenty years, the charge being reduced to manslaughter on the ground that there had been a quarrel.

" A PERFECT HELL" THROUGH " DRINK !''

Sir,—Such i the town of Warrington according to his Worship the Mayor's title of it given on rhursday last at the Brewster Sessions. By no means a flAttering title for Warrington, which is not easy for thoughtful and observ- ing people to refute aotwithstanding. The Chief Con- stable in his report, as contained in your I let issue declares himself "happy to say" there is a decrease of 64 persons proceeded against for the offence of drunken- ness during the year. While the Chief is "happy," the Mayor is evidently unhappy at seeing and being in the midst of our town—" a perfect hell" of drunkenness. Surely the Mayor would not have made such a state- ment unless it was based upon what he had personally and painfully witnessed of drunkenness, and the Chief Constable surely must not have seen, or somehow differs with the view of the Mayor as to what is " a perfect hell" of drunken persons. The views of the chief magistrate and the Chief Constable, or the figures of the latter gentleman in reference to drunken persons are causing many people who have the welfare of the inhabitants and the true honour of this town deeply at heart, to long to see something of a far higher kind then a mere decrease in figures of per- sons "proceeded against for the offence of drunken- ness," while our town remains "a perfect hell." Let us hope that in the coming jubilee of the:borough,for such improvement in the sober, moral and spiritual tone of our town, that its drink victims may decrease, not in mere figures on paper only, but in the homes of the rich and of the poor alike, so that our town ean merit a better title than" a perfect hell," and that we may see on every hand some pleasing signs of a heaven in our midst instead of " a perfect hell." Why should not those who make the people commit the offence of drunkenness be prosecuted also? None are fined for such offence, so it is not unreasonable and un- just as well as unlawful to allow so many persons to sell drink to their victims until they are a public danger and curse and then simply prosecute the drunkards and never heed those who have caused them to he so ? Yours faithfully, Warrington. Sept. 2, 1896.
HUMANITY.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

Some interesting particulars on the mushroom industry in France have recently been prepared by the United States Consul at NAntes. The annual crop of mushrooms in France is valued at £400,000. and in Paris alone there are said to be sixty wholesale firms dealing exclusively with them. As is well known the mushroom loves a place that is cool, damp, and dark, sunshine turning it from a pure white colour to a reddish brown. For this reason the mushroom is almost invariably cultivated in subterranean excavations throughout France. In the department of Seine there are over 3,000 caves in which mushroomOare grown, and in these places about 300 people. called champignonistes, live, who rarely see the daylight. The descent into these caves is by way of rope ladders. the caves being generally exhausted stone quarries. The beds are most carefully and systetuati- %ally prepared, leng experience having shown the inv. portance of this. We learn from the." Society of Arts Journal" that an experiment to transplant to Germaoy the growing of mushrooms has been made in Wiesbaden after the method of the Paris catacombs.

Transactions in real estate at Johannesburg are freg quently conducted on a colcssal scale. Mr. Abe Bailer, who was one of the" Reform " prisoners, and who re- cently returned to his country, is credited in the Cape papers with having purchased the Ford and Jeppe estates for the sum of £300,000. Fordsburgand Jeppes- town are suburbs on the main reef, and are named, the former after a gentleman who was Attorney-General in the Transvaal when it was under British rule, and the latter in honour of Mr. Jeppe, the representative of Johannesburg in the VolkSraad. Mr. Bailey is a very popular sporting Randite, who has built up an immense fortune, and his new purchasP, on present calculations, will bring him in some £50,000 a year.

It will be remembered that Princess Maud of Wales and the Duchess of York, before being married, ordered silk from the hand-loom weavers of Spitalfields. In con- sequence of this patronage the trade of the interesting descendants of the Huguenots IS improving. Fftv years ago there were more than 3,000 looms in Spitalfields ; and dwellings with long windows like those seen in Lan- cashire before steam machinery became universal were common in this part of East London. Some may still be found, for 700 or 800 hand-looms are now at work.

The blackness of the atmosphere in many factory towns seems to have more considerable cause even than most of us would have guessed. The smoke-stack of a German sugar factory was recently provided with a soot-catcher,from which 6,700 pounds of soot was taken at the end of six days; and it is concluded that the stack of such a factory pours 200 tons of carbon dust annually into the air.

Li's joke in America about the number of the generals (writes a correspondent) was anticipated years aLo by John Bright. General Hawley, a member of the Ameri- can Senate, was introduced to Mr. Bright, in London, and the first thing the English statesman said was, "1 believe you have a great many generals in America, General Hawley ?" This made the senator very irate, and he was about to discourse upon it as a personal injury.

Funny stories of proffered curiosities are told by the officials at the Natural History Museum, South Kensinx- ton. Quite lately theyoreceived a letter from a person in America saying that the writer was ready to take £lOO for the unbroken ash of a cigar with a tiny uncon- surned stump still adhering. The money was not sent. A catterpillar of the death's head moth, a double apple and several birds' eggs have just arrived in one parcel, the sender trusting to the generosity of the Curator. They were not wanted, neither are any more king-fishers nests, though some people seem to think them in con- stant demand. Other persous are steadily of opinion that the Museum wants creatures with an unusual uum- ber of limbs,but it is a mistake. A belief that a tomcat -of the tortoiseshell brigade will fetch more than its weight in gold at South Kensington has spread to the uttermost ends of the earth. The latest offer of such a treazstre came from Russia. Hearing that one English eccentricity had a desire to pay 200.000 roubles for a tortoiseshell' "torn," the writer communicates the im- portant fact that a lady near Karkoff has one ; and he adds, "please send your agent to secure this precious cat." The agent has not yet started.

With regard to our statement in a recent issue con- cerning the growth of trees on church tower', a corres- pondent, says the " Daily Chronicle," points out that there are, at least, two other instances, besides the ono mentioned,of tree life thriving in such unusual surround- ings in Great Britain. The village of Fishteft, which lies about two miles south-east of Boston,in Lincolnshire, possesses a fine church built of stone in the Norman and early English styles, which has a square embattled tower on the top of which is a remarkably healthy beech tree some twelve feet high. The other case is the tower of the parish church of Bicknoller, in Somersetshire, on which is gr- wing a fine tree—a yew—now about five or six feet high. In both instances it is supposed that the seed was originally carried there by a bird. There is something stranger still, however, to be seen in the old church of Ross, in Herefordshire, where two thriving elms are growing, one oh each side of a passage between the pews in the building itself. They are said to have sprung up from the pavement beside the pew once occu- pied by John Kyle, a gentleman who spent a consider- able sum of money in planting elms about his native town.

There are also many such arboricultural curiosities abroad, one of the most notable of which may be seen at Goslar, in Germany. In this case the building is not a ehurcb, but a tower, whicli serves the unromantic pur- pose of a beer shop. The whole tlp of the tower is al- most covered with luxuriant vegetation, amongst which are several sturdy trees, which, when in fall foliage in summer, form a unique and attractive canopy. In the season the strange sight draws visitors from all around the county, and the proprietor of the beer-garden below reaps the reward of a harvest which he never sowed. Another curiosity of vegetation, in the shape of a pine- tree, is growing on a ledge of the facade of the ancient calthedral church of Fenioux (Charente Inferieure), France. Though hardly belonging to the same category, it may be mentioned that there is a church in Washing- ton which has a " steeple " formed of a tree. The church was built under a tall poplar, and an ingenious member of the congregation suggested that the tree should become the" belfry "of the building. The novel idea" took " at once, and, accordingly the tree was deprived of its head, and a bell hung on the mutilated stump.
THE FORTHCOMING MARRIAGE OF MAJOR WALKER.

The marriage of Major Hall Walker, of Gateacre Grange, and Miss Sophie Sheridan, daughter of Mr. Brinsley Sheridan, of Frampton Court, Dorset, has been fixed to take place at Frampton Court on the 30th inst. The lady is a neice of Sir William Har- court. In celebration of the wedding the employee ot Messrs. Peter Walker and Son and of Messrs. B. Walker and Co., Limited, will enjoy a holiday, and it is understood that Major Walker has made arrangements to entertain his workpeople in a liberal manner. At Gateacre the event will be ob- served by village festivities. Major Walker's name has been mentioned in connection with the Lord Mayoralty of Liverpool for the ensuing year. His selection for that honour is stated to be decidedly -probable.

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
DRUNKENNESS.

At the Police Station. Earlestown, on Monday morning,before Mr. C. B. F. Barron, James Cunniffe of Earlestown, was fined 53. and costs for being drunk. He appeared in answer to a summons at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday morning, but was in too drunken a condition to be dealt with. WARGRAVE DAY SCHOOL. _ _

The Inspector's report on the recent examination in cohnection with the above school has been re- ceived, and it appears the excellent grant has been obtained. The report reads :—" The school con- tinues to make satisfactory progress, the children are orderly and attentive,and the work is carefully and steadily carried on with very good results." Mr. R. Ckandley, head master,is to be congratulated upon having gained such an excellent report.

div.head: WESLEYAN JUVENILE MISSIONARY SOCIETY.
div.p: WESLEYAN JUVENILE MISSIONARY SOCIETY.

The collectors of the Earlestown branch of the above society were entertained to tea in the Wes- leyan schoolroom on Saturday afternoon. About 30 children sat down to tea, to which they did full justice. Afterwards they enjoyed themselves with games and racing in the school yard. Mrs. Ennt- ing, secretary, and Mr. J. Yorke (assistant secre- tary) had charge of the arrangements.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT THE VIADUCT WORKS.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT THE VIADUCT WORKS.

On Tuesday morning, a young fellow named Isaac Boon,a labourer employed in the Forge at the Viaduct Works, met with a very serious accident. He was removing a bloom weighing 1201bs. on a trolly when from some cause the trolly tilted up, and Boon in trying to save himself placed his hand on the trolly,and the bloom coming forward fell on his left hand and arm, badly smashing both. The arm was temporarily set by members of the works ambulance corps, and the young fallow was sent to Dr. Handyside, who attended to his injuries. 1.0.G.T. EARLINTOWN EBRNBZBUI LODGE. This Lodge held the usual weekly session in the Co-operative Hall Earlestown on Tuesday evening. Bro. J. Taylor, C.T., presided over 4 very good attendance of members and visitors. Bro. W. J. Taylor L.D., read digest of No. 1 Convention to be held at Ashton on Saturday, September 12th. The programme for the evening was sing, recite or pay a penny. Bro. P. Topping being responsible. The following took part: Song, Sister Mrs. Owens; recitation, " The Voiceless Chimes" Sister Mrs. Hopkins ;song. Bro. J. Woods; recitation in Lanca- shire dialect; Bro. E. Kenyon ; song, 80. J. Taylor; song, Sister A. Newman.; song, ,Sister Witty. Bro. :W. ,J Taylor also gave a humorous reading, L PRXSENTA.TION AT NEWrON. On Friday evening several ,of the office.staff of Messrs. McCorquodale and C 0.,. Newton, together with a few friends assembled at the Hand and Banner Hotel for the purpose of presentipg Mr. John Cook with a memento of their respect and esteem, on his promotion to the London office of „the Arra. The proceedings included a tea, after 'which Mr. W. Hindley presided and explained in a few choice words the objieit for which they were gathered together. He then presented, on behalf of the stih4dril)ellita gold-watch guard to Mr. COOK, and expressed the hope tbat he might be long spared to wear it. Mr. Cook suitably acknowledged the gift, and eulogistic remarks were made bx others of the company assembled. The evening was passed in a sociable manner and proved most enjoyable.

div.head: GOOD TRISPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TRISPLARY.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening.—Bro. W. Wilson,C.T., presided, and there was a large attendance of mem- bers; Bro. B. C. Jones. of Widnes was also present. Two candidates were admitted to membership. The digest of business foc the meeting of the District Juvenile Council to be held at Ashton was read by the Secretary. Bro. Jones gave a short address.and tendered greetings from the Consolation lodge. Bro. G. Clarke, P.C.T. read a paper • entitled" Our lodge and its success," which was of an interesting character, and was well received. A discussion fol- lowed, in which Bros. Newman, and Dale took part, and at the close a vote of thanks was accorded Bro. Clarke for his paper.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY, EARLESTOWN,
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY, EARLESTOWN,

On Monday evening, the Wesleyan Chapel at Earlestown was crowded with a curious audience, who had assembled because of the attractions offered by the local corps of the Salvation Army, in the way of a missionary meeting conducted by Major Otway (circle secretary, United Kingdom) The notices of the meeting invited people to "Come, see, and hear these real living Miracles." The said miracles consisted of Adjutant Clarke (from Zoluland,and his Africander wife) : Kvcengee Zulu Warrior; Munu, Zulu girl drummer; Panel Tyaka (Ked Kaffir), (daptain Ferriara (Boer), and Captain Govaars of Holland. These people, who assisted Major Otway in the mission, were attired in their native costumes, and as they had pre- viously made a tour of the streets, the public flocked to the Wesleyan Chapel to see and hear what was taking place. The meeting was con- ducted in the usual manner, most of the foreign visitors giving addresses in their native tongue.

div.head: LITE MR. ARTHUR EVANS.
div.p: THE LITE MR. ARTHUR EVANS.

Mr. Arthur Evans, merchant, of Haydock, who has just died at Oberammergau, where he was ac- corded a public funeral—nearly the whole of the villagers following him to the grave—was, says a contemporary, a very remarkable personage. It would he difficult to, conceive two more different places than Haydock:with its smoke and the lovely valley of Oberammergau; where the deceased had a chalet,and where he was beloved by the in- habitants, to whose interests tie was devoted. Mr. Arthur Evans was a v.ery staunch Churchman, and when first public attention was drawn to the miracle plays he Went over to. see them, and was so convinced of their value as aiding the cause of re- ligion that he devoted his life to making the place, the actors, and the various scenes depicted known in England. Some years ago he accidently heard in the North of England of a clergyman and his wife in very straightened circumstances who needed rest and change, and he wrote to the rural dean of the district asking him to utilise a £5O note to get them a thorough holiday and provide the duty at the same time,but on no account to divulge his name. We understand that the Vicar of Bay dock has appointed Mr. Peter Cunliffe to be his warden in place of Mr. Evans.
_ BRITAIN'S NIED DIVISION OF THE ORDER OF
SONS OF rEMPERSNCE.

The twenty-seventh anniversary of the above society was celebrated on Wednesday evening last in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestowzi. The proceed- ings commenced at 6 p.m. with a public teaparty, when over 100 members and friends sat down to a I nicely arranged tea. At 730 an entertainment was ! held, Bro. S. Eaton W.P. Presiding, being supported on the platform by the officers of the Division wear- ing their official badges. After the opening hymn, " Love at home," the chairman save a few brief remarks on the object of the meeting. Bro. George Clarke then sang a temperance melody " Publican and paupers "—responding to an encore. Miss E. Hughes recited very nicely "The bunch of Flowers," and was followed by Mr. Joseph Howard whom his usual acceptable style gave a whistling solo "Killarney," responding ,to an enthusiastic re-call with "The Lost Chord." A Lancashire reading, "The Queer Funeral," by Bro. C. Pickett was well received ; after which the chairman called upon Bro. Wm. Wheatley, G.W.P., on behalf of the divi- sion, to present to Bro. Isaac T. Judson, P.W.P., a neatly framed emblem of the Order, Bro. Judson having recently completed 2i years official service, entitling him to the recognition. Bro. D. H. Robinson recited " My young days," and was fol- lowed by Bro. George E. Warburton who very im- pressively rendered "The songs my Mother used to sing." Being recalled he recited" Ask Mama." Mr. Joseph Howard received well-merited applause for his whistling solo. " Love's Golden Dream." A reci- tation "Exce-ssive Drinking," by Miss Jane Pickett nicely given being the concluding item. Miss Kate Hughes was a very efficient accompanist. Thanks to entertainers and all taking part in tea arrange- ments were moved by Bro. Wm. Pearson, G.S.c., who referred to the "'Sons "as second to none, in offer- ing good benefits for a minimum premium and being from the public-house influences. Bro. Jelin Judson, G. Patron, in seconding spoke of the juven- ile section of Cadets. He was pleased to say that since its formation upwards of 39 had been passed on into the adult branch, many of them now being amongst their best anti mot active workers. The meeting concluded about 9 p.m. the rest of the evening being spent in a social manner.
