div.head: EXAMINERI SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 5, 1896
div.p: THE EXAMINERI SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 5, 1896

where a body could be taken to await an inquest. Mr. Browne alluded to the case of a carter who was killed last week at Winwick and whose body had to be con- veyed to Warrington as there was no one in the district who would take the body in. The Borough of Warring- ton had no light to be put to the trouble of getting a jury in such a case, and the inquest should have been held in the same district. If the application was granted they intended to erect a thoroughly resp.ctable good hotel to cost from £2,500 to £3,000. A bowling green would be provided together with good stable accommodation, and the hotel would be so set back that horses travelling on the road could be refreshed without interrupting the traffic. William Owen, architect of Warrington District Coun- cil, produced plans of the proposed house at Winwick. We confirmed Mr. Brown's statement as to the number of houses to be erected near the site. In the plans pro- duced he had provided ample stable accommodation,and proper sanitary conveniences. He had put the house back so as to allow carts and carriages to stand opposite without disturbing the traffic on the highway. A bowl- ing green would also be provided. The Horse and Jockey would be the nearest public-house and that was over 1000 yards away. There was only the Swan Inn, and the Horse and Jockey within a reasonable distanc. He es- timated that the house would cost between £2,500 and £3,000. _ _

Deas, civil engineer, manager of the Longford depot and also water engineer to the War- rington Corporation stated that a very large number of deputations came to visit Long- ford Depot. There was one from Portsmouth during that week. They had had deputations from a great many places including London, Swansea, Lan- caster, Taunton, Glasgow, Edinburgh, and Leicester. They came to experiment and ascertain whether the process of the Warrington Sanitary Committee was good or not. Some of the engineers stayed for 24 hours. There was no place where they could get any refresh- ment vlbarer than Warrington, and he thoueht a place was required. It would be an advantage sn far as large deputations were concerned, and he as manager of the works had no objection to the erection of the hotel. He. would not say that there was sufficient to support one there. They had had as many as three deputations in one day. Sometimes they consisted of six persons and sometimes twenty.

Mr. F. R. Roberts said he was present to oppose the application on behalf of Mrs. Beamont and the Rev. W. R. Hartwright, of Orford.—Mr. Browne said those two were not property owners in Winwick, and his friend would have to search for someone else.—Mr. Roberts said he begged to submit that as Mrs. Beamont was a property owner in that parish he was entitled to appear on her behalf.—Mr. Browne: Orford is not Winwick.—Mr. Roberts: My information is that Mrs. Beamont is a pro- perty owner in the township of Winwick.—The Clerk : Can you prove it.—Mr. Roberts said he could not. He was in their worships hands. He did not know how far it was true or not.—The Chairman: I am afraid you have no locus standi unless you are prepared to prove that Mrs. Beamont is a property owner in the township of Winwick.--Mr. Roberts : It is my information. I can only say it will be very unfair if their objection is not heard, and it afterwards turned out that they were property owners in Winwick. Mv clients have instructed me to appear on their behalf. Mr. Browne: It is the Warrington Temperance Federation that is opposing the application, not Mrs. Beamont.—Mr. Roberts: My friend has not the slightest justification for saying so.—Mr. Browne: He has been following me about all week.— Mr. Roberts: I don't follow Mr. Browne anywhere.— The magistrates agreed that Mr. Roberts had no locus standi and the hearing of the application was proceeded with.

James Norman, Samuel Porter, David Ashcroft, J. Blackledge, and James Johnson, all resid-nts at Winwick gave evidence in support of the applioa- tion, a licensed house in that neighbourhood being necessary in their opinion.—Richard Walter Groate, foreman at Longford Depot, spoke of the accident to a man at the works, and the difficulty in obtaining brandy. It took 15 minutes to fetch some from the Horse and Jockey. He had no objection to the erection of a licensed house near the depot. He thought a house was required. The witness also gave evidence of the number of deputations to Longford. Alderman Francomb said he was a member of the Lunatic Asylums Committee of the County Council and owner of the adjoining land to the house proposed to be built at Winwick. Plans for 12 and 18 houses respec- tively had been passed, and three acres of land bad been let recently for building purposes. He did not wish to say anything on behalf of the Asylums Committee but he thought a house was fully required at Winwiek for the neighbourhood, and others passing on the road. The Chairman said the magistrates were quite satis- fied. The witnesses seemed to get stronger as the case proceeded.—Mr. Browne said he had other witnesses. He intended calling P.C. Groarke who was unable to get a body taken in at Winwick.—The Chairman said the nrigistrates did not req .ire any further evidence. They were unanimous in granting the application. James Wm. gotten, clerk for Mr. Bruwoe,then proved the service of the requisite notices. THE BRICKLAYERS' -INN, GOLBORNE. -

Mr. Widows, solicitor, Leigh, applied on behalf of Mr. J. B. Almond, Standish, owner of the Bricklayers' Inn, Bank-street,. Golborne, to rebuild the house in accordance with the plans he now submitted which had been prepared by Messrs. Heaton, Ralph and Heaton, architects of Wigan. The plans were explained and Superintendent Brassington said be agreed with them as the alteration would mean the closing of a aide door. There would now be only one entrance to the house.— The plans were approved of.

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS AT NEWTON.
div.p: LICENSING SESSIONS AT NEWTON.
TWO NEW LICENSES GRANTED.

The annual licensing sessions for the Warrington Petty Sessional Division were held in the Court House, Newton-le•Willows, on Saturday. The magistrates on the bench were Captain Withington (chairman), Colonel Wood, Messrs. F. J. Gillespie, C. B. F. Borron, William Houghton, J. Hartley, and S. S. Brown.
TRE REPORTS.

Superintendent Higginbotham in his annual report for the Warrington division, stated that the number of licensed persons was the same as last year :—Licensed victuallers, 45; beer sellers (on premises), 16 ; beer sellers (off premises), 5 ; grocers and wine licenses, 2 ; t0ta1,63. During the year one licensed victualler was proceeded against,and dismissed. There were two new applications for licenses—that of Joseph Hatton, of 10, Rolleston-street, Warrington,engine driver, who applies for a licensed victualler's license for a new house pro- posed to be erected at Winwick—and that of Richard Forshaw,brewer, of Burtonwood,who applies for an off. beer license. It would be observed that there was an increase of 31 persons proceeded against for drunken- ness compared with last year. Generally, the licensed persons have conducted their houses satisfactorily, and there have been few complaints. A comparative return of licensed persons and persons" proceeded against for drunkenness showed that in 1895 the number pro- ceeded against was 244 against 275 In 1896. Superintendent Brassington in his report stated that there were within the townships of Golborne and Hay- dock, which form the Wigan portion of Warrington Petty Sessional Division, 32 licensed persons, viz.: 13 innkeepers, 1 spirit grocer, and 18 beersellers (13 on and sof the premises), tring the same as compared with last year. 177 persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness and drunk and disorderly conduct, being an increase of 60 as compared with last year. The houses generally speaking had been well conducted, and he had no objection to make to the renewal of any of the licenses. With regard to the increase of drunkenness alluded to, the Superintendent remarked that it was chiefly in Haydock where sinew pit—the gPrince's pit— had been opened, and a good many strangers had been brought into the district.—No objections were raised to the renewal of the existing licensee, and the Chairman said in granting the whole of the licenses to hich there was no objection, he might say on behalf 4f the Bench that the reports read were satisfactory. The increase of drunkenness was accounted for by the increased popu- lation, and perhaps the police had been more active in attending to their duties by looking after drunken people. He thought on the whole the licensed victual- lers might be congratulated in conducting their houses satisfactorily, and the Bench had pleasure in renewing the licenses of all. MR. RICHARD FORSHAW'S APPLICATION.

Mr. Warsley. solicitor, Warrington, said he made an application on behalf of Mr. Richard Forshaw who was a brewer carrying on an extensive business at Collins Green Brewery. The brewery had been established a great number of years, and was conducted before Mr. Forshaw's time by his uncle. The application was for a certificate to enable Mr. Forshaw to sell strong beer in casks and betties and the application was a somewhat peculiar one, inasmuch as he believed it was the first of the kind which had been heard in that division. Notices had to be given in the same way as though it was really an application for an off-license, but it was a license which could only be held by brewers and which was pro- vided by the legislature to meet the difficulty which Mr. Forshaw at the present moment found in his business. By the excise license which he held he was allowed to sell beer in any quantity not less than 4 gallons, and in bottles in not less than two dozen quarts. He now ap- plied for an additional license under the Act of 26 and 27 Victoria. chapter 30. The reason the license was ap- plied for was that it had been found inconvenient to be unable to supply customers with a 1 as quantity than two dozen quarts. The trade of the brewer had very much altered, and there was an increasing demand for beer in bottles delivered in boxes containing a smaller qUantity than two dozen reputed quarts as allowed by the excise license. A great trade was done in porter and as this did not keep it was a great inconvenience to be unable to supply it in small quantities. It had been found that there was an objection raised to the granting of the additional license as it was contended that it was really the granting of an off license to a brewer which opened an opportunity for him to se!l a single bottle of beer off the premises if he so liked. The way that difficulty had been met by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company wheu they applied for a similar license was to give an undertaking that they would not sell a smaller quantity than a dozen reputed half-pints. That undertaking Mr. Forshaw was prepared to give and the Superintendent had no objection to the granting of the license.—Richard Forshaw, brewer, of Burtenwood said the brewery had been established since 1857. He felt the disadvantage of not being able to supply in smaller quantities than he was allowed under the excise license. There was a large demand for beer and porter in bottles, and the reason of his application was in consequence of being unable to supply in small quanti- ties. Ile would give an undertaking that he would not supply in smaller quantities than one dozen half-pints. He was assessed at £3l 103.—George Liogard proved the services of the necessary notices.—William Owen,valuer for the Warrington Union, said he could not swear what were the exact figures of the applicant's assessment but he knew the premises were worth that much money.— The Chairman said the magistrates granted the applica- tion subject to the undertaking which had been given vert ally.

div.head: EXTENSIONS TO THE SWAN INN. WINWICIC
div.p: EXTENSIONS TO THE SWAN INN. WINWICIC

Mr. Worsley said he submitted plans on behalf of Mr. Cooper, of the Swan Inn, for the approval of the magis- trates, of a contempla'ed extension to be mad of his premises. The Swan Inn was, perhaps, one of the old- est inns in that part of the country, and he would not care to dilate on its antiquity. It was last enlarged in the last century by the Rev. Jeffrey Hornby who was owner of the tewnship. Since then it had not been enlarged, audit had f iltilled the wants of the district up to very recently. But lately, the business of the country inn in such a picturesque place as Winwick had been much increased by the fact that it was a great resort of cyclists, and further accommodation was necessary.— The magistrates approved of the extension ,the Chairman remark;ng tt,at he looked upon it more in the light of a temporary enlargement. MESSRS. GRERNALL'S APPICATION.-A NEW LICENSE GRANTED.

Mr. Arthur Browne said he was instructed to apply by Messrs. Greenell Whitley and Co., for a license to new premises about to be erected just outside the borough of Warrington at the corner of Long-lane in winwick-with-Hulme, and on the Winwick-road. The actual locality was right opposite the Longford depot of the Warrington Corporation. The magistrates would be aware that it was on the highway between War- rington and Wigan and Preston which was very much used. Th4re 'Wei rio licensed house from the Horse and IJockey in the Borough of Warrington until the Swan Inn at Winwicle which must be a distanee of from 2-4 miles to 21 mites.lt was proposed to erect the house 1200 yards from the Horse and Jockey which was almost half way between the two he had named, and he would call a large number of witnesses who would speak of the necessity of such a house. There was no licensed house in the hamlet of Orford. If the license was granted the nearest house en the Winwick-road after leaving War- rington would be the Swan Inn. Going in the other direction to Burtorawood the nearest was the Cat and Fiddle, 4.300 yards away, and in the opposite direction was the,King and Queen at Padgate,which was over miles away. The inhabitants in the neighbourhood of the proposed house had not the slightest chance of get- tiug a drink either in case of necessity or for pleasure. large number of houses were going to be erected im- mediately around the spot where it WIIS proposed to build the new public-house. The owner of the land had let the ground sufficient for twelve houses adjoining it, and also for eighteen on the other side. Only this week a large of land had been taken for buildingotlher" other houses. A great number of men would lee em- ployed in erecting the asylum at Win wick. and the dice tance would be too great to walk to Warrington. The 'house would meet the requirements of the people ie that particular neighbourhood, and he would bring before the magistrites residents in the district who would speak of the necessity of the house. The owner of the land would also eive evidence as well as the managers of Longford depot who would give strong evidence as:to the necessity of a public-house more especially for the convenience of deputations which came to that place from all parts to see the vast improvements made by the Sanitary Committee of the Warrington Corporation in doing away with the objec- tionable smells in the destruction of refuse. A depute- ticn -visited the place during the present week from •Pereemoutle—Mr. Gillespie jocularly referred to the smell still existing at Longford.—Mr. Browne said their worships might blame the Warrington Corporation but he was ectlng to stick up for them. It was not only the Corporation that was respeneible for a smell existing there but there were others.—Continuing, he said depu- tations came great distances, and engineers from differ- ent parts also visited the works, and experimented for several hours together. When they required refresh- ment there was no hone nearer than the Horse and Jockey, a distance of 1260 yards, and he was sure there ought to be a house nearer than that. If the licence was granted, they would give an undertakiug net only to supply good liquors but also proper and reasonable re- freshments in the way of dinners, luncheons and teas Mr. Hetton,who would be in charge of the house.was an engine driver on the London and North-Western Rail- way Comnany, and had been employed by that com- pany a great many years. There was no objection to his character, and therefore there could b 3 no objection lon the part Of the police. Mr. Browne proceeded to I sneak of the difficulties experienced by the inhabitants 'in the neighbeurhood in getting brandy in cases of emer- gency. At Loneford during the past week one of the workmen fell off a ladder.—Mr. Gillespie In conse- quence of the smell ? (Laughter.)—Mr. Browne : No, there are other causes. The man was very seriously hurt,and someone was despatched to the Horse and Jockey for brandy. It took fifteen minutes to bring it, and during that time the man might have died from want of proper restoratives. Another difficulty experi- enced in the neighbourhood was the want of a house

div.head: LIVERPOOL ST. HELENS, AND SOUTH LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.
div.p: LIVERPOOL ST. HELENS, AND SOUTH LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.

The half-yearly meetinr, of the shareholders of this Company was held on Thursday at the London-road Station, Manchester ; Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., presiding. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said it was now about a yeer singe the line was opened, and it had not yet been handed over by the contractor. Only a single line had been opened, and a number of the connections and sidings had not yet been made. In these circumstances they could not expect to show very good results, and the figures for the year could not be taken as a test of the earning capacity of the tine when com- plete. During the halt-year they had carried 17,539 tons of merchandis^ and 80,000 font of coal. Phe income for the halt-year had been £2,725. and the expenditure £3,390. Certain items of the expenditure he described as exceptional. The directors had not taken, and would not take, any money for their services till the line could afford it They had every confidence in the future of the undertaking, and he thought the figures for the half-year were encouraging enough in the circumstancei. It might be asked why they did not complete the line as a double line, and open it for passenger traffic. There were several reasons why the work was not being hurrie.i on. At the present moment they were suffering front an insufficiency of capital, for there was a debit balance of £9,000 en the capital account. Moreover, they desired to see how the single line turned out before completing the line as a double one. Then the Sheffield Company had a very large controlling interest in the shares, and the directors had naturally to consult them as to financial arrangements. And next session the di- rectors intended to apply to Parliament for further bor- rowing powers. When the line was finished he had nm doubt it would be a very valuable property.—Mr. E. Chapman seconded, and the report was adopted.—Mr. Leach and Mr. Leith,both of St. Flelens.urged the direc- tors to lose no time in reeking sidings to certain works on the line.—A vote of thanks was given to the directors on the motion of Mr. Leith, beconded by Mr. W. Barker.

div.head: DROWNING CASE Al MOORE.
div.p: THE DROWNING CASE Al MOORE.
THE BODY IDENTIFIED.

It will be remembered that the body of a man was found drowned at Moore ladt week, and at the inquest on Thursday last, evidence was given by a boatman that he engaged the deceased on the Monday previous at Manchester to go with him to Runcorn, and to load and unload a flat. When going under Moore bridge, the deceased was engaged with a " fender " to prevent a collision with another boat, and somehow or other he got into the water and was drowned. The deceased was not identified at the inquest, but it now transpires that his name was Alfred Hayes, of Mill-street, Bradford, Manchester. He was a married man, and leaves a wife and family. He was 45 years of age.

div.head: COST OF MAINTAINING PAUPERS.
div.p: THE COST OF MAINTAINING PAUPERS.

div.head: BAZAAR AT EA.RLESTOWN.
div.p: BAZAAR AT EA.RLESTOWN.
LORD NEWTON ON VOLUNTARY EDUCATION.

A three days' bazaar in aid of the Wargrave Church and schools was opened in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Thursday afternoon by the Right Hon. Lord Newton. The objects of the bazaar as set forth in the official pro- gramme were to raise funds for the necssary repairs and decoration of Emmanuel Church, and to increase the accommodation and renovate internally Wargrave School. For the Parish Church there are exceptionally necessary repairs required to the fabric as well as inter- nal decoration, the cost of which will largely exceed the ordinary amount collected yearly for its maintenance. The Wargrave National School requires increased ac- commodation for infants and internal reconstruction to meet the requirements of the present period. As may be supposed the preparations for the bazaar have entailed a vast amount of labour,but it is only fair to say that this has been generously and freely given by a band of willing helpers. A large committee of ladies and gentlemen was organised to work the affair into shape, the executive committee being Messrs. C. B. F. Borron. E. Leyland, Moss, Norman Slee, Thompson, Jun., Wright; Misses Carson ; Mesdames Collingwood, Molyneux, Norman,Purnell,Slee,aad W. Thompson,with the Rev. J.Carson as chairman. The laborious work of secretary fell to Mr.R.Chandley, who performed his task most creditably, whilst Mr. Purnell undertook the task of taking care of the finances. The hall was very prettily laid out, and when the stalls were opened for business they presented a charming appearance. The first was "The Rectory Stall," presided over by Mrs. Car- son and the Misses Carson "The General Stall," under the superintendence of Mrs. C. B. F. Herron; "The fancy and useful stall," under the care of Mes- dames Norman, Thompson,Leyland and Miss Thompson, another stall of the same kind was in care of Mesdames Molyneux, Slee and Purnell ; " Glass and fancy stall," Mrs. Walton and Miss Hughes; "Flower and fruit stall," Mrs. Collingwood; "Grocery stall," Miss Gutteridge and Miss Shepherd ; " Doll stall," Miss Carson and Miss R. Appleton; " Ice-cream stall," Miss Molyneux ; " Bran tub," Mrs. Oubridge ; "Fish pond," the Misses Laith- waite*; "Refreshment stall," Mesdames Shaw, White, Sweetlove, Fairclough and Miss Halsou. The stalls, without exception were well laden with articles of a varied descriptinn,common to bazaars. There were also various side shows, including an electrical exhibition, consisting of cooking, motors and other apparatus, which were under the superintendence of Mr. G. H. Bentley, of Earlestown. During the evening the hall was lighted by electricity, but it was hardly a success, owing chiefly to the want of power when the full force was turned on. A large company assembled on Thurs- day afternoon at the opening, including Mr. and Mrs. Collingwood, Captain and Mrs. Royse, Mr. and Mrs. Norman, Mr. W. Thompson (sen.), Rev. T. R. Matthews,

The Rev. J. Carson presided,and on the platform there were Lord and Lady Newton, Captain Withington and Miss Withington, Mr. C. B. F. Horror', J.P.,Mrs. Carson, Mrs. Handyside. Mrs. Street, Miss Garvin, Rev. Canon and Mrs. Penrhyn. As soon as all was seated on the platform, a little girl, Miss Marjorie CoHingwood handed a beautiful bouquet of flowers to Lady Newton. The Rev. J. Carson, rector of Newton, in opening the proceedings said it fell upon him as chairman of the Bazaar Committee to tender in their name a hearty wel- come to Lord Newton for having come to them on that auspicious occasion, and they were deeply gratified in- deed that Lady Newton had been able to come with him. When he approached Lord Newton to open this bazaar.he at once promised to do so, as he would be in this country at the time. He was then going away for a change, and he (Mr. Carson) was glad to see that the change had been beneficial. (Applause.) He had re- ceived several letters of apology, one from Lady Gerard who was unable to be present, as she was away in the south, but she showed her appreciation by sending a parcel of go. ds. (Hear, hear.) He had another letter front the Hon. T. W. Legh in which ha said he was leaving for Scotland on Monday next. Mrs. Legh had prepared some artieles which she would send to Mr. Carson, together with soine other things made by his little girl. The church,after over half a century, needed internal repairs, but being plain people at Wargrave they did not require adornment, but they liked to be de- cent and homely, and they could not colour the walls until they had removed the plaster, &c. The schools also needed enlargement, because of the increase in the population between the rail way and the church. An old scholar of the school had taken a classroom in hand, and renovated it throughout himself. It was appro- priate that Lord Newton should be wita them that day, because the church was built on land given by his pre- decessor Thomas Legh, Esq., and the deeds were kept in the safe,and he was greatly pleased to notice in the drawing up of the deeds in connection with the school it said that the Christian religion should be upheld in all its fulness in the schools, ;and it provided that a Sunday school should also be held. In conclesion he would say "Our things are good, our work is just, the times are hard, we cannot trust." (Applause.) Lord Newton said it seemed to him that there must be some strange fascination about a bazaar. The moment a bazaar was mentioned it seemed to bring out all the latent energies and zeal from all parts and from all the inhabitants of the district, from the oldest to the young- est, and in nine times out of tea the success of a bazaar was always assured.He hoped it might be so that day. It all depended upon the object the bazaar was held for. The object they were called upon that day to assist,they would all agree could not be a higher one. First of all they had the church to repair and re-decorate. They knew what the Church of England had always doce,that the members of that body had always fulfilled their duty and it really fell upon them a great deal that their church should be kept in a proper and efficient state. With reeled to the schoole,up to now they had done their duty, everyone would allow, but the requirements of the Educational Board were so great that it was with diffi- culty the Committee could carry on the schools and do it effectually. It seemed to him that for the purpose of raising funds, nothing answered so much as a bazaar. The attractions were so great that the visitors who came there were bound to open their purses to spend, and the fascination, as he had stated, was difficult to understand. Now the great question of to-day was of school education. Were the voluntary schools to be carried on as effectually as they had been, and yet meet the extraordinary requirements they were called upon by the Education Board to carry out. If the expenses increased in the way they had done of late years, he could not see that it would be possible to do so on the +oluntary system. They asked for nothing more than their rights, and he thought they might always trust the members of the Church of England to do their duty to the highest point that anybody could expect from them. Two or three months after the present Government came into power they were led to believe that great help would be given to the voluntary schools. As a Conservative he could not say that their action this time " had been very satisfactory. Whoever drew the new Education Bill, and those who brought it in, he did not think had properly stated the facts of the bill throughout the couutry, and it had not been accepted with any great acclamation by anybody. He thought fairness should be meted out to the Church of England and voluntary schools, The Government had promised that before this financial year was through, a bill should be passed which would not suffer from the failure of the first bill. All he could say was he hoped and trusted that would be th case. This was a very serious question, and he looked upon it that the education question of the day was such a large one, that it was not to be trifled with. The Church of England had done more than its share in the education of the country, and he could not see that it should be neglected in the bill. (Hear, hear.) He saw from the report which was issned last year that the maintenance in Church voluntary schools had increased from LI 7s. 3d. to £1 184. llid. per head and in the Board schools from £1 Bs. 4d. to £2 103. 111. How was it possible that the voluntary system could go ' on if it had to compete with the .Board schools. They I knew what the difficulties were in keeping up with the present requirements,and they all had their duty to per- form. He then formally declared the bazaar open, and wished it every success and he felt sure that from the numbers he saw present, and the way the stalls were got up,that it would be a decided success. (Applause.) Mr. C. B. F. Borron in preposing a vote of thanks to Lord Newton for his presence, and to Lady Newton,said the Wargrave people were a small body i nthat district, but they were a united body and desirous of strewing that they were determined to maintain both the church and schools which were built by their predecessors—and he was sure his Lordship did his duty as a peer of the realm, and supported all those who endeavoured to sur port themeelves. (Applause.) The business of the baz iar was then proceeded with briskly and sales were rapidly made. Half-hourly concerts were given by Mr. Leyland and Miss Greenall, and Mr. Peplow's string band gate selec- tions during the afternoon. The total takings for the day were £ll6.

div.head: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

At the Warrington Occasional Court-, on Monday, before Mr. W. Houghton, Josiah Clayton, Glaze- brook, was summoned for having, on the 28th ult., stolen 21b of apples, valued at 4d., the property of Henry Bridg.—P.C. Cameron said that he and another constable were at Mr. Bridge's house. They saw prisoner and 14 other lads come to the orchard with stick., and stones and beat down a quantity of apples. They then chased the lads, but were only successful in catching one ot them.—Prisoner was fined is. and costs, or in default seven days' im- prisonment.

FOOTBALL IN AUSTRALIA.
AN EXCITING TIME FOR THE REFEREE.

A football match between Collingwood and North Melbourne was played at North Melbourne on July 25, and the incidents which occurred show tkat the lot of a football referee in Australia is no better than that of his English confrere. The" Melbourne Argus " says : Owing to a disturbance which took place on the Col- linrsood ground when these two teams met there last year, there was probabk soine ill-feeling between their partisans at starting, and this was raised to fever heat by the exciting events of one of the hardest games played this season. In the early stages of the match J. Roberts,formerly a well-known Carlton player,who acted as umpire, was severe on the players for passing the ball for little marks instead of kicking it, and the local twenty were the chief sufferers by it. There was some hooting at that stage, but later on, when North Mel- bourne, by a fine effort, had made the game almost even again, this was forgotten. Had they won all would have been well, but unfortunately for the umpire they were beaten by a goal, and someone had to suffer. The moment that the final bell rang there was a rush of people in the reserve to the pay gate. As it was evident that some of them meant mischief,several of the Coiling- wood players and a few North Melbourne quietly got round the umpire, who had to run the gauntlet of this ruffianism to reach the dressing-room. It was well that they did so, or Roberts would either have been killed or seriously injured, for the moment he stepped through the gate scores of men rushed at him like wolves, and a scene of indescribable tumult followed. Fists and sticks were going, and one man in the thick of the crowd,with some implement wrapped in paper, was making des- perate efforts to fracture someone's skull. In the first rush Roberts was seized by the hair, and dragged down, but esalendid help was given him just then, notably by Proudfoot, of Collingwood, who, holding one arm over his head to shield himself against a rain of blows and with the other round the umpire, literally carried him through the pack with one of his football rushes. Even when the players and umpire had reached the pavilion their troubles were not over, for they had still to get to their cabs, and the crowd were waiting for a chance to renew the attack, but fresh police were brought and the ground cleared. . _

A" lady" bad the enviable honour of starting this disturbance. As the players were coming in at half- time she waited near the gate and struck Roberts in the face. Afterwards her shrill voice, as she leaned over the fence, added a high treble to the torrent of abuse rained on the untortunate umpire whenever he ap- proached the Pavilion, which strangely enough seemed to be the mustering point of the roughs. The woman " barrac'zer," indeed, has become one of the most objec- tionable of football surroundings. On some grounds they actually spit in the faces of players as they come to the dressing rooms, or wreak their spite much more maliciously with long hat pins. In the height of this vane some of the women screamed with fear, others screamed" kill him." One of these gentle maidens at the close of the struggle remarked regretfully that it was a pity they "let off" the umpire in the Geelong match, as they should have killed him. Yet these women con- sider themselves respectable, and they " support " foot- ball, which is consequently in a serious decline.

div.head: PLEA FOR SUNLIGHT.
div.p: A PLEA FOR SUNLIGHT.

The health-giving power of sunlight has long been be- lieved in, but the belief has been acted on in a half- hearted way. With one hand we enlarge our windows, says '6 Natural Science," with the other we draw cur- tains across them ; we send our children to the seaside fora summer holiday, encouraging them to bathe and paddle,while for the rest of the year we make them wear boots and shoes and all other necessary evils of civilisa- tion, and coddle them up indoors as much as possible. A special retreat even has been prcvided among the mountains of Illyria, far from the eye of the police, where, as in paradise regained, the sedentary sufferers of city life may wear no other covering than that which nature has provided, and may bathe themselves in pure sunshine. The belief then exists' but only recently has it been set upon a scientific basis. In his address as president of the Chemistry and Engineering Section at the recent meeting in Glasgow of the British Institute of Public Health, Profe sor William Ramsay explained how the violet rays of sunlight act upon moist organic matter, producing hydrogen peroxide; bow this peroxide becomes water, and hands on the remaining portion of oxygen to the organic matter, which it thus destroys or changes. Now these changes are destructive to the life of minute organisms, such as the baiteria in sewerage, and the germs of many, perhaps all, zymotic diseases, such as typhus and anthrax. These are the conclusions to be gathered from the recent work of Pro- fessor Marshall Ward, Dr. Arthur Richardson, and Dr. E. Frankland. We must have sunlight. In our rapidly growing cities its admission is a necessity for the com- monweal, its exclusion a crime. But hitherto the condi- tions of city life, in England at least, have tended more and more towards theexclusion of sunlight. The.smoke that goes up, not only from our factories but frem every private house that stretches over London like a veil even on the clearest summer Sunday, this net merely acts directly as a screen against the sun, but condenses around its particles the vapour of the atmosphere.form- ing mists, peasoup fogs, and rain-clouds, all which shut off from us just those violet rays that we need for the destruction of the rapidly incea sing bacteria. Professor Ramsay, speaking in the smoke-vomiting city of the north, urged the same remedies as have been urged by all who have thought on this subject ; first, one strin- gent enforeement of the Smoky Chimneys Act, and of municipal by-laws against smoke ; secondly, the adop- tion of smokeless fuel, such as coke or coal-gas. Pro- fessor Ramsay's valuable and thorougbly interesting address should be studied by all town and county councillors, and we should like to see it reprinted and placed in the hands of all householders, and especially housewives. The gas companies might undertake its distribution along with the quarter's notice.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS H. CRAMPTON, OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS H. CRAMPTON, OF WARRINGTON.

An interesting wedding took place at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-st., on Thursday afternoon last, the contracting partiesjbeing Mr.Thornas R.Dootson,soli- citor,of Leigh,and Miss Helen Crampton,daughter of Mr. W. Crampton of Parker-st.,Warrington. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. B. Dain, ot Chorley, assisted by the Revs. C. Finch and J. Benson. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a costume of silver grey silk trimmed with white chiffon, white hat trim- med with white ostrich tips, and diamond brAoch, the gift of the bridegroom. She also carried a handsome shower boquet. The bridesmaids were Miss Mary Crampton (sister of the bride) Miss Dotson (sister of the bridegroom) who wore pale reseda dresses trim- med with silk and lace, white hats trimmed with white tips, each carrying boquets. Miss Mabel Cramp- ton and Mies Ethel Crampton (nieces of the bride were attired in dresses of cream silk with bats to match) and carried small baskets of flowers. Mr. William Crampton (brother of the bride) attended as best man, Mr. John Dootsou,and Mr. Paul Newton Peters officiated as groomsmen. As the newly married couple left the chapel, Mr. Arthur Finch, played the Wedding March. At the conclusion of the ceremony the bridal party (numbering upwards of sixty), drove to the Masonic Hall, where the reception was held. Subsequently the bride and bridegroom left for London and Brighton, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's going away dress was of dark green cloth, and white felt hat.

Amcngst those present at the" Wedding Breakfast," were the Rev. B. and Mrs. Dain (Chorley), Rev. C. and Mrs, Finch, Rev. A. and Mrs. Benson (Leigh), Rev. W E. Lead, Mr. A. Hunsworth (Leigh), Mr. A. W. Wyatt, (Leigh), Mr.T.Unsworth(Sale),Mr. and Mrs.J.C. Cramp- ton (Stretford), Mrs. Whitelegge (Carrington), Miss Cal- vert (Southport), Mr. P. Hampson (Leigh),Mr. J. Turner (Leigh). Mr. A. Graham (Widnes),Mr. J.Midwocei (Wid- nes), Mr. Arthur Finch, Miss Whitley,Mr. r. N. Peters. Mr. Gerard (Leigh), Mr. and Mrs. Collier, Mr. and Mrs. Dootson, Leigh, Mr. John Dootson, Leigh. Miss M. E. COUNTY COUNCIL SCHOLARSHIPS AND GRANTS. At a meeting of the Technical instruction Com- mittee held at Crewe on Friday, August 28th, the results of the examinations for various classes ef scholarships were declared, and the same awarded. Special day scholarships tenable at Owen's College,: Manchester, or University College. Liverpool, or similar institution, and of the maximum value of .£5O per annum were awarded to Walter Cheshire 9f Crewe, who has held a County Council scholarship at Sandbach Grammar School for three years. Ernest Ludlam of Winniugton, Ncrthwich ; Ewen Kerr .of Crewe; James Atherton of Liscard. The sPecil scholarship in art, to encourage the application art to industry, was awarded to Marion Broadhead of Macclesfield, whose work showed great care and skill. The scholarship in music, tenable at the Royal College of Music, Manchester, was awarded to Ellen Arthan of Tattenhall, near Chester, whose work received special praise from the examiner. The scholarship in cookery, dressmaking, and laun- dry work tenable for eight months at the School of Domestic Economy, Chester, was awarded to EmilY Bott of Crewe. Included amongst the grants for technical inatruction purposes was one of £313 for Runcorn.
